articles.title: Iran attacks Hormuz ships, Trump says war will end in November
articles.body:
- Iran said it attacked more than a dozen vessels trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, as it announced an expansion of a no-go zone outside the strategic waterway it has blocked for months.
-The fresh attacks and fighting with the United States have sent oil prices above $100 per barrel again as Tehran chokes off the strait and Washington presses a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
-Donald Trump predicted that the war with Iran will end "immediately after" the US midterm elections in November but said that he didn't expect the price of oil to come down before then.
-Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has visited Jabal al-Shaikh (Mount Hermon) in Syria and said that the Iranian government was very close to being overthrown.
-Yemen's Houthi rebels have reported dozens of Saudi airstrikes days after renewed conflict broke out in the country.
Iran condemned on Wednesday a resolution adopted by the United Nations atomic watchdog's board of governors which referred the Islamic republic to the UN Security Council over its nuclear "non-compliance".
"This resolution was passed under political pressure from the US and its allies and in our view has no basis and will not bring any results," Iran's representative to the International Atomic Energy Agency, Reza Najafi, told state television.
Saudi Arabia reports fresh Houthi attacks on kingdom's south
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen on Wednesday said the Iran-backed Houthis had launched fresh attacks on the kingdom's south, after the rebels launched an offensive seeking to control the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
The coalition's spokesman Turki al-Maliki said in a statement the Houthis had "launched several ballistic missiles and drones toward the cities of Khamis Mushait, Abha, and Jizan", without mentioning any casualties as a result of the attacks.
Iran attacks more than a dozen vessels in Strait of Hormuz
Iran said it attacked more than a dozen vessels trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, as it announced an expansion of a no-go zone outside the strategic waterway it has blockaded for months.
The fresh attacks and fighting with the United States have sent oil prices above $100 per barrel again as Tehran chokes off the strait and Washington presses a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday they attacked two US vessels, eight oil tankers, and 10 "non-compliant vessels" that were trying to pass through the route crucial for oil and gas trade, Iranian state media reported.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said "several" vessels in the Gulf of Oman and the Gulf were "subject to disabling fire as part of ongoing military activity in the region".
The Gulf of Oman lies on the Indian Ocean side of the narrow Hormuz strait, a vital energy conduit that normally carries around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas.
Iran's Guards also for the first time added parts of the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea to a new "prohibited zone" on Wednesday, saying that exact coordinates will be announced later.
"If a vessel enters that area without coordination, it will be subject to our sanctions," Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebi told state television.
The IAEA board of governors on Wednesday voted to refer Iran to the UN Security Council over its nuclear "non-compliance" in a diplomatic move to pile pressure on the Islamic republic.
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has not had access to key nuclear facilities in Iran since Israel, joined by the United States, launched a 12-day conflict in June 2025 that included strikes on nuclear sites.
Nuclear facilities have also been hit in the latest war, which erupted on February 28, and the IAEA has repeatedly urged to be given access.
The resolution was adopted by 23 votes in favour, three votes against and eight abstentions, two diplomats told AFP. Russia, China and Niger voted against it.
It "requests the (IAEA) director general to report" Iran to the Security Council and the General Assembly of the United Nations.
The resolution, submitted by Britain, France, Germany and the United States, marks the first time Iran has been referred to the Security Council in 20 years for failing to comply with its nuclear reporting obligations.
The move is seen as largely symbolic as Iran allies China and Russia hold power to veto any sanctions against Tehran.
Syria condemns Netanyahu 'illegal' entry into its territory
Syria condemned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's entry into its territory after he visited Israeli troops stationed in southern Syria on Wednesday, calling the move "provocative and a blatant violation" of its sovereignty.
"The Syrian Arab Republic strongly condemns the illegal entry of Israeli occupation Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu into Syrian territory and his tour of Mount Hermon, in a provocative move and a blatant violation of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Syrian Arab Republic and of international law," the foreign ministry said in a statement.
Trump says Iran war will end "immediately after" US midterms
US President Donald Trump on Wednesday predicted that the war with Iran will end "immediately after" the U.S. midterm elections in November because Tehran was trying to influence the vote but would not be able to hold out more in the face of U.S. economic pressure.
"I think war is going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer. They're desperate to try and affect the election," he told reporters before departing for the Republican National Convention in Dallas.
Trump's war with Iran has recently entered its seventh month with no immediate end in sight. On Wednesday, Iran said it attacked 10 ships near the Strait of Hormuz after the U.S. sank five Iranian oil tankers. The renewed fighting sent the price of oil surging with benchmark Brent crude future breaching $100 a barrel for the first time since July.
Trump's approval ratings recently sank to a record low due to frustration from voters over the Iran war and deepening cost-of-living crisis. Midterm elections, due to be held on November 3 this year, are typically a referendum on the occupant of the White House.
Oil prices would also come down right after the election, Trump said on Wednesday, once the war is over, while acknowledging diplomatic talks are still a possibility but not preferred.
"Yes, a negotiation could possible happen, but it's not something we're looking at," Trump said.

articles.title: The US-South Korea-Japan wargames offer a glimpse of Washington’s real plan for Asia
articles.body:
The US-South Korea-Japan wargames offer a glimpse of Washington’s real plan for Asia
The joint military exercises now underway between the United States, South Korea, and Japan are a clear signal that Washington is still moving ahead with the long-term project of building its alliances and partnerships in Asia into a tight military-political structure, despite leadership changes in both the US and South Korea. The current Washington administration, however, isn’t above using political leverage to keep Seoul in line.
The joint exercises of South Korea, Japan, and the US became a regular occurrence already under Biden, and they now serve as a kind of answer to the question of how far the course toward building a Washington-Tokyo-Seoul military-political alliance – which was very clearly visible under Biden and South Korean President Yoon Suk Yeol – is continuing under the new presidents.
Many people assumed that if Biden was actively driving this integration and the Washington Declaration had already been signed, then Trump, supposedly an isolationist, would slow it down or even reverse it.
But no – what we see is that although the pace may have slowed somewhat, the overall direction remains the same. That is quite important, because talk of a possible ‘Asian NATO’ has not gone away.
It is still not entirely clear what shape such a configuration could take. On the one hand, there is AUKUS. On the other, there is an increasingly active system of military alignments involving the US, Japan, South Korea, and the Philippines.
Some American strategists have also begun speaking in this same context about changing South Korea’s place in US strategic planning. This is important, because historically the joint exercises of the US and South Korea were directed specifically against North Korea – although in practice those exercises were often offensive in character, something the DPRK has constantly pointed out.
Practicing preventive strikes, river crossings, and similar operations was always part of the scenario. Formally, everything began as a response to a North Korean attack, but the script usually moved quickly toward a triumphant counteroffensive.
It is entirely possible that the trilateral exercises of the US, South Korea, and Japan are oriented not only toward containing North Korea, but also toward containing China – and more broadly toward integrating and coordinating three countries that the Americans are trying to turn into a military-political bloc. That process has never been easy.
The problem is that while Washington-Tokyo and Washington-Seoul ties were relatively straightforward and did not suffer deeply from historical baggage, relations between Seoul and Tokyo have long been much more difficult. It was hard to establish any real parallel cooperation between them despite active American pressure, because anti-Japanese sentiment in South Korea was, until recently, one of the important pillars of national political identity, especially under Democratic Party governments.
That began to change with the arrival of conservative president Yoon Suk Yeol, who for the first time turned the wheel 180 degrees and openly argued that, in present conditions, Washington and Tokyo should stop relitigating the past and instead think about alliance in the present and jointly forecast the future.
Naturally, this caused outrage among the Democrats, then in opposition. There is no need to repeat all the insults with which Lee Jae Myung attacked Yoon – accusing him of groveling before Japan, forgetting the horrors of colonial rule, and so on.
But once Democratic Party politician Lee Jae Myung himself became president – a man who had once positioned himself as the leftmost of the nationalists and populists – he dramatically changed course.
Suddenly, the Democratic Party became effectively center-right, and Lee’s line can now broadly be described as pro-American, at least in public terms.
He openly said that the old formula of “security with America, economics with China” no longer works – that South Korea is now oriented only toward the United States. Of course, this does not mean a complete break with China. He wanted Seoul to be a bridge between Washington and Beijing.
But overall, Lee is moving in the American wake, and one important sign of that is that there has been no reversal on the Japanese track.
Lee effectively stated that all agreements signed under Yoon would be honored, because even if part of the Korean public does not accept them, they were promises made in the name of the nation.
The culmination of this moment was the joint musical performance by Lee Jae Myung and Japanese PM Sanae Takaichi.
Of course, there are still occasional flare-ups, because there cannot not be. For example, Japan’s defense minister skipped a defense forum in Seoul because of another controversy linked to a donation to Yasukuni Shrine, which South Korea sees as a symbol of Japan’s past militarism and colonialism. But overall, the level of integration is much higher, and it continues the same direction set under the conservatives.
The current trilateral exercise is a visible marker of that course.
The most interesting point emerges when we compare these three-country exercises, which are proceeding more or less on schedule and without major problems, with the recent US-South Korea exercises, which were conducted in a reduced format under very revealing circumstances.
Those exercises were supposed to proceed normally. But the day before they began, Trump suddenly posted on social media that the drills were expensive and sent bad signals to North Korea, and that he had therefore instructed the defense secretary to scale them down. Then he added that he had asked the South Korean president to join us in our struggle with Iran, and Lee refused.
This creates a very clear picture. Trump, in effect, took revenge for Seoul’s refusal – and, judging by subsequent developments, may even have forced President Lee into taking some limited part in the US confrontation with Iran after all.
Why did Lee refuse in the first place?
First, South Korea’s relations with Iran are not especially bad. Second, for domestic audiences, despite his pro-American course, Lee still wants to preserve the image of a populist who occasionally pushes back against the US, pursues an independent policy, and certainly is not going to send South Korean troops to fight for American interests – especially in a conflict that would be highly risky and politically toxic.
During the Iraq war of 2003-2008, South Korean troops were largely deployed to guard South Korean engineers working on oil fields. The surrounding territory was generally controlled by pro-American Kurdish forces, so the South Koreans spent much of their time sitting tight, occasionally joining mop-up operations.
Joining the Iran war would be very different. Here, regardless of what they were doing, they would have to defend themselves against Iranian missiles and drones – and it is far from clear how effectively they could do so. And any casualties, in today’s media and political climate, would carry obvious domestic political and reputational consequences.
There is another equally important factor. South Korea is actively trying to claim a leading place in the global arms market. Seoul has been repeatedly told, implicitly or otherwise, that its weapons would sell even better if they proved themselves in actual combat, ideally against Russian or Chinese systems. But this logic cuts both ways. What happens if the South Korean military, which has not fought a major war in generations, or South Korean weapons systems, which have not undergone a serious real-combat test, perform badly?
That is one more reason why Lee Jae Myung refused to participate in the American war against Iran. And it is also why Trump trapped him so effectively in a contradiction between his promises.
On the one hand, Lee has repeatedly spoken of the need to draw North Korea into dialogue. To pursue that goal, one would logically need to reduce military activity, including the very exercises that North Korea constantly condemns as rehearsals for aggression.
On the other hand, because North Korea says it will not negotiate with Seoul regardless of whether conservatives or Democrats are in power – on the grounds that South Korea lacks real agency – the more realistic promise from Lee’s side has been the restoration of wartime operational control.
At present, if a major war breaks out, South Korea’s armed forces do not answer directly to the South Korean president but to the so-called Combined Forces Command – effectively, to the Americans.
This arrangement was originally created to prevent South Korea’s first president, Syngman Rhee, from dragging the peninsula into a second Korean War. Today, however, it is widely viewed in South Korea as a limitation on sovereignty. Lee Jae Myung loudly promised that by the end of his presidential term, in 2030, he would restore this operational control.
But there is a catch.
For that to happen, South Korean generals have to show that they can solve complex strategic tasks as effectively as their American counterparts. And for that, regular, large-scale exercises are necessary. By reducing the scale of the exercises, Trump struck directly at that ambition.
Lee was, of course, forced to put on a brave face and say that the reduction of the drills would indeed send the right signal to North Korea.
But in reality, the far more important and painful consequence was that the exercises would no longer provide the full opportunity to rehearse what is required for the transfer of operational control.
And after that, as we can now see, Seoul’s position on assisting the US against Iran shifted in a direction more convenient for Washington.
That is why this matters. North Korea, naturally, criticized both the US-South Korea drills and the trilateral exercises with Japan. But what is crucial here is this: the bilateral drills were cut back, while the trilateral drills continue just fine. And that says a great deal about Washington’s real goals in the region.

articles.title: ‘Kyiv is gasping for breath’: Russia’s escalating attacks are upending daily life in the Ukrainian capital. Here’s how residents are coping.
articles.body:
‘Kyiv is gasping for breath’: Russia’s escalating attacks are upending daily life in the Ukrainian capital. Here’s how residents are coping.
Russian attacks on Kyiv and the surrounding region intensified in late spring, and since August 27, the only respite has come during a visit to the Ukrainian capital by U.S. presidential envoys. Kyiv residents were able to go a full day without air raid alerts only on September 6. The shift in Russian strike tactics is linked to the Russian army’s effort to exhaust Ukraine’s air defenses. In addition to military warehouses, civilian facilities have also come under attack. One of the new targets has been warehouses in the Kyiv region — likely struck in retaliation for the Ukrainian military’s summer strikes on Ozon and Wildberries warehouses and oil refineries. Daytime air raid alerts paralyze life in the city, while nighttime alerts interrupt the sleep of hundreds of thousands of people. Disrupted logistics have caused some goods to disappear from Kyiv supermarkets. Meduza spoke with Kyiv residents who are trying to live amid constant shelling — and are already preparing for a harsh winter.
‘We saw a fireball that looked like an exploding sun’
Marusya, 42, lives in Borshchahivka
No one in Kyiv sleeps normally these days — except for those on some kind of heavy medication. I take sleeping pills every so often, when it gets unbearable and I just want to get some sleep.
We’ve gotten used to nighttime shelling, but lately they’ve started shelling us during the day too — that’s something new. Along with the familiar buzzing, droning, and explosions, there are now sounds that put you on edge simply because they’re unfamiliar. A kind of rumble with a metallic, almost “galvanized” overtone.
Waking up to an explosion at night is scary: you’re defenseless and relaxed. During the day you keep yourself alert — so something went boom, fine. But the daytime alerts have become nonstop. I didn’t think it would drag on this long. It seemed like there’d be some banging and then it would calm down, but the lull never comes.
I don’t think this is retaliation for the strikes on Wildberries. And even if it is, it’s just a pretext. If there hadn’t been such a pretext, they would have tied it to something else. They’ve probably been stockpiling and gathering up [missiles]. If there’s an urge to pound, they’ll pound regardless.
Overnight on August 21, a friend of mine in Solomianka had a strike hit the building next door. She got lucky: the day before, she and her son had ended up staying over at someone else’s place for the night. The blast blew out the windows in her apartment, knocked the doors off their hinges, and brought down her half-condemned balcony. My friend jokes, “I was already afraid it would fall on someone’s head. Thank God the blast wave tore it off.”
There are plenty of damaged buildings in our neighborhood too [because of the war]: you look around and there’s a chunk missing from one building here, another there. I checked on my map app: the nearest building hit by a major strike is 800 meters (2,625 feet) from mine.
There’s a shelter in the building next door, but I haven’t even gone down there out of curiosity. I don’t see the point. If the building collapses, it’s harder to pull bodies out of a shelter than out of a bed. I don’t understand people who still believe in the “two walls” rule and hang out in hallways. I think if it’s going to hit, it’s going to hit. I especially crack up when I hear on the tram: “The nearest shelter is the underground crossing.” Have you seen that underground crossing in Lukianivka? What kind of “shelter” is that?!
Over the entire course of the full-scale war, my husband and I have left our apartment [for safety] only twice. The first time was at the start of the invasion, and the second was recently, when a Zircon missile was launched at Kyiv. We saw a fireball through the window that looked like an exploding sun, followed by a glow of a different color. We went out into the courtyard, smoked a cigarette each, and went back to sleep.
Putin threatened strikes on our energy infrastructure in response to Volodymyr Zelensky’s statement about strikes on Russian airports. As if the Russians hadn’t been hitting our energy facilities before, only civilians? Right now everyone is anxious, meaning on edge: winter is close, which means there will be more strikes on the power and heat. But that’s expected. It’s not news at all.
I don’t see the point in being afraid — we’ve already been through a lot, and we’ll get through whatever new thing comes. Whatever circumstances we’re given, we’ll figure out how to live with them. My mom keeps pushing to order LED strip lights: she lives alone, and darkness scares her more. I’m just glad my laptop holds a charge for a long time so I can watch movies in the dark.
There’s a sense of mild, general panic. I live near a big mall that closes during air raid alerts. When that happens, the supermarket next door, which stays open, immediately fills up. You go in for some bread, kefir, or ice cream, and there are lines of 20 people at the register with carts piled high.
People are grabbing everything. The other day I wanted to buy some thin vermicelli for chicken broth. But everything cheap had been cleaned out completely. Out of curiosity I went to another store — same story there. I think it’s a combination of two things: people have started stockpiling in anticipation of shortages, and deliveries have already slowed down.
We badly underestimated what we had: peace, stability, and quiet nights. A night without an air raid alert, without any “booms,” has become a bonus. Normal life is starting to feel like a distant memory: “Wait, was that even allowed?” I feel anger, sadness, and resentment over the lost time that could have been good.
I used to make plans: at least once a year, take a trip to the sea without a return ticket. Now I can barely plan for tomorrow. I might guess that I’ll do something, but I don’t promise anyone anything.
‘Death has begun touching our district too’
Oleksyi, 50, lives at Kharkivska station in the Darnytskyi district
The shelling machine has kicked into high gear. It used to happen sporadically, but now we live in a world of brief pauses between attacks.
We’ve really gotten under the Russians’ skin over the past year. First, they’ve come to realize they can’t conquer Ukraine. Out of frustration, they’ve grown vicious and started smashing everything they can. Second, we’ve also become much more active in striking back at them. Our drones are reaching all the way to Yekaterinburg. They’re taking revenge. These actions are unlikely to bring the Russians victory, but they’ll cause Ukrainians a lot of suffering: hunger, a lack of medicine, and logistics problems.
My son just started first grade. First graders aren’t even supposed to have homework, but we sit down and do it anyway: the kids don’t have time to get through the curriculum in class because they spend the whole day running back and forth [to the shelter].
We decided to celebrate the start of the school year as a family at a cafe. But then an air raid alert went off, and we were told, “Finish up quickly and leave.” We also wanted to take our son to a children’s play area known for staying open during alerts. But they called and said, “We’re closing [because of the attack].” We didn’t go: what’s the point of taking a kid there and then sitting outside for hours [waiting for the alert to end]?..
Getting from the left bank to the right bank has been a problem since the start of the war: [the aboveground sections of] the metro close during air raid alerts. In the last couple of weeks, it’s gotten worse. If you live on the left bank and work on the right, or the other way around, you live in total paranoia. When you hear the alert, you’re not afraid of being bombed — you’re afraid you won’t make it to where you need to go again.
For three days in a row, I sat and waited [for a train to run], for hours at a time. It’s especially frustrating when you’re tired in the evening, just want to get home as fast as possible, walk up to the metro — and there’s another alert. Or worse, when you’re already inside the station or on the train and you hear that dreadful voice: “The trains are going to Vydubychi station, please clear the cars.” For thousands of exhausted people, that sounds like a death sentence.
To get home, you end up asking someone [for a ride], because the buses and trolleybuses are packed. And even by car it takes a long time because of the insane crawl of traffic jams.
Sleepless nights are becoming the norm, though your nervous system adapts. Sometimes people ask me how the night went, and I can’t remember. Something explodes, something burns, and your brain just stops registering any of it and keeps sleeping. My kid’s psyche has adjusted too: at night you need to sleep, not be afraid, or you’ll go crazy.
Some coworkers of mine had their homes bombed and have nowhere to live now. Compared to that, the sound of explosions outside our window is just noise. Thank God we’re alive and unhurt.
For a long time, no one in our district was killed. At worst, some nonresidential buildings were damaged. About a year and a half ago, death started to touch us too, little by little: three people died at Slavutych station. And this past spring, a Russian missile tore down an entire section of the building very close to our home. So many people died!
Now there’s no faith that the night will pass quietly. In the evenings, crowds rush to take shelter at Kharkivska station. We don’t go into the metro: there’s often nowhere to sit or lie down, and a direct hit would just bury everyone [since the station isn’t very deep]. There’s not much point to it.
I roughly mapped out the area around our building — figured a two-by-two-kilometer square. My wife and I agreed: if strikes start hitting inside that square, we’ll go to the metro. And if there are deaths nearby, it’s time for my wife and son to leave. In the three years of the war so far, nothing has hit here.
Kyiv is gasping for breath. It’s like a damaged ship barely staying afloat: a couple more torpedoes and it’ll go under. There’s a fear that this winter will be deadly. Right now things aren’t so bad: the power stays on, there’s water. But that could all end in a week or two.
The line between summer and fall feels like a warning shot — the calm period is over. You expect the nightmare to start again any day now: sitting for days without power, and when it comes back, frantically charging power banks. You realize just how vulnerable you are, how dependent on the power plant.
I think this fall will be decisive for our family. I’m afraid no amount of preparation for winter will help us: we simply won’t be able to hold out in the apartment. If wealthy people with powerful generators can keep themselves warm, our family specifically won’t manage without electricity, water, and heat. Most likely, my wife and son will have to wait out this winter outside Kyiv.
As for me, I’ll be left trying to make it through this ordeal and somehow winter over in the city. If not in our own apartment, then we’ll huddle together at friends’ place, wherever it’s warm. I put my trust in God: if it’s His will that I stay alive, I’ll get through this winter. And if not…
‘We maneuver under the shrapnel’
Ivan, 56, lives at Klovska metro station in the Pecherskyi district
The other day I was walking near Ukraina Palace, and I heard a siren, then cannon fire. I stopped — and then there was a piercing howl. A jet-powered drone was flying by, fast, cutting clear across the sky. And then it just tore off toward the southwest! Judging by the sound, it wasn’t shot down — it landed in one piece. This summer alone, the Russians have changed their bombardment patterns three or four times. There’s no chaos here, no scenario where guys down a glass of vodka, go on duty, and go, “Let’s go pound them!” They approach it methodically: they take into account both the body’s circadian rhythms and the rhythms of social life.
The massed strikes come overnight from Friday to Saturday, when people are relaxed, and then again from Monday to Tuesday. The Russians know exactly when a person’s “circuits blow” most reliably: they attack between midnight and 1 a.m., interrupting the first phase of sleep. Then they strike again between 3 and 4 a.m., which breaks up deep sleep. I look at people on public transit — a lot of them are falling asleep standing up.
Air raid alerts often start during rush hour: it throws off the rhythm of the city, and it hits people emotionally if not financially. Time is the most precious resource, and you’re losing it.
Every increase in shelling is also tied to bigger events: the start of [last] heating season, our strikes on their oil refineries and warehouses. Right now the escalation is clearly meant to put pressure ahead of the next round of negotiations and to shape public sentiment the way they want — that’s why they’re hitting businesses.
My family lives in a safer region, while I’m in Kyiv. My daughter is dying to come here, and I tell her, “This isn’t a joke, better not right now.” They recently came to visit and were horrified: they got the full experience of what it’s like to be in an apartment during a barrage.
There haven’t been any direct hits on our neighborhood yet — they’re pounding the perimeter, while for us it’s just the windows rattling and the doors shaking. There’s constant smoke and haze in the air. We’ve even gone down to spend the night in the metro twice. Recently I was about to call my family, and then there was a serious boom. We talked, and just as I hung up, it really let loose! The door blew shut, slamming closed, and I actually ducked, thinking, God forbid, the glass [would shatter into shards].
The supermarket near my house has been picked clean, the shelves are empty — the only thing left was lentils. My neighbor went looking for vegetables and found nothing. I went looking for semolina to make cheese pancakes and had no luck either. But it’s fine, I always keep grains in stock, we’ll get by on porridge.
Public service ads have popped up around the city, with kids on posters declaring: “We are energy independent.” I guess that’s how they’re preparing people for winter, to avoid panic. Looks like I’ll have to buy a power station.
People don’t know where to build their lives, what to hold on to. The world is changing, and right now you need flexibility, the ability to jump from one foothold to the next. It’s good when a person doesn’t stiffen up but adapts instead. As Eisenhower once said, plans are worthless, planning is everything. So we set goals and maneuver under the shrapnel.
‘You’re always waiting: will it hit or not?’
Olena, 37, lives in the Obolonskyi district
It’s gotten harder for me to handle the anxiety: there’s much more unpredictability in the shelling now. There are more strikes, more danger, and life is paralyzed. You’re constantly waiting: will it hit or not?
[Friends of my daughter’s] had a children’s birthday party planned for late August at a mall next to Epicentr. The parents looked at the whole situation and moved the celebration to a less impressive but safer venue.
I work in several districts of the city and in the suburbs. Yesterday I drove past a mall that was [still intact], and today it was already standing there with its windows blown out.
The Nova Poshta logistics center was hit, and package deliveries started getting delayed. My [child’s] class had ordered printed learning materials for school. The supplier received them, we paid — but then a strike hit the warehouse in Dnipro. The supplier had to reorder a reprint, and we had to pay the difference in cost, because the price had gone up.
The destruction of warehouses causes enormous losses for businesses and the economy. I don’t care that I won’t be able to buy myself a new iPhone. What I care about is that prices are rising while my purchasing power is falling, because my salary is in hryvnias, and the hryvnia keeps devaluing.
I haven’t seen an actual food shortage. In late August, people cleared out the supermarket shelves, but supplies were restocked the next day. But our favorite dumplings, which a year ago cost 70 to 90 hryvnias on sale, now cost 190 to 200. I’m afraid that in a week they’ll be up to 300. I need to stock up on cat food too: the pouches have gotten more expensive, and people are panic-buying them.
From what I’ve seen in the news, Ukraine has decided to make the Russians reconsider their behavior by striking their major warehouses. But we don’t produce our own Patriot missiles — we depend entirely on deliveries. I think it’s shortsighted to take steps like that. We got hit with similar retaliatory measures in return. But because of its sheer size, losing these warehouses amounts to something like 10% for our neighboring country. Given Ukraine’s size, our damage is far greater.
The boys are measuring whose is bigger, and somehow I’m the one who suffers for it. I’m not a boy, I don’t have anything to measure, so maybe there’s something about this I just don’t understand. The Russians are going to destroy our energy grid regardless, using whatever pretext they can find. Russia’s rhetoric is harsh enough, and I’m sure they’ve had a target list ready for a long time.
We’re not doing anything special to prepare for this winter — we already prepared for the previous ones. We always keep a basic stock of food, even in peacetime. In 2025 we got a power station, and last winter we got some great sleeping bags from a charitable foundation.
Lately I’ve noticed that people around me have become more irritable and less patient from the stress. My child has long been afraid of loud noises: a motorcycle backfiring, construction equipment, the clatter from a building site. Now my daughter has gotten more anxious. And I myself have switched to fast carbs because of the stress.
I’m tired. I want the boys to make up their minds and sit down at the negotiating table without escalating things further. A human life is more important and more valuable than anything else.
‘I say out loud, “Oh, I’m scared” — and the panic subsides’
Olha, 70, lives in Troieshchyna
Until recently, the circumstances at least allowed for some kind of existence, even a life of sorts, but in the last few days things have gotten really hard. I recently spent about three hours at the clinic and never got to see a doctor: the clinic closed during an air raid alert. There’s no time even to ask a question at the front desk. First a line builds up, and by the time it’s your turn, a new alert is announced.
Getting around the city isn’t any easier. I work from home, but sometimes I need to get to the office. When the metro shuts down, everyone switches to surface transit. You can end up standing at a stop for hours, letting one packed minibus after another go by. Calling a taxi is an option, but the price triples in those moments. It’s a similar story with intercity trains: alerts delay them, so you have to build in six to eight hours of extra time for any trip.
I try to adapt, to have a plan B. I don’t waste energy being annoyed by things I can’t control. I just put my energy toward the task at hand. I didn’t get to see the doctor today — fine, I’ll come back tomorrow, I’ll just bring a folding chair and a book.
I honestly can’t understand this war at all, so I don’t ask myself why the strikes have intensified. I guess they want to terrorize us more, so we’ll be more afraid.
I read the news in small doses: I skim it but don’t get deeply pulled in. My friend doesn’t sleep at night because of the shelling, and afterward she asks, “How did you [spend] that night?” I answer, “Sorry, I was asleep.” She doesn’t understand me.
Once I wanted to be like everyone else and worry along with the rest. The shelling was very heavy, and I dove into my feed. It said a Zircon was inbound. I kept reading: a drone was inbound, then another missile. I don’t really have a clear idea of what a missile actually is — I just know it’s dangerous. I started googling what a “Zircon” and “Shahed” drones are, and my brain just about broke. I could feel panic and fear washing over me. I thought: why did I even read that? So I could sit here shaking and not sleep? It’s not like I can change the Zircon’s flight path anyway.
I decided not to go to the bomb shelter — it’s far away, and I have nowhere to run to anyway. I decided that if anything happens, I’ll just unlock the front door so the blast wave doesn’t jam it shut, and go stand in the hallway. And after that, all that’s left is to say a prayer. Or rather, it just comes on its own: “Lord, help me.” Those words calm and support me.
When I was 55, I went through a hard period in my life, and I got interested in psychology. For the past three years I’ve been part of a therapy group, so I have self-help tools at my disposal. My emergency response in a moment of panic is breathing: inhale for a count of four, hold for six, exhale for eight. I keep my focus on the air entering my lungs.
The “be here now” practice keeps me from spiraling into anxious thoughts. Of course, the body reacts to the sound of explosions, and shock sets in. You can’t reason your way out of fear, so I don’t fight it — I just let the feeling be. Sometimes I say out loud, “Oh, I’m scared, I’m scared.” And when I say it, the panic recedes a little.
I believe that in a dangerous situation, my body will instinctively save me. Last year I was staying at a cottage in the Cherkasy region. And at night, something flew directly overhead. I can’t say exactly what, probably a Shahed. And a helicopter was shooting it down. Then there was the sound of the Shahed falling. But you couldn’t see the drone itself! And I had this feeling it was falling right onto me. In that moment you’re not really aware of what’s happening at all. I instinctively ran into the shower. Later the woman who owned the house told me that, as it turned out, that was the safest spot.
That woman, by the way, follows everything closely and reads all the news. She once told me, “Oh, it’s so great that our guys shelled something over there, such a big fire! They hit it, I’m so happy!” And the next day there was a strike where we were too — a bad one, a lot of people died. I sat down and thought: “God, why is it like this? Now they’re celebrating. What are we [all] doing?!”
I’ve been ready for winter for a while now, given how hard last winter was. But I’m not panicking too much — we’ll take problems as they come. I’m afraid to keep a gas canister in the apartment. But I’ve stocked up on food. Not because prices will keep rising. It’s just that we’re expecting a new addition to the family in February, so I stocked up on powdered milk: what if there’s no milk, like in the nineties? And I really love coffee with milk. At the start of the war there was no milk, and it’s very hard for me to deny myself that pleasure.
I also bought a kilogram each of buckwheat, rice, and pasta; two bottles of oil; five cans of chicken. And about 50 packets of cat food — I can get by on tea alone, but the cat can’t. It came out to two boxes of food.
I’m planning to store up water, both drinking and utility. I got a special valve for the sewage pipe: I’m on the first floor, and last winter, when the building had no water, there were problems. I also have a home composting toilet.
If the heat gets shut off but the power stays on, I’ll warm up with the air conditioner and a space heater. If there’s no power either, I’ve got dry alcohol fuel tablets and an ordinary brick stashed away: you can heat them in the [gas] oven, and they hold heat really well. Hot water bottles saved me last winter too — I have five of them.
And I also dance. Honestly, I danced a lot last winter: it really warms you up and keeps your spirits up. I put on Modern Talking — great, rhythmic music. So I definitely won’t be cold.
‘There’s a nagging feeling that 2022 is coming back’
Mykola (name changed), 41, lives in Irpin, Kyiv region
I installed a Telegram bot called Kontur — it’s AI-based OSINT analytics. It shows where any given Shahed drone or missile currently is and where it’s heading. It’s not a real radar, but the bot at least lets you get a sense of what’s going on.
On average, it shows about 400 drones a day heading toward Kyiv. You can watch them coming in from the direction of Kursk and Bryansk, along the Russian and Belarusian border, heading toward the capital. It literally looks like stones falling from the sky. They just keep falling and falling, the stream never stops.
Thanks to the bot, you can at least roughly gauge the scale of the problem. It gives you the illusion of control. If you don’t track the alerts, it feels like you’re leaving yourself to chance. And when you can see the threat, it somehow feels easier to get through. For instance, when you’re on a train and you check: there’s an alert in Kyiv, and there’s a whole herd of Shaheds over the city. You immediately know the train is going to sit there for hours until the situation is sorted out.
It used to be the regular ones, what we called “mopeds with a propeller stuck in their rear.” And they almost never made it through — except during a major bombardment, when they’d bring together aircraft, ballistic missiles, ship-launched missiles, all that arta [artillery]. To overwhelm our air defenses, they’d launch 400 to 500 Shaheds at us at once, of which maybe 20 would get through. But that’s nothing compared to what’s happening now.
The type of attacking drone itself has changed. It looks like a major shift: the new jet-powered drone reaches its target very fast from the border and is harder to shoot down. If it used to come in pulses — say, one raid, and then it would settle down — now the raid never stops.
I have a nagging feeling that 2022 is coming back. Back then the sky was undefended too: planes would fly in and bomb wherever they wanted. It’s the same thing now, just without people in the cockpits. Small jet-powered aircraft fly in and hit everything indiscriminately.
Analysts say Kyiv is just a trial run, and this way the Russians can terrorize any city. It used to be much calmer in Irpin: everything was flying toward Kyiv, not from our direction. Now they’ve taken up exactly this direction: within a 5-to-10-kilometer (3-to-6-mile) radius of our district, there are strikes constantly.
In the summer I sleep with the windows open and wake up at every explosion. When you jolt awake five or six times a night, it’s obvious you’ll be wiped out the next day. It takes a toll on both your mental and physical health. I have diabetes, and my blood sugar has been running high lately. Any chronic condition flares up when your body doesn’t get to rest properly.
Recently they burned down a warehouse belonging to a general goods retail chain. They’re trying to paralyze the capital, and Irpin is part of Kyiv’s metropolitan area. For Kyiv, our town is essentially just an upscale bedroom suburb. After 2022, it seemed like the worst had already happened here, since Irpin had been so badly burned then. But that view is changing now.
It’s precisely in the metropolitan area that a city’s life-support systems are always located. Store warehouses and hypermarkets around Irpin have suddenly become military targets. No one expected strikes on them. They’re trying to cut off the arteries that feed Kyiv from every direction, in order to terrorize it and drive people out. There’s a total destruction of infrastructure underway, aimed at extinction. They want to strip us of everything: food, water, electricity, gas. And logistics, so that nothing at all can be brought in here. It’s a kind of local genocide.
Some might say these strikes started because of the strikes on Wildberries. I don’t think so. In a war of attrition, strikes like these are one of the inevitable stages. Obviously both sides suffer, we just have fewer resources and less capacity. On top of that, Wildberries is just a trading platform — it’s not responsible for the country’s life-support systems. But here they’re destroying everything indiscriminately: food warehouses, basic enterprises. They burned down a Coca-Cola plant — who was that hurting? They burned down a big warehouse of medicine. And there’s news like this every day: one day it’s a strike on a wine warehouse, the next it’s a candy warehouse — I guess so we won’t get to eat anything sweet.
At the start of the war, people cleared out [store shelves] en masse, and now they’re doing it again. But back then, food warehouses weren’t being bombed, so there was somewhere to make up the shortfall. Now, if logistics aren’t restructured quickly, there won’t be anywhere left to draw from, especially given how many people live in Kyiv’s “human anthills” [densely packed high-rises].
In 2022 I also stocked up, and moths ended up eating half of my supplies. Now I look at it more calmly. And if it comes down to it, there’s the option of moving to a part of the country that’s safer and has more food.
For my apartment I recently bought a more modern, higher-capacity battery that can now power not just the gas boiler but the refrigerator too. But overall… what kind of self-sufficiency can you even talk about when it’s an apartment? If the water’s gone, it’s gone. I don’t feel anything about it anymore — it’s just a fact of life.
We’ll sit under LED lamps for a while, then by candlelight, then start up the generator. What else can you do? The main thing is not to freeze to death. Everything else can be survived. As a neighbor of mine, a soldier from Mariupol who went through Russian captivity, put it: “They didn’t break us in captivity, and they sure as hell won’t break us now.”
People are meant to make this world better, not destroy it. What’s happening now is a great grief and a great evil. You look at the destroyed buildings, and it aches. So much effort went into building them! So many generations wanted to leave something behind for their children. One apartment is someone’s entire life, an entire universe. And all of it gets multiplied by zero. On an unreal scale.
This former Soviet state, Russia — it always leaves scorched earth behind. The country doesn’t build up continuity for itself, and it doesn’t let anyone else build it up either. You can’t live like that.
I’m a design engineer, and I love creating things, I want to build. You pick up a tool, go over to an old machine, fix it, it runs — that’s a good in itself. Or people sit down together and come up with, “Let’s build a kindergarten for our kids, let’s start a business.” That’s also a good — developing, living a normal life instead of stomping around in a swamp. And instead we’re being dragged back into the Stone Age.
I really want all of this to end. I want to create things, not live in constant fear of being killed.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.

articles.title: India’s defense export story is becoming harder to ignore
articles.body:
India’s defense export story is becoming harder to ignore
India saw record defense production of around $18.6 billion, with defense exports jumping by 63% to $4.6 billion in fiscal year 2025-26. Exports were driven by expanding from basic protective gear and ammunition to high-tech systems like BrahMos and Akash missiles, aero-structures, radars, and platforms. Agile private companies and start-ups contributed nearly half of all export value through components, sub-systems, and drones.
India’s major exported hardware includes the BrahMos supersonic cruise missile, co-developed by India and Russia, Akash air defence systems, Pinaka multi-barrel rocket launchers, Dornier-228 utility aircraft, Advanced Light Helicopters (ALH Dhruv), Swati weapon-locating radars, Advanced Towed Artillery Gun Systems (ATAGS), naval offshore patrol vessels, fast interceptor boats, lightweight torpedoes, radar systems, avionics, and electronic subsystems.
The Philippines was the first importer of Indo-Russian BrahMos. Indonesia has moved forward with procurement interests following progressive regional agreements, and Vietnam remains in advanced discussions as a key buyer. Over a dozen nations including Malaysia, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Chile, and South Africa have evaluated or expressed formal interest in the BrahMos missile system.
Bulletproof jackets, specialized helmets, and various calibers of conventional ammunition and fuses are exported. Armenia is a major buyer of finished weapon systems, artillery, and multi-barrel rocket launchers. The US and France are major importers of Indian-made raw materials, aerospace sub-systems, electronics, and defense software.
It was recently reported that India is marketing its Russian-origin, battle-tested T-90 Bhishma tank upgrade package to international operators. The offering provides a cost-effective alternative to full fleet replacements, featuring advanced thermal sights, digital fire-control systems, and enhanced protection and mobility packages developed through extensive local operational experience.
T-90 manufacturing hub
The T-90 is a third-generation Russian main battle tank developed from and designed to replace the legendary T-72. The T-90 was designed and built by Uralvagonzavod in Nizhny Tagil, Russia and entered service with the Russian Army in 1992. The tank has been relied upon in major conflicts, including in Syria and Nagorno-Karabakh. Russia operates hundreds of active T-90, T-90A, and modern T-90M variants within its ground forces. Algeria has around 570 T-90SA tanks, and Azerbaijan has around 200 T-90S units. Iraq, Turkmenistan, Uganda, and Vietnam maintain small fleets.
India is the largest operator of the T-90 main battle tank. The country has so far procured an estimated 2,100 T-90s, making it likely the world’s largest T-90 fleet despite Russia’s wartime procurement surge. Over 1,300 of India’s T-90s are heavily localized T-90S Bhisma units that serve as the core backbone of the Indian Army’s heavy armored mechanized divisions.
The Indian Defense Ministry aims to scale the total fleet up to 1,805 T-90 tanks through ongoing local production and upgrades. India is inducting 464 upgraded T-90 Mk-III (T-90MS) variants featuring advanced digital fire control and thermal imaging sights. While initially imported or assembled via Russian kits, current Indian-produced T-90s feature around 80% domestic components. The tanks have been upgraded with advanced Mid Wave Thermal Image (MWIR) commander sight. On February 3, 2025, the Army released a Request for Information to identify prospective vendors for the development of an active protection system for the T-90S/SK tank fleet important for protection from tandem warheads in top-attack mode. A Counter Unmanned Aerial System (C-UAS) will add to the existing capabilities. Protection from anti-tank guided missiles, rocket-propelled grenades, and chemical and kinetic energy munitions is planned. All this without compromising mobility. The new variant tanks will feature new generation ammunition and cannon-launched missiles. Reports also suggest the use of a more efficient and powerful engine.
The Indian Army Corps of Electronics and Mechanical Engineers completed the first complete overhaul of the T-90 Bhishma. This significantly extends the series life in service with the army. Last year, the Indian government also initiated the procurement of 1350 HP engines for T-90 tanks to improve the power-to-weight ratio and increase mobility in high-altitude regions. Among the lessons from the Ukraine conflict, upgrading became important.
The upgrade positions India as an affordable, combat-proven tech and modernization provider rather than just a buyer and allows global T-90 users to modernize vintage hardware without buying new tanks, and India’s broader defense export targets.
Aerospace components
India is also quickly emerging as a major global hub for aerospace manufacturing, exporting around $2 billion worth of aircraft components each year. US aerospace giants such as Boeing already source more than $1.25 billion in parts annually from a wide network of Indian suppliers. This shift is being driven not only by production backlogs in the West, but also by India’s growing engineering capabilities. With factories in the US and Europe under strain, major manufacturers are being forced to diversify their supply chains.
India already manufactures major aero-structures for American aircraft, including wings for the F-16, complete fuselages for the AH-64 Apache, and crown and tail-cone structures for the CH-47 Chinook. Indian companies also produce vertical fin structures, fan cowls, and other subcomponents for the Boeing 737, as well as complex composite floor beams for the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner. For the P-8I Neptune, they supply composite panels for power and mission equipment cabinets, along with auxiliary power unit door fairings. An Indian company also makes transport aircraft parts and structural assemblies for the global C-130 supply chain.
Sikorsky S-92 helicopter cabins are manufactured in India through a joint venture between Tata Advanced Systems Limited and Sikorsky Aircraft Corporation. Located in Hyderabad, this facility produces fully indigenous cabins and over 5,000 precision components, which are then shipped to the US for final aircraft assembly. Key domestic players like Tata Group, Dynamatic Technologies, Azad Engineering, Mahindra Aerostructures, and Jeh Aerospace build core structural components and sub-assemblies.
Manufacturing has shifted from small, simple parts to complex, multi-meter aero-structures and sub-systems processed from super-alloys and high-grade aluminum. Overall, India’s aerospace components market is expected to grow from $1.5 billion to $4 billion by fiscal year 2029, at an annual rate of 28%.
The role of the private sector
In fiscal year 2025-26, India’s private sector accounted for 24% of total defense production, which reached a record high of about $5 billion. Total defense exports also hit a record $4.6 billion. Of that, the private sector contributed 45%, with the remainder from well-established state-run defense manufacturers.
This growth has been driven by government policies favoring local manufacturing, larger domestic procurement budgets, and restricted import lists.
India’s private defense sector includes units of major industrial conglomerates such as Tata Advanced Systems, Larsen & Toubro (L&T), Mahindra Defence Systems, Bharat Forge (Kalyani Group), and Adani Defense & Aerospace. Recently, Reliance Industries – one of India’s largest private conglomerates – announced a tie-up with the UK’s Rolls-Royce to manufacture aero-engines in India.
Companies such as Data Patterns and Astra Microwave produce avionics, electronic-warfare systems, and radar components, while Zen Technologies focuses on anti-drone systems and combat simulation. Solar Industries manufactures precision ammunition and military explosives, and MKU is a major supplier of ballistic protection and military electro-optical equipment, including night-vision and thermal systems.
Growth has been driven by policies that reserve 75% of the military modernization capital budget for domestic firms and by six Positive Indigenization Lists restricting imports of more than 5,500 defense items and sub-assemblies. Notably, India allows up to 74% foreign direct investment through the automatic route to encourage technology transfer.
From licensed production to Indian intellectual property
For decades, India has manufactured Russian defense equipment under license. Much of what is still produced in India is in the ‘build-to-print’ category, where the design – and often the raw materials – are supplied by the foreign original equipment manufacturer (OEM). In effect, India performs the manufacturing work, but control over the end use remains with the OEM. Licensed production grants only a temporary and limited right to make or sell a product; the core technology, source codes, design data, and patents remain with the foreign licensor. This means India cannot freely modify or export the product without permission.
Even in the case of BrahMos, the original design is Russian, though Indian-led improvements are now being incorporated. Because it is an independent joint venture, it offers greater flexibility, especially for exports. Similarly, the T-90 upgrades offered by India are largely based on systems developed domestically. This makes the Indo-Russian model a practical win-win. But defense technology is at the cutting edge: It takes years of research to develop, becomes obsolete quickly, and is rarely shared freely. Countries guard these types of capabilities closely. If India wants to become a genuine defense manufacturer and exporter in its own right, it must build its own design base.
This means investing far more in research and development. India currently spends just 0.6% of GDP on research and development, compared with 2.7% in China and 3.6% in the US. To build real intellectual property at home, India must move beyond assembly-line production and toward original design, software development, and domestic ownership of patents and know-how. Future contracts, joint ventures, and employment arrangements should ensure that intellectual property generated in India remains with Indian entities, rather than defaulting to foreign partners.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1659: Fedorov returns from the US with plans for Ukraine’s largest defense-tech fund
articles.body:
Exclusives
Military
Far from any front line: Russia has hit at least five of Ukraine's western border crossings with Moldova and NATO member since late August. During one strike, a drone flew into Moldova toward Romania and NATO jets scrambled.
"Neither pickup nor Bradley can enter": retreating Russians have mined sector where three Ukrainian oblasts meet so heavily that only ground robots can cross. On the junction of the Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia oblasts, Russian forces lace their old positions and roads with mines and FPVs.
Ukraine's top commander scrapped more than 30 obsolete General Staff orders, freeing field commanders from paperwork built for different war. Many of the cancelled rules dated to the trench fighting of 2016-2020.
Ukraine reported hitting warships and an oil terminal in a Russian port city whose mayor claimed only falling debris. Orbital heat detection and eyewitness cameras placed more than one blaze across Novorossiysk overnight, in a port that carries a large share of Russia's seaborne export trade.
"In the best blockbusters you wouldn't see this": Ukrainian soldier on fighting off a Russian drone from a moving Humvee. The soldier commands a squad that hauls wrecked armor off the battlefield, and this run cost the crew their own vehicle and a walk out on foot through mined ground.
Intelligence and technology
"We found the key to the Russians": Ex-Defense Minister Fedorov returns from the US, planning Ukraine's largest venture fund for defense tech and war think tank. Fedorov credited contacts built around Palantir with helping raise it. No name, size, or date yet.
Osa air defense missile stocks are running low, but Ukraine has developed the RK-19 as a replacement. Ukraine's Osa launchers stay in the fight with a domestically built RK-19 interceptor as the Soviet 9M33 stock runs down.
Russia's new ballistic missile could reach western Ukraine—and it may be tested there within months. Russia is building more ballistic missiles as well as longer-ranged ones, part of a push to tip Ukraine into a social and economic crisis, Kyiv's military intelligence says.
20% to 70%: Ukraine's National Guard rewired its drone war around cables. Fiber-optic drones trail a cable with no signal to jam—and now account for 70% of the drones the National Guard uses, up from about a fifth.
1,000 Patriot missiles arrive too late for this winter, so Ukraine asked the Ramstein arms coalition to open its warehouses. The swap Kyiv proposed would move rounds out of allied warehouses immediately and hand those governments newer replacements once its own orders come through.
Can Ukraine's newly shown Koral become home-built answer to Patriot? Expert evaluates system displayed at Poland's MSPO expo. The new missile looks a tier below the newest Patriot and has yet to prove it can stop Russian ballistics.
International
Norway sends 69 Russians home without their ship, held for Ukraine. The vessel stays tied up in a Russian settlement on Svalbard while Kyiv's state gas company works to collect a compensation award.
Humanitarian and social impact
Mines and unexploded munitions have harmed 1,688 civilians since Russia's full-scale invasion, Ukraine says. Farmers were the worst-hit occupation, in a country the UN's mine action service calls the most heavily contaminated since the Second World War.
Political and legal developments
Ukraine moves to restore anti-money-laundering safeguard that it quietly weakened, alarming EU and IMF. The IMF said the previous version pulled Ukraine out of global anti-money-laundering standards.
New developments
Romania trailed a Russian agent for seven months—then revealed what he was filming. Romania watched a man filming NATO bases and Ukraine's giant Antonov cargo planes for months.
A drone nearly hit Zelenskyy's plane taking off from Moldova on his way to a king's funeral, Norway's PM says. Zelenskyy arrived in Oslo having spent much of the night on the phone about strikes on his own country.
Read our earlier daily review here.

articles.title: Russia’s new ballistic missile could reach western Ukraine—and it may be tested there within months
articles.body:
Russia plans to test-fire a new type of ballistic missile before the end of 2026, one built to fly farther than the Iskander missiles it now launches at Ukraine, according to Ukraine's military intelligence. Its deputy chief outlined the plan at a Ukraine-NATO meeting on 8 September, ZN reported.
A longer-range missile would erode the relative safety of western Ukraine, where the routes carrying Western aid run beyond the front, and stretch air defenses already struggling against ballistic strikes.
A longer reach into western Ukraine
Russia plans final tests of a new ballistic missile with a range of up to 800 kilometers, or about 500 miles, by year's end, Vadym Skibitskyi, deputy head of the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine (HUR), told the Ukraine-NATO Interparliamentary Council, citing the agency's own assessments. Russian forces may try to hit targets in western Ukraine during those tests, he said.
The deputy chief noted that Moscow is raising both the output and the range of its ballistic missiles to intensify strikes and push Ukraine into a social and economic crisis. He urged partners to tighten sanctions until Russia loses access to the foreign components in its long-range weapons.
Russia's modernized 9M723-2, also called the Iskander-1000, reaches up to 550 km, HUR says, and the older 9M723-1 covers 390 km. An 800-km weapon would carry strikes well past the front.
The missile Russia already fields
Russia already fields a longer-range Iskander variant. This summer, its forces first fired the modernized 9M723-2—part of the Bora-M system—in a combined missile strike on Kyiv. A bigger engine and a larger launcher gave that missile its extended reach, HUR said. Ballistic missiles are the hardest of Russia's strikes for Ukraine to stop, and Moscow has poured them out in recent months, running its plants above quota and firing them in larger salvos.
Losing more soldiers than it signs up
Russia is waging a war of attrition despite heavy losses and has not given up on destroying Ukrainian statehood, Skibitskyi said. Skibitskyi put Russia's August losses at 43,000 soldiers against 39,000 recruited. Russia has struggled to fill its ranks for months. Russia's General Staff sees intensified mobilization as the only way to reach its main goals—fully occupying the Ukrainian Donbas and seizing the strategic initiative—he explained.
The Kremlin plans to mobilize about 600,000 people across 2026 and 2027, half of them by the end of this year, he said. Russia will also try to close the Black Sea to Ukraine and to drag Belarus into the war and into hybrid operations against NATO, he added, though HUR sees no signs of Russian strike groupings forming there yet.
Each new kilometer of range puts more of Ukraine within reach from deep inside Russia, without moving a launcher closer to the border.

articles.title: Ukraine Revives Osa Air Defense Systems With New Domestically Made RK-19 Missile
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Revives Osa Air Defense Systems With New Domestically Made RK-19 Missile
Ukraine has developed a new domestically produced surface-to-air missile designed to replace Soviet 9M33-series interceptors used by the Osa-AKM short-range air defense system.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Militarnyi on September 8, the RK-19 missile was displayed at Ukraine’s defense industry stand during the MSPO defense exhibition in Poland, where its intended role and key technical specifications were disclosed publicly.
The RK-19 can engage aerial targets at ranges of up to 10 kilometers and altitudes of up to 5 kilometers. Its maximum flight speed is listed at 600 meters per second, exceeding the roughly 500-meter-per-second maximum speed of the Soviet 9M33M3 missile it is intended to replace.
Like the original Osa ammunition, the Ukrainian missile uses radio-command guidance. The RK-19 carries a 14.3-kilogram warhead, while the missile and its launch container have a combined weight of 163 kilograms. The container measures 3,255 mm in length, 320 mm in width, and 303 mm in height.
The missile was first shown publicly in April 2026 during a video address by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy marking Ukraine’s Gunsmith Day. At the time, its specific launch platform had not been officially detailed.
The latest presentation confirms that the RK-19 was developed as a replacement for the Soviet-made 9M33 family used by the Osa-AKM, potentially allowing Ukraine to keep the existing air defense systems operational without relying on dwindling stocks of Soviet missiles.
The Osa-AKM is a mobile, short-range surface-to-air missile system designed to protect troops and infrastructure from aircraft and cruise missiles. Each combat vehicle carries six 9M33M3 missiles and can engage targets at ranges of up to 10 kilometers and altitudes of up to 5 kilometers.
Ukraine has operated Osa systems extensively during Russia’s full-scale invasion, including against Russian drones and cruise missiles. However, stocks of compatible Soviet-produced interceptors have declined during the war, limiting the intensity with which the systems can be employed.
Earlier, Ukraine unveiled the launcher for its domestically developed Koral surface-to-air missile, a significantly redesigned interceptor intended to engage both conventional aerial threats and ballistic targets. The latest version weighs about 450 kilograms, carries a 36-kilogram warhead, and uses inertial navigation, radio-command correction, and an active radar seeker.
