articles.title: Trump says Iran war will end ‘immediately’ after US midterms
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump said Wednesday that he expects the war with Iran to end “immediately after the election,” arguing that Tehran is trying to hold out until the November 3 midterms in hopes that Democrats will regain control of Congress.
Trump made the remarks while speaking to reporters before departing for a Republican conference in Dallas, as crude oil prices climbed above $100 a barrel amid renewed escalation with Iran. “I think the war is going to end immediately after the election,” he said. Asked why, Trump replied: “Because they can't hold out any longer. They're desperate to try and affect the election so that we can get a nice weak group of people in there and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon. All they want is a nuclear weapon. And if they had a nuclear weapon, the whole world is in deep trouble.”
Trump also took responsibility for recent U.S. attacks on Iranian vessels and suggested more strikes were coming. “Well, the attacks are made by us. We've knocked out nine of their ships,” he said. “And you're going to see a lot more.” At the same time, he signaled that Washington’s objectives go beyond another nuclear agreement, saying the U.S. was “not looking for a deal” and was seeking “much more than a nuclear deal,” while adding that negotiations could still take place.
The president also said he would speak with Israel about sanctions imposed on Israeli settlements in the West Bank. Britain announced new economic measures this week targeting companies and individuals involved in settlement activity, while Canada and France have also moved against settlement goods as part of coordinated pressure on Israel. The British move has sparked a diplomatic row with Jerusalem and criticism from leading Jewish communal figures in the UK.
Trump’s remarks came as Tehran faced a separate escalation on the diplomatic front. For the first time in 20 years, the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Board of Governors voted Wednesday to refer Iran to the UN Security Council after determining that Tehran had violated its obligations under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. The resolution was backed by 23 of the board’s 35 member states, with Russia, China and Niger voting against, eight abstaining and one not participating.
The referral is not expected to produce immediate sanctions because Russia and China, both Iranian allies and permanent members of the Security Council, could block such measures. Still, sending the issue to the UN’s most powerful body marks a significant diplomatic escalation and follows an IAEA resolution adopted on June 12, 2025, one day before Israel launched its war against Iran, which found Tehran in violation of its nonproliferation commitments.
The dispute centers in part on long-running IAEA investigations into uranium traces found at undeclared Iranian sites and Tehran’s refusal to allow inspectors full access to facilities damaged in the war. Iran has consistently denied pursuing nuclear weapons, but since its nuclear sites were bombed in June 2025 it has sharply restricted cooperation with the agency.
A central unresolved question is the fate of Iran’s stockpile of uranium enriched to 60%, close to the 90% level associated with weapons-grade material. Before the 2025 war, Iran possessed 440.9 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60%, an amount estimated to be sufficient for at least 10 nuclear weapons if enriched further. Much of the material was reportedly buried underground near the damaged Isfahan facility, while Iran has denied inspectors access to Isfahan, Natanz and Fordow.
The survival of that stockpile remains a major concern in Israel, where officials fear Tehran could eventually move the material to a secret facility and enrich it rapidly to weapons grade. One site that has drawn particular attention is a deeply buried complex known in Israel as “Pickaxe Mountain,” which Israeli officials fear could be difficult to destroy even with bunker-busting bombs.
Iran had threatened to respond if the IAEA referred the issue to the Security Council, though no concrete retaliatory step had been announced by Wednesday evening. Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi accused Western countries of exploiting conditions created by attacks on Iran’s nuclear facilities, while Iran’s mission to the IAEA denounced the decision as political and blamed the United States and Israel for the current crisis.

articles.title: F-16 and Patriot Missiles: Key Outcomes of the 36th Ramstein Meeting
articles.body:
Following the 36th Ukraine Contact Group meeting in the Ramstein format, Ukraine will receive missiles for F-16 fighter jets and Patriot air defense systems, along with funding for weapons procurement programs.
Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense reported the development.
During the meeting, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Mykhailo Drapatyi presented Ukraine’s “War Plan” to international partners for the first time. The plan outlines the strategy guiding the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
Following the latest Ramstein meeting, Germany announced new deliveries of interceptor missiles for Patriot air defense systems, missiles for F-16 fighter jets, and funding for the procurement of drones.
The United Kingdom will allocate $135.6 million to purchase U.S. weapons under the PURL program and will also deliver 95,000 drones by the end of the year.
London announced the delivery of tens of thousands of extended-range artillery shells purchased with funding from other countries.
The Netherlands will allocate $300 million to the Drone Line project and to procure 300 anti-drone missiles.
Estonia announced that it would continue supporting Ukraine in 2027 and allocate at least 0.25% of its GDP to aid for Ukraine.
Sweden and Lithuania will contribute $14 million and $10 million, respectively, to the PURL program, while Norway will allocate $200 million to purchase missiles for Patriot air defense systems.
Spain will provide $2.3 million to purchase fuel through the NATO Support and Procurement Agency and deliver air defense missiles and artillery ammunition.
Poland will also provide Ukraine with $58.13 million in assistance. Part of the funding will be allocated, among other things, to air defense systems.

articles.title: Germany to Supply Ukraine with PAC-2 Patriot Missiles from Bundeswehr Stocks
articles.body:
Germany will supply Ukraine with PAC-2 interceptor missiles for Patriot SAM systems from Bundeswehr stocks.
Boris Pistorius, German Minister of Defense, stated this in an interview with Suspilne.
According to him, the decision was made at a meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group in light of Ukraine’s urgent need to strengthen its air defenses ahead of the winter season.
“I have decided to urgently provide Ukraine with the much-needed PAC-2 interceptor missiles from Bundeswehr stocks, in parallel with the NATO summit,” Pistorius said.
“Today’s second step with our partners on air defense: Germany is ready to support Ukraine with missiles for the Patriots,” Volodymyr Zelensky stated.
In addition, Germany plans to supply Ukraine with AIM-9 air-to-air missiles.
Pistorius also announced that Ukraine plans to order several thousand additional IRIS-T guided missiles. Their procurement is expected to be financed through the European Union’s defense loan for Ukraine.
Germany will also join the City Dome project, which aims to strengthen the protection of Ukrainian cities against Russian drones and missiles.
According to Tagesschau, Berlin is funding the purchase of tens of thousands of rounds of ammunition for Ukraine’s long-range artillery through a British consortium.
Germany has stepped up cooperation with Ukraine amid the August 4 incident at Leipzig Airport, where an FPV drone carrying explosives crashed near a Ukrainian An-124 Ruslan aircraft.
After identifying the involvement of Russian intelligence services in the sabotage, Germany began considering providing Ukraine with data from the country’s BND intelligence service, including precise coordinates for retaliatory strikes against targets in Russia.
Germany’s Federal Ministry of the Interior (BMI) also plans to establish a comprehensive set of measures to counter Russian sabotage, including cyberattacks.

articles.title: Osa air defense missile stocks are running low, but Ukraine has developed the RK-19 as a replacement
articles.body:
At the MSPO 2026 arms exhibition in Poland, the Luch Design Bureau, part of the state conglomerate Ukroboronprom, presented the RK-19 surface-to-air missile for the Soviet-made Osa air defense systems and disclosed its specifications for the first time, Defense Express reports.
The Osa-AKM forms the backbone of Ukraine's remaining Soviet Osa fleet, and it is the missiles rather than the launchers that are running out, so a Ukrainian-built interceptor lets those launchers keep engaging jet drones and cruise missiles as the Soviet stock runs down.
Its maker's materials describe the RK-19 as designed to intercept subsonic and supersonic targets "at medium range," Defense Express reports. The missile uses radio-command guidance and proximity detonation and carries a 14.3-kg high-explosive fragmentation warhead.
The missile is similar to the original, but slightly faster
On its main specifications, the RK-19 is similar to the standard missile used by the Osa-AKM, although its maximum speed is somewhat higher, Defense Express notes. Both engage targets at ranges of up to 10 km and altitudes of up to 5 km.
However, their speeds differ: the upgraded missile reaches 600 m/s, while the standard 9M33M3 reaches 500 m/s. Their weights also differ: the transport-launch container with the new missile weighs 163 kg, compared with 157 kg for the standard missile, the outlet reports.
Domestic missile keeps Osa launchers firing at jet drones
The RK-19 will allow the older air defense systems to continue protecting Ukrainian skies and intercepting aerodynamic targets, including jet-powered drones and cruise missiles such as the Banderol, according to Defense Express. The price of the Ukrainian surface-to-air missile for the Osa systems and its production volumes have not yet been disclosed.
The Osa systems were effective through 2022 and into 2023, destroying a significant number of Russian drones and cruise missiles, Militarnyi notes. However, the stock of standard missiles for the Osa systems later began to run out, significantly reducing the intensity of their use, the outlet reports.
With interceptors limited, Ukraine's Armed Forces had to use older missiles for the Osa systems, which had poorer specifications, and integrated short-range air-to-air missiles such as the R-73. That route carried its own drawbacks: reduced range, and reliance on the missile's own seeker, Defense Express reports.

articles.title: Can Ukraine’s newly shown Koral become home-built answer to Patriot? Expert evaluates system displayed at Poland’s MSPO expo
articles.body:
Ukraine's newly shown Koral missile could become a home-built answer to the Patriot in addition to the "Freya" project. However, the system has yet to prove it can stop Russian ballistic missiles, Ivan Kyrychevsky, an arms expert at Defense Express and a soldier in the 413th REID regiment of the Unmanned Systems Forces, said on a YouTube broadcast.
Currently, the PAC-3 version of the Patriot is the only weapon in Ukraine's arsenal that reliably stops Russia's maneuvering Iskander ballistic missiles, and its interceptors are scarce, costly, and rationed for Ukraine by the US.
But in the podcast, Kyrychevsky places Koral, on the data available so far, at roughly the older PAC-2 level. A PAC-2-class interceptor can handle aircraft and simpler ballistic targets, yet it is not the ideal tool against the fast, maneuvering Iskander and Kinzhal that do the most damage. That leaves Koral a hedge against dependence, not a replacement.
The missile sits a tier below Patriot
Kyrychevsky based the judgment on photos released at the expo. The Koral missile lacks the gas-dynamic surfaces that would let it maneuver in flight, he said, and it carries a different warhead from the "hit-to-kill" round on the PAC-3. He did not treat that as disqualifying.
"We are in a situation where we do not just need means against ballistics, but means of at least some technological level," he said.
Cost tilts Ukraine toward its own missile
The economics push in the same direction. A PAC-3 interceptor runs about $10 million for export, and Kyrychevsky noted that even the US Army finds the missiles expensive to spend at the rate the fighting around Iran has demanded.
"We are better off building our own analog of the Patriot, even a mediocre one, than staying dependent on the regularity of external deliveries," he believes.
Winter still hinges on the Patriot
For all that, Kyrychevsky was blunt about the near term. Koral still needs to be tested against Russian ballistic missiles, even experimentally, to confirm its claimed performance, and power cuts at the plants that build it could slow production.
“My assessment for now is roughly this: hopefully, we’ll be able to put the ‘Koral’ to the test against Russian ballistic missiles on an experimental basis," he said.
This winter, he said, Ukraine will need Patriot interceptors regardless of whether it develops its own. Work on Koral began in 2016, and the system was first shown in 2021, a fast pace for a weapon of its kind, and a separate European project, Freya, is advancing on a parallel track.
In July, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine, in cooperation with other European countries, was working on an anti-ballistic missile defense system called “Freya". It is intended to serve as a cheaper and more widely deployable alternative to Patriot air defense systems.
Zelenskyy noted that, in theory, Ukraine could develop “Freya” on its own, but doing so would take significantly more time — potentially years. The system would require not only a missile and launcher, but also radars, command-and-control systems, and many other components. Even with European partners, the process will not be quick.

articles.title: Sybiha, amid new Russian attacks, urges partners to boost air defense, weapons and sanctions
articles.body:
Following another round of Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called on international partners to strengthen Ukraine's air defense, increase weapons deliveries, and step up sanctions pressure on Russia.
"Russia should enter this winter knowing that the sky over Ukraine is getting harder to penetrate, that the missiles and drones it produces will be intercepted more and more often, and that the industry, technology, revenues and supply chains sustaining its attacks will face growing disruption and cost," Sybiha wrote on X.
He said Russia attacked Ukraine overnight, targeting cities and communities across the country with missiles and drones, with the attacks continuing into the morning.
"This is exactly what Russia does when it sees that repeated attacks carry too few consequences. It widens the geography and increases the frequency of strikes, testing how far it can go," the foreign minister said.
According to Sybiha, international partners need to make decisions now, including on additional air defense systems and interceptors, particularly to counter ballistic missiles.
Sybiha also called for providing more missiles for F-16s and additional aircraft to bolster Ukraine's ability to defend its skies, as well as for imposing tougher sanctions against Russia's military-industrial complex and sanctions-evasion networks.
"The world cannot stand idly by while Russia treats Ukrainians as targets on a shooting range," Sybiha said.
He stressed that closing Ukraine's skies should no longer be a matter of reacting to individual Russian attacks, but must instead involve depriving Russia of the confidence that it can keep terrorizing Ukraine indefinitely at an acceptable cost.
"The longer Moscow sees hesitation, the more it will try. The task is to change that calculation," the foreign minister concluded.

articles.title: Ukraine seeks 300 Patriot missiles from allies
articles.body:
Ukraine has asked allied countries to provide 300 Patriot interceptor missiles from their existing stocks as Kyiv attempts to strengthen its air defences before another winter of Russian missile and drone attacks.
Ukrainian Defence Minister Evgeniy Khmara set out the requirement during his first appearance at the Ukraine Defence Contact Group, alongside requests for 500 air-to-air interceptors capable of engaging cruise missiles and $2 billion in funding for drones.
Khmara said a recent Russian attack had involved cruise missiles, ballistic missiles and jet-powered Shahed-type drones. Ukrainian air defences had intercepted 31 of 32 cruise missiles, he said, but ballistic missiles were proving more difficult to counter because of shortages of Patriot ammunition.
He said: “Our air defence managed, among other things, to intercept 31 of the 32 cruise missiles, but the situation with ballistics is much more difficult, and that difficulty is precisely down to the lack of Patriot missiles.”
Ukraine is already contracting around 1,000 Patriot missiles with support from partner countries and through European Union financing, according to Khmara, but most of those weapons are not expected to arrive immediately.
He therefore appealed to countries to transfer missiles currently held in their own inventories, saying: “we ask that you supply us the missiles from your stockpiles today, in exchange for future improved missiles from our contracts.”
Khmara also warned that Ukraine faces a substantial defence funding gap. He said €70 billion in security assistance had been promised this year, with around €62 billion currently expected from bilateral assistance and European funding.
That leaves €8 billion of the earlier commitment outstanding, while Khmara put the wider Ukrainian defence funding shortfall at €23 billion, equivalent to around $27 billion. He asked partners to take the necessary funding decisions by November so that equipment could reach the battlefield during the winter.
Drones also featured prominently in the Ukrainian presentation. Khmara said: “Up to 90 percent of our success in the battlefield is down to drones.”
He said Ukrainian companies were developing lower-cost methods of intercepting jet-powered Shahed-type drones, with some interceptor systems already being tested in combat. Khmara also said Ukrainian assessments indicated that Russia was planning to mobilise around 300,000 additional personnel on top of existing recruitment and could seek a similar mobilisation effort in 2027.
He argued that Moscow was attempting to turn the conflict into a competition over manpower and resources, while Ukraine intended to rely increasingly on technology, drones and rapid battlefield adaptation.

articles.title: UK brings forward maritime role for Protector drones
articles.body:
Britain is bringing forward plans to give the RAF’s Protector drone a maritime capability, with a review of the programme now under way and revised milestones expected by December 2026.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard disclosed the move in response to a written parliamentary question from Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked what progress had been made towards integrating Protector with P-8 Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft and Type 26 frigates.
Pollard said: “The Defence Investment Plan directed Maritime capabilities for the PROTECTOR RG Mk1 be brought forward, and a review of PROTECTOR is therefore currently underway. Rebaselined milestones are expected by December 2026, with a Review Note to follow.”
He added: “In the interim the Capability Sponsor, Cyber and Specialist Operations Command, is progressing capability development activity.”
The 2025 Strategic Defence Review recommended exploring a maritime surveillance capability for Protector, integrated with the RAF’s P-8 Poseidon fleet and the Royal Navy’s new Type 26 anti-submarine warfare frigates.
The review said Protector should be enhanced with maritime surveillance equipment and improved connectivity to give the long-endurance remotely piloted aircraft wider utility. It also placed Protector within the planned evolution of Britain’s anti-submarine warfare force under Atlantic Bastion, envisaging underwater, surface and airborne drones operating alongside Type 26 frigates, P-8 maritime patrol aircraft and nuclear-powered attack submarines.
The concept would use Protector’s endurance to provide persistent surveillance over large maritime areas while connecting its sensor picture with crewed aircraft and warships. The aircraft can remain airborne for more than 30 hours, providing a potentially useful means of maintaining coverage without continuously committing a P-8 to the same task.
The concept is not entirely new to British forces, of course. In 2021, a maritime-configured MQ-9B SeaGuardian, the maritime variant of the aircraft family on which Protector is based, took part in a series of demonstrations in the UK.
During Exercise Joint Warrior, SeaGuardian operated with an RAF P-8 in a manned-unmanned teaming demonstration supporting anti-submarine warfare activity, including the tracking, monitoring and reporting of sonobuoys.
The maritime MQ-9B configuration demonstrated at the time included a maritime surface-search radar, Automatic Identification System receiver and electro-optical and infrared sensors. General Atomics has also developed an anti-submarine warfare mission kit capable of working with sonobuoys.
Those capabilities should not be taken as confirmation of the final equipment fit for British Protector aircraft, which has yet to be disclosed or properly evaluated.
Defence had already begun examining a wider maritime role before publication of the Strategic Defence Review. In January 2025, ministers said Britain was working with the NATO Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance Force to scope options for using Protector in the North Atlantic and Arctic.
After the Strategic Defence Review, however, the Government stopped short of giving a timetable. Asked in October 2025 when Protector would be integrated with P-8 Poseidon and Type 26, Pollard said the maritime capability was being considered through the forthcoming Defence Investment Plan.
The published Investment Plan subsequently allocated £590 million to Protector over the four years to 2029-30, but did not explicitly describe the maritime surveillance programme. It separately committed £260 million to upgrade the RAF’s P-8 Poseidon aircraft and equip them with the UK-built Sting Ray torpedo.
The latest answer now confirms that the Investment Plan actually resulted in a direction to bring Protector’s maritime capabilities forward, with detailed programme milestones being reconsidered as part of the wider Protector review.
That review comes as the overall aircraft programme works through a number of outstanding issues. The latest government major-projects assessment rated Protector Red, citing its pending programme rebaseline alongside trained crew numbers, Full Motion Video metadata dissemination and delays to weapons testing.
Some of those issues have since moved forward. Protector is already being employed operationally, Paveway IV has been operationally available since March 2026 and Brimstone 3 testing has progressed to analysis ahead of operational clearance.
By December, Defence now expects to have rebaselined the milestones governing the programme, including the work intended to turn Protector from a predominantly land-focused persistent surveillance and strike aircraft into another sensor within Britain’s increasingly integrated North Atlantic maritime force.

articles.title: Battlefield sees 263 clashes over past day – Ukraine's General Staff
articles.body:
Battlefield sees 263 clashes over past day – Ukraine's General Staff
A total of 263 combat clashes have occurred on the battlefield over the past day. Ukrainian defence forces have hit seven clusters of Russian military personnel, eight UAV ground control stations and an artillery piece belonging to the Russians.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on Facebook, information as of 08:00 on 9 September
Quote: "In total, 263 combat clashes were recorded over the past day. Yesterday, the enemy launched two missile strikes and conducted 79 airstrikes, dropping 302 guided aerial bombs. In addition, the invaders deployed 9,233 kamikaze drones and conducted 2,601 strikes on Ukrainian settlements and positions, including 42 from multiple-launch rocket systems."
Details: Ukrainian defence forces hit seven areas where Russian military personnel were concentrated, eight UAV ground control stations and an artillery piece belonging to the Russians over the past 24 hours.
On the North Slobozhanshchyna front and in the operational zone in Russia's Kursk Oblast, two Russian assaults were recorded. The Russians conducted 79 strikes on Ukrainian positions and settlements; they also carried out one airstrike, dropping one guided bomb.
On the South Slobozhanshchyna front, Ukrainian forces repelled 10 Russian attacks. The Russians attempted to advance towards the settlements of Lyman, Starytsia, Vovchansk, Chaikivka Mala Vovcha, Rubizhne and Ustynivka.
On the Kupiansk front, the Russians attempted to improve their positions six times, conducting assaults towards the settlements of Kupiansk, Kurylivka, Hlushkivka and Novoosynove.
On the Lyman front, Russian forces launched 11 attacks towards the settlements of Shyikivka, Druzheliubivka, Novoselivka, Lyman and Dibrova. All attacks were repelled.
On the Sloviansk front, the Russians conducted seven offensive actions near the settlements of Yampil, Kryva Luka, Kalenyky, Mykolaivka and Rai-Oleksandrivka.
On the Kramatorsk front, Russian troops conducted one attack towards the village of Yurkivka.
On the Kostiantynivka front, 17 Russian attacks were recorded. The Russians conducted assaults near the town of Kostiantynivka and towards the settlements of Novoselivka, Mykolaipillia, Sofiivka, Rusyn Yar, Illinivka and Kucheriv Yar.
On the Pokrovsk front, the Russians conducted 49 attacks. They attempted to advance towards the settlements of Dorozhnia, Bilytske, Novyi Donbas, Vodianske, Shevchenko, Nadiia, Myrne, Serhiivka, Udachne, Novomykolaivka, Novopidhorodnie, Dobropillia, Hannivka, Krasnopodillia and Novopavlivka.
On the Oleksandrivka front, the Russians conducted two assaults towards the villages of Rybne and Shevchenko.
On the Huliaipole front, Russian forces launched nine attacks on Ukrainian positions. They attempted to advance towards the settlements of Dobropillia, Rizdvianka, Kosivtseve, Tsvitkove and Charivne.

articles.title: Lithuania Moves Toward Lifting Constitutional Ban on Nuclear Deployments
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Lithuania Moves Toward Lifting Constitutional Ban on Nuclear Deployments
Lithuania’s parliamentary Committee on Legal Affairs has voted 7–2 to approve a proposal removing constitutional restrictions against hosting foreign military bases and weapons of mass destruction, according to tv3.lv on September 9.
The decision moves the Baltic nation closer to allowing NATO nuclear forces on its territory, following a broader political consensus reached by parliamentary parties earlier this summer.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
If passed by the full Seimas and signed by the president, the measure will strike Article 137 from the Lithuanian Constitution. The clause currently prohibits the deployment of weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases, regardless of NATO collective defense arrangements or security threats from Russia.
Lawmakers supporting the constitutional amendment emphasized that lifting the restriction is essential for regional security and deterrence. Lithuanian Parliamentary Speaker Juozas Olekas highlighted the country's unique position among allies: “When agreeing on common collective defense plans, and especially deterrence, Lithuania looks like a black sheep in the Alliance, as it is the only one with such a restriction.”
Olekas added during the committee hearing: “Nuclear weapons today are the most powerful deterrent capable of stopping an aggressor crossing our borders.”
The Ministry of Justice has voiced strong backing for the change, with Deputy Minister Martynas Dobrovolskis confirming full support during the meeting.
However, some opposition remains within parliament. Raimondas Šukys, a committee member from the Reminisce of Nemunas party, urged lawmakers to hold a consultative referendum before finalizing the constitutional update.
The initiative follows similar action taken by Finland in June, when the Finnish parliament passed legislation permitting the import, transit, and storage of nuclear weapons for national defense purposes. The bill was later signed into law by Finnish President Alexander Stubb.
Finnish Defense Minister Antti Häkkänen previously noted that ending the ban strengthens national defense capabilities and ensures full access to NATO's nuclear deterrence framework. The Finnish government stated that its decision came in response to deteriorating European security conditions.

articles.title: Russian drone strike near Ukraine-Moldova border kills at least two as Ukraine targets oil terminal
articles.body:
Russian drone strike near Ukraine-Moldova border kills at least two as Ukraine targets oil terminal
An overnight Russian drone strike at a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova killed at least two people, Odesa's regional governor said Wednesday. Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan said that 17 drones had hit Moldovan territory in August alone as both Kyiv and Moscow ramp up long-range strikes on military and energy infrastructure.
Two civilians were killed in a Russian drone strike at a checkpoint on Ukraine's border with Moldova, the regional governor said Wednesday.
"Tonight, enemy drones attacked the Starokozache international road checkpoint on the border with Moldova," Odesa regional governor Oleg Kiper wrote on social media.
"Sadly, there are casualties among the civilians who were near the checkpoint: according to preliminary information, two people were killed and three wounded."
An image attached to Kiper's message showed a deserted border post littered with debris.
The attack forced the closure of the checkpoint located around 500 kilometres south of Kyiv, Ukraine's State Border Guard Service said.
A Moldovan driver was also injured in the attack, according to the country's foreign ministry.
Read morePutin tells Trump that Russia has no 'aggressive plans' towards Europe
Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan on Wednesday said Russia's war against Ukraine was "increasingly endangering the lives of our citizens as well".
Tofan said 17 drones had hit Moldovan territory in August alone, more than during the whole of last year.
"The attacks have intensified so much," he said in a video of a cabinet meeting posted on Facebook. "It's becoming the norm, yet at the same time it's clearly an extremely worrying development."
Ukraine hits Russian oil terminal, naval base
Both Ukraine and Russia continued to exchange air strikes on each other's infrastructure.
Ukrainian forces struck targets in Russia's Black Sea port city of Novorossiysk and in the Krasnodar region, including a naval base and a terminal for loading oil, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Wednesday.
Zelensky said military port facilities and warships allegedly carrying missiles had also been struck.
For its part, the Russian defence ministry said that its forces had struck a Ukrainian cargo vessel carrying what it alleged was military equipment in the Black Sea en route to the port of Odesa, as well as a warehouse in Kyiv belonging to a company manufacturing drones, Russian news agencies reported.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and Reuters)

articles.title: Middle East on brink of World War III, warns Iranian lawmaker among escalating tensions - report
articles.body:
Iranian lawmaker Kamran Ghazanfari said that the region is “practically on the brink of World War III.”
The report of his comments appeared in Iran International. Ghazanfari has been known for some outlandish claims. For instance, he claimed in the past that Iran’s president Ebrahim Raisi was assassinated by Israel and its allies in 2024.
The Ghazanfari comments are interesting because they likely illustrate how some of Iran’s more extremist politicians and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) elites view the war. They see it as a regional and global conflict.
The Islamic Republic has worked with Russia and China and has hopes that it can challenge the US-led world order. Iran has long portrayed its Islamic Revolution as a unique event that would transform the region and the world.
This goes back to the fact that Iranian Islamists believed they were presenting a new path during the Cold War that was different from those of the American and Soviet blocs. That changed in the 1990s when the Soviet Union declined.
Iran positions itself on side of a new world order
While Iran has at times considered reconciliation with the United States, it has also sought to position itself alongside countries that want a new world order. Weakening the US and pushing it out of the Middle East is a key goal of Tehran.
Iran International noted on September 9: “Ghazanfari, a Tehran representative in the parliament, said that we are ‘practically on the brink of World War III’ and considered the expansion of the war between Russia and Ukraine and the increase in tension between world powers as grounds for the formation of a widespread conflict.”
The report noted that he made the comments in an interview with the official Iranian Labour News Agency (ILNA).
“Ghazanfari said that NATO’s support for Ukraine in its war with Russia - and Moscow’s tensions with Britain and Germany - have increased the possibility of the conflict spreading to other European countries. He also called the US-China dispute over Taiwan another area of widespread conflict in the world.”
In the interview, Ghazanfari also focused on Iran’s plan to withdraw from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT). “According to him, there is a possibility that this issue will be put on the parliament’s agenda again.”
In the past, he has critiqued the chances of a US deal. For instance, in June he criticized the memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the US. At the time, it seemed America and Iran might be able to reach an agreement. Ghazanfari said that any deal with the US would lack legitimacy and not be binding.
At the time, Iran International reported that “Iranian lawmaker Kamran Ghazanfari” said in a “warning to the negotiating team” that they should not cross any of the supreme leader’s red lines.
US reportedly threatens Iran, members of negotiation team
“Ghazanfari added that the United States had repeatedly threatened Iran and members of its negotiating team during the two-month talks, saying any deal reached under such conditions would have no validity under international law,” Iran International said.
Ghazanfari has also warned in the past about American and Israeli plans for a broader military operation. He claimed that the US might seize Iranian islands.”
“Evidence and signs show that the United States and Israel are planning a large-scale operation. They probably intend to seize some of our islands in the south and have brought many forces and equipment into the region,” he said.
Iran’s regime is currently continuing attacks in the region. Its recent attacks on Jordan and threats to attack tankers indicate that it wants to show that it can respond in kind to any US strikes and is telegraphing that it will not back down.

articles.title: Defense Forces down 165 Russian UAVs – Air Force
articles.body:
On the night of September 9, Russians attacked the territory of Ukraine with Iskander-M ballistic missiles, S8000 "Banderol" missiles, as well as 196 strike UAVs of the Shahed and Gerbera types, and "Parodiya"-type decoy drones, reported the Air Force Command of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
"According to preliminary data, as of 08:30, air defense shot down/suppressed 165 Russian UAVs of the Shahed and Gerbera types and drones of other types," according to a statement on Telegram.
In addition, impacts of Russian missiles and strike UAVs were recorded at 23 locations, as well as the fall of downed targets (debris) at 4 locations.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
The attack is ongoing, with enemy UAVs remaining in the airspace. The number of missiles launched by Russian was not reported.
Thus, the efficiency of Ukrainian air defense against drones on Wednesday night exceeded 84%.

articles.title: Despite Russian strikes, Ukraine’s BTR-4 maker built 600 vehicles
articles.body:
- Ukraine's KhKBM has built more than 600 BTR-4 armored personnel carriers since the 2022 invasion, with capacity for about 200 a year.
- The state currently has no active contract for new BTR-4Es, though the company has parts in stock for 100 to 200 more vehicles.
A Ukrainian armored vehicle maker has built more than 600 BTR-4 troop carriers since Russia’s full-scale invasion began, working through repeated missile strikes on the country’s defense industry.
The Kharkiv Morozov Machine Building Design Bureau, known as KhKBM, disclosed the production figure to a Militarnyi correspondent at the MSPO defense exhibition in Kielce, Poland.
The company relocated its operations after the 2022 invasion put its home city of Kharkiv within range of Russian strikes, and it has kept building the eight-wheeled BTR-4 armored personnel carrier throughout the war.
KhKBM says it can build about 200 BTR-4s a year at current capacity. The vehicle’s BTR-4E variant is roughly 80% Ukrainian-made by component count, according to the company representative, a level of domestic content that has let the plant keep working even as some imported parts became harder to source during the war.
Despite that output, the state currently has no active contract to buy more BTR-4Es, the KhKBM representative said. Militarnyi first reported the funding gap in June, when plant workers said they were finishing the last government order on their production lines.
Ukraine’s Defense Ministry has not placed new armored vehicle orders since the start of 2026, according to earlier Militarnyi reporting, with procurement officials saying deliveries are continuing under contracts signed in prior years while the General Staff works out this year’s requirements. KhKBM says it has enough parts in stock to build another 100 to 200 vehicles even without a new order.
The company used MSPO to show an updated BTR-4E fitted with a rear ramp built to a specification the military requested, which KhKBM plans to make standard on future production vehicles. The armor meets NATO’s STANAG 4569 standard, with frontal protection rated to stop 12.7 mm armor-piercing incendiary rounds and side and rear armor rated against 7.62 mm rounds. Mine protection comes from layered armored plates rated to STANAG levels 3a and 3b, backed by an aramid anti-spall liner inside the hull.
The updated vehicle also carries slat armor around its perimeter and upper hull to defeat shaped-charge weapons, along with chain and rod curtains meant to counter loitering drones that wait above a target before striking. KhKBM has fitted the vehicle with a Ukrainian-made electronic warfare system and says it plans to eventually add an active protection system and additional anti-drone netting to both the hull and its gun turret.
The exhibited BTR-4 also carries a new turret called Topaz, which KhKBM said is still undergoing testing.

articles.title: Ukrainian Navy: Russia's Admiral Essen frigate in Novorossiysk hit by Neptune missile
articles.body:
Ukrainian Navy: Russia's Admiral Essen frigate in Novorossiysk hit by Neptune missile
The Russian frigate Admiral Essen, which was struck on the night of 8-9 September, was hit by a Ukrainian-made Neptune missile.
Source: Ukrainian Navy; a Ukrainian OSINT project Exilenova+
Details: Ukrainian forces attacked the Russian warship with a missile during a combined strike by Ukraine's defence forces involving units of the Unmanned Systems Forces, Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU), the Security Service of Ukraine (SSU) and other elements of the Ukrainian military.
Quote from the Navy: "Navy personnel used a Neptune missile to hit the Admiral Essen frigate, a carrier of Kalibr cruise missiles."
More details: OSINT project Exilenova+ posted a satellite image of the Russian base in the city of Novorossiysk following the overnight attack. DIU reported that the frigate's superstructure was hit.
For reference: The Admiral Essen is a Russian Project 11356R Burevestnik-class frigate, launched in 2014 and commissioned into Russia's Black Sea Fleet. The vessel took part in missile strikes on Syria in 2017 and has been involved in strikes on Ukraine since 2022. It is armed with 3M14 Kalibr cruise missiles, the Shtil-1 surface-to-air missile system and a 100mm A-190 gun.
The R-360 Neptune cruise missile is designed to destroy ships with a displacement of up to 5,000 tonnes and, like other missiles of its class, can be launched from land, surface and air platforms. In April 2022, a Neptune missile was used to sink the Russian cruiser Moskva.
In late 2025, Zelenskyy confirmed that Ukraine was also using the upgraded Long Neptune version. The Neptune-D system uses RK360L cruise missiles with a range of up to 1,000 km and a 260kg warhead. The missile is designed to strike both land and maritime targets.
Background: It was reported earlier that Ukraine's defence forces and the Unmanned Systems Forces struck a number of Russian military assets in Novorossiysk and Anapa on the night of 8-9 September. Confirmed hits included a Su-33 carrier-based fighter and an Mi-8 helicopter, two Russian radars – a Kasta-2E2 and a 92N6 radar from an S-300/S-400 air defence system – near Gelendzhik, as well as the Project 11356 frigate Admiral Essen.

articles.title: Ukraine fighting for our freedom too warns UK
articles.body:
Britain will not flinch in its support for Ukraine, the Defence Secretary told allies as he announced a £100 million contribution towards the rapid delivery of air defence interceptors before winter, at a virtual meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group on Tuesday.
Wes Streeting, co-chairing the meeting alongside German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius, put the money into the PURL mechanism, under which allies fund American weaponry for Ukraine. The announcement came against a requirement Kyiv had set out minutes earlier for 300 Patriot missiles from partner stocks, 500 air-to-air interceptors with counter-cruise missile capability and $2 billion for drones.
Attending as, in his own description, the still relatively new Secretary of State, he said the commitment felt across the country was unshakable. “Our Prime Minister Andy Burnham and I, and in fact our entire country, feel to Ukraine, to its people and to its government as they fight on the front line, not just for Ukrainian freedom and democracy, but for all of our freedom and democracy.”
Having hosted President Zelensky in Britain over the summer and visited Kyiv alongside the Prime Minister, he said he had seen the consequences of Russian aggression at first hand along with “the resilience and strength and the courage that the people of Ukraine are showing”.
The message he wanted heard in Moscow was that the winter would change nothing. “We know that this will only end through a negotiated peace. It’s really important that Russia understands that we won’t flinch in terms of our support for Ukraine as they continue to fight for their freedom and, for that matter, for ours.”
On drones, where Britain committed to supplying 120,000 this year, progress is running at more than 25,000 delivered so far with thousands more due before winter. Those cover a range of capabilities, in his account, helping Ukraine “to take the fight directly to Russia, defend itself by taking out Russian drones, and also to see what’s happening both on the battlefield and behind enemy lines”.
Britain delivered its millionth round of large calibre artillery ammunition in July, with tens of thousands more to follow, funded by Germany, Denmark, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden.
The Ukrainian ask
Evgeniy Khmara, attending his first meeting as Ukraine’s Defence Minister, opened by thanking partners for the munitions, the funding and the technology, but above all for the time it had bought. “We are still standing because we have strong people and we have strong friends,” he told the group. His assessment of the front was that Russia has failed to achieve strategic success and is compensating through terror against civilians. “We have built a drone kill zone. It halts the enemy’s advance and destroys over 30,000 Russian military personnel every month,” he said.
Describing the previous night’s attack, in which cruise missiles, ballistic missiles and jet-powered Shahed drones were launched, he said Ukrainian air defences intercepted 31 of 32 cruise missiles. “The situation with ballistics is much more difficult, and that difficulty is precisely down to the lack of Patriot missiles. Russia is aware of this, which is why it’s trying to exhaust our air defence, our economy, and our society.”
Russia is planning to mobilise something in the order of 300,000 personnel on top of those already recruited, according to Ukrainian assessments, with the same expected for 2027, alongside increased production intended to turn the war into a competition of resources. Kyiv’s answer, Khmara said, is “smart technology and speed”. On money, of the 70 billion euros promised at Ankara, partners are so far providing 62 billion including bilateral assistance and the EU loan, leaving 8 billion outstanding against the declaration while the overall defence deficit stands at 23 billion euros. He asked that the necessary decisions be taken by November so results can be seen on the battlefield this winter, noting that up to 90 per cent of Ukrainian battlefield success now rests on drones.
Ukraine is contracting around 1,000 Patriot missiles with partner help and through the EU loan, but the majority will not ship for some years, which is why he asked allies to supply from existing stockpiles now in exchange for improved missiles from those future contracts. “The support for Ukraine is not a subsidy; it is an investment,” he said.
“We are offering a win-win partnership. Together, we’re creating new capacities for the security of the free world.”

articles.title: US destroys five Iranian tankers as Tehran launches retaliatory strikes on Jordan
articles.body:
US CENTCOM said crews were warned to abandon ship before its strikes after the IRGC fired missiles at a US Navy warship twice in two days. Tehran launched missile strikes on US targets in Jordan and warned tankers near Kuwait and Bahrain to evacuate.
US forces destroyed five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday after the Revolutionary Guards fired ballistic missiles at a US Navy warship twice in two days, as Iran launched missile strikes on US targets in Jordan.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) said the crews of all five vessels — the Kivik, Charminar, Horizon 1, Riesco and Derya — were warned to abandon ship before the strikes.
The targeted warship evaded both Iranian attacks without casualties, CENTCOM said.
Iranian state-affiliated news agency confirmed one oil tanker was struck near Jask and another tanker four miles off Kharg Island. Iran's state broadcaster has reported that a commercial vessel was also attacked in the coastal waters of Jask county.
According to Tasnim, citing local sources, the attack on the tanker near Kharg caused no casualties.
Iran launched missiles at US targets in Jordan following the tanker strikes, according to Iranian state-run television.
"Given the malign actions of the terrorist US military in targeting several oil tankers of the Islamic Republic of Iran, we warn all tanker crews in the area of the ports of Kuwait and Bahrain, which host these terrorists and are partners in their aggression, to leave their vessels immediately, whether at anchorage or at the quays, as they will be targeted," IRGC said.
The Khatam al-Anbiya central command followed with a threat to US bases in the region.
"The US military has ordered Iranian oil tankers to evacuate so that it can strike them; therefore I declare that any attack on Iranian oil tankers will result in US bases in the region being targeted by the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran," Major General Abdollahi said in a statement.
Jordan's military said its air defence systems intercepted 18 ballistic missiles launched toward its territory and that two others landed in uninhabited areas. No casualties were reported.
Jordan hosts several US military installations and has been a repeated target of Iranian strikes since the war began on 28 February.
Iran also said it had captured a US unmanned underwater vessel at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz before dawn, broadcasting images of what it described as the captured drone on state television. Iran had claimed to have struck a US Navy sea drone on Sunday.
The Trump administration separately announced new sanctions on more than two dozen Iranian commercial and private airlines and foreign cargo providers, in a further effort to isolate Tehran from its remaining trading partners.
The exchange marks one of the sharpest escalations since the framework deal the two sides signed in June broke down the following month.
Both sides have been attempting to assert control over the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway through which roughly one-fifth of the world's traded oil passed before the war began.
The US has been enforcing a naval blockade of Iranian ports while Tehran has sought to impose its own transit regime on commercial shipping through the strait.

articles.title: US Patriot Batteries Go Into “Machine-Gun Mode” Against Iranian Ballistic Missile Attack, Video
articles.body:
- Category
- World
US Patriot Batteries Go Into “Machine-Gun Mode” Against Iranian Ballistic Missile Attack, Video
US-operated Patriot batteries may have fired roughly 60 interceptor missiles to counter an Iranian barrage of just 20 ballistic missiles over Jordan, highlighting the enormous ammunition demands involved in defending against sustained ballistic attacks, Defense Express reported on September 9.
Iran struck Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan overnight, a facility used by US forces. Jordanian authorities said air defenses intercepted 18 of 20 incoming ballistic missiles, while two fell before reaching their intended targets.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Footage from the attack, however, provides an unusually revealing look at how intensely Patriot batteries were operating during the engagement.
Defense Express estimated from available videos that approximately 60 Patriot interceptors may have been launched during the defense. Claims circulating online that as many as 100 were fired appear exaggerated, the outlet noted.
Even the lower estimate would mean roughly three interceptors launched for every Iranian ballistic missile in the salvo, although the exact number of Patriot missiles fired has not been officially confirmed.
Defense Express described several Patriot batteries as effectively operating in a “machine-gun” mode as they attempted to defeat the incoming missiles.
Video from the attack also appears to show Iran using ballistic missiles carrying cluster submunitions, adding another layer of difficulty to the interception effort.
The scale of Patriot expenditure is particularly notable because the systems protecting the area are believed to be operated by US forces rather than Jordanian crews.
Jordan has never publicly declared Patriot systems as part of its own inventory. The United States, however, has deployed Patriot batteries in the country when necessary to defend US facilities and support Jordanian airspace protection.
That distinction matters, Defense Express noted.
Previous cases of unusually high Patriot interceptor consumption against Iranian ballistic attacks could potentially be explained by limited experience among foreign operators.
US air-defense personnel have already spent more than six months responding to repeated Iranian ballistic missile attacks against American military installations since the beginning of Operation Epic Fury on February 28.
The crews therefore have substantial practical experience with this particular threat environment.
If the estimate of roughly 60 Patriot interceptors is accurate, the September 9 engagement illustrates that high missile consumption may be an inherent feature of defending against modern ballistic salvos rather than simply a consequence of inexperienced operators.
For Ukraine, which relies heavily on Patriot to stop Russian ballistic missiles, the episode also underscores a familiar problem: successful air defense can consume enormous quantities of some of the world’s most expensive and difficult-to-produce interceptors in a matter of minutes.
As Defense Express noted, the question is therefore not only whether Patriot can stop ballistic missiles, but how many interceptors must be available when a sustained barrage arrives.
Earlier, reports emerged that US forces may have used as many as 96 to 128 PAC-3 interceptor missiles in a single night while defending military bases in Jordan from an Iranian ballistic missile attack—potentially consuming up to 17% of estimated US stocks.
Discuss this article:

articles.title: Berlin slams Kiev for not spending aid cash on German guns
articles.body:
Berlin slams Kiev for not spending aid cash on German guns
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has criticized Kiev for failing to spend enough of its Western-provided procurement money on German weapons, arguing that the country’s massive support for Ukraine should at least benefit its defense industry.
Germany is one of Ukraine’s largest bilateral supporters, providing or earmarking more than €43 billion ($50 billion) in “civilian” assistance and around €58 billion in military aid since the conflict escalated in 2022.
“We are now the strongest supporter of Ukraine in terms of financial and military support. And naturally, the German defense industry must benefit from this,” Wadephul told Bild in an interview published on Tuesday.
The minister said he raised the issue with Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky during a visit to Kiev last month.
“We stand by you, we support you. But I also have to explain this to German taxpayers, and the very least you can do is to involve the German defense industry in all procurement measures,” Wadephul said he told Zelensky.
“At the moment, we are not entirely satisfied with the level of orders in Germany,” he added, saying Kiev has been asked to review its purchases and ensure that the situation “gets better.”
Germany’s demands that the money spent on Kiev flow back to its own weapons makers mirror US President Donald Trump’s approach to Ukraine aid. Since returning to the White House, Trump has largely shifted the financial burden of supplying US weapons to European NATO members and Canada. Under the PURL mechanism, the bloc’s members now pay Washington for US-made arms that are then delivered to Kiev.
Moscow has criticized the unprecedented military buildup by Germany and the wider EU on the pretext of the ‘Russian threat’. President Vladimir Putin said in June that Western governments are no longer concealing their intentions and are “openly saying that they are preparing for war with us.”
Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has warned that Germany and the rest of Europe under their current leadership are “transforming into a Fourth Reich” and seek fight Russia “to the last Ukrainian.”
Berlin has also stepped up pressure on Ukrainian men of military age living in Germany to return home “without coercion.” Wadephul backed calls by Bavarian leader Markus Soeder and suggested that the German authorities could provide Kiev with information identifying Ukrainians receiving welfare benefits or holding registered residency status so they can be contacted for mobilization. Germany has separately backed stripping newly arriving draft-age Ukrainian men of the automatic temporary-protection privileges granted to refugees.

articles.title: The World's Best Companies of 2026
articles.body:
The economy built around AI has continued to boom even as experts and leaders work to hammer out the technology's execution problem and debate the guardrails that should be put around it. Demand for AI chips remains strong, as Nvidia holds its top spot in TIME and Statista’s 2026 statistical ranking of the World’s Best Companies, highlighting top performing companies around the globe based on evaluations of employee satisfaction, revenue growth, and sustainability transparency. But new companies are also entering the scene as the AI boom reaches down the supply chain.
Companies like Wistron (no. 16), Lenovo (no. 51) and Zurich Insurance Group (no. 70) are new additions to the 2026 list. Major Nvidia supplier Wistron reports that the demand for its AI servers continues to exceed supply. The Taiwan-based manufacturing company recently opened a plant in Texas to ramp up production. Chinese computer company Lenovo, known for being a maker of devices like PCs, smartphones and tablets, saw annual profits rise to record sales driven by the newer AI server part of their business. And the wave of growing demand for physical infrastructure to support AI has created an opportunity for firms like Zurich Insurance Group to cash in on selling more data center construction-related insurance. Zurich plans to expand its dedicated insurance and risk management solution for large-scale data center projects soon into Europe and Latin America. S&P Global puts total insurable values for each data center at up to $30 billion per location.
Beyond AI, European defense technology companies are seeing cashflow as a result of European NATO allies committing in 2025 to spend a projected €800 billion on defense readiness by 2030. “The increased defense spending in Europe is actually one of the largest demand signals we have seen in generations,” says Hugues Lavandier, senior partner in McKinsey’s Aerospace & Defense Practice. A good portion of that spending is still going outside of Europe, but Lavandier “won't be surprised that we increasingly see more of that spend going to Europe for sovereignty reasons.” The war in Ukraine among other recent geopolitical tensions has shown Europe that the art of war fighting and the equipment needed is also changing. “The share of that money being spent on equipment is actually going up,” Lavandier says, especially on new technologies like drones and unmanned vehicles, and addressing technical challenges like navigation, electronic warfare, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance.
Traditional companies in the space like French defense electronics maker Thales (no. 22; up from no. 224 in 2025) and Italian defense and aerospace company Leonardo (no. 25; up from a no. 126 in 2025) are seeing uptick in orders. At the same time, “non-traditional players are entering into the field, especially as suppliers,” Lavandier says. “In particular, a number of automotive players have entered into the fray…sometimes even selling plants, making capacity available.” Thales, for example, recently announced a sovereign drone partnership with French carmaker Renault (no. 42). A number of new startups are also taking this opportunity to translate the investment into innovations, sometimes as standalone products or in partnership with other companies, similar to Anduril’s ventures in the U.S. For example, German drone-maker Quantum Systems, which is currently supplying armed forces in Ukraine, announced significant investment from German telecomm giant Deutsche Telekom (no. 7), which owns the T-mobile brand, and also announced a new partnership with Rheinmetall (no. 287) to co-create an anti-drone shield.

articles.title: Ukroboronprom Reveals Designation of Palianytsia Missile-Drone
articles.body:
Ukroboronprom has revealed the designation of the Ukrainian-made Palianytsia missile-drone, which Ukraine’s Defense Forces use to strike targets in Russia.
The weapon was displayed under the designation UAV-290 at MSPO 2026, an international defense exhibition in Kielce, Poland.
Previously, the missile-drone was displayed at various exhibitions and events, sometimes as Palianytsia and other times as UAV-290.
It has now been officially confirmed for the first time that the two names refer to the same weapon, developed and manufactured by the state-owned Luch Design Bureau.
UAV-290 Palianytsia is designed to autonomously strike various stationary ground targets at the enemy’s tactical depth.
The missile-drone is equipped with a turbojet engine that provides a cruising speed of up to 800 km/h.
Palianytsia is launched from a trailer or semitrailer using a solid-fuel booster.
After launch, it switches to autonomous flight using an integrated INS+GPS navigation system.
The UAV-290 carries a 100 kg warhead and weighs 350 kg. Its stated range is 650 km.
The missile-drone is 3.5 meters long, with a 1.7-meter wingspan.
The manufacturer states that navigation and terminal guidance are performed using a combination of an autonomous inertial navigation system, immune to electronic warfare, and satellite navigation to correct deviations.
In August 2026, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reported that Ukraine’s Defense Forces had used, among other weapons, the UAV-290 to strike a Russian Navy base and port in Novorossiysk.

articles.title: Ukrainian commander, whose unit destroyed 57,000 Russia’s targets: US telling allies to brace for years of war at Ramstein means no “miraculous de-escalation” is coming
articles.body:
The US told Ukraine's allies to prepare for a war lasting years at the latest Ramstein meeting, the forum where Kyiv's partners decide the military aid it gets. Yurii Fedorenko, commander of the 429th "Achilles" Unmanned Systems Brigade, said that the message confirms there will be no "miraculous de-escalation" from the latest round of US-Russia talks.
Fedorenko commands one of Ukraine's most effective drone units, a brigade credited with more than 57,000 strikes, as per Militarnyi. The unit was formed around volunteers who, on 24 February, 2022, established a rifle company within the 128th Battalion of the 112th Territorial Defense Brigade.
Fedorenko reads a long war
He took the message from US defense policy chief Elbridge Colby, who told the 36th Ramstein contact group to prepare for a protracted war.
“A cold shower for everyone hoping for a quick peace: the US representatives urge preparation for years of war," Fedorenko says.
It means that the allies must brace for a hard winter in Ukraine, for Russia sharpening its hybrid war against Europe, and for Ukraine's military needs lasting a long time.
Colby, he says, dispelled the illusions of anyone still hoping for a "miraculous de-escalation" and made clear no timeline for a settlement is in view.
Peace talks hinge on side deals
A real peace process is unlikely in the coming months, Fedorenko argues. Recalling NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte’s remarks, he says that, in his view, the collective West should not simply maintain its current level of support for Ukraine, but strengthen it.
“Western media, quoting these remarks, conclude that the attempt to revive negotiations with the Kremlin has failed. In reality, that is too categorical a statement,” the commander says.
He explains that any long-term track of so-called “peace negotiations” is inevitably linked to resolving “parallel", yet highly important issues, such as the exchange of prisoners of war, navigation in the Black Sea, and the need for temporary ceasefires during visits to Kyiv or Moscow by international delegations, among others.
“At the same time, Russia will use — and is already using — this mechanism to manipulate and advance its own interests. We need to be prepared for that as well,” Fedorenko adds.
Force alone moves the Kremlin
His bottom line is stark. Grounds for a serious conversation will appear, he said, only when Russia exhausts its reserves and its ability to attack and begins to fall back.
"Whatever signals the Kremlin sends, our partners and we should firmly remember: the aggressor understands only the language of force," Fedorenko says.
Until the moment of its weakness comes, he adds, the West should do two specific things before the cold sets in: tighten sanctions on Russia and send Ukraine more support.

articles.title: A drone nearly hit Zelenskyy’s plane taking off from Moldova on his way to a king’s funeral, Norway’s PM says
articles.body:
An unknown drone nearly struck President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's plane as it took off from Moldova on his way to King Harald's funeral in Oslo. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who received him the next morning, told the broadcaster NRK that his plane "was nearly hit by a drone during takeoff."
The account, so far only Norway's, points to how far Russia's air war now reaches. If confirmed, it means a Russian drone came close to a head of state as he left the region, somehow reaching Moldova, Ukraine's neighboring state.
"That is the reality he faces," Støre added.
A drone shadows the president's flight
Details of the near-miss remain thin. Støre did not say how close the drone came or what happened to it, and Ukraine has not commented publicly.
While the drone could come from the territory of Ukraine, it may also echo an episode from five weeks earlier in Leipzig that Germany has since formally pinned on Moscow.
On the night of 4 August, an airport worker at Leipzig/Halle found a drone carrying roughly 800 grams of explosive parked near a Ukrainian An-124 cargo plane.
Zelenskyy arrives after a hard night
Støre said he asked Zelenskyy how the night had been.
"He said it hadn't been a good night, because he had been on the phone receiving information about where the missiles had hit," Støre said, calling the situation in Ukraine "very dramatic."
Zelenskyy met Støre, Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg, the former NATO secretary general, and Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide soon after landing.
The drone war reaches into Moldova
The reported near-miss fits a widening pattern on Ukraine's southwestern edge. Russian drones have struck the border crossings that tie Odesa Oblast to Moldova and Romania and have strayed into Moldovan and Romanian airspace during strikes on Ukraine, forcing both countries to close their skies and scramble jets.
Moldova, which lacks the air defenses to stop such incursions, has been investing in building them. On 27 August, the Institute for the Study of War said the crossings show Russia working to normalize the threat its strikes pose to European states.

articles.title: Ukraine's Defence Intelligence strikes Kalibr missile carrier Admiral Essen again: details of Novorossiysk attack
articles.body:
Ukraine's Defence Intelligence strikes Kalibr missile carrier Admiral Essen again: details of Novorossiysk attack
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has reported that on the night of 8-9 September, operators from its Active Operations Department, as part of a joint deep-strike operation with other components of Ukraine's defence forces, struck infrastructure at the Russian naval base in Novorossiysk, as well as the Russian Project 11356 frigate Admiral Essen.
Source: Defence Intelligence of Ukraine
Details: The DIU reported that the strikes caused a fire on the superstructure of the Admiral Essen.
The Admiral Essen is a carrier of Kalibr cruise missiles, which Russia regularly uses to attack civilian infrastructure in Ukraine.
Ukraine's defence forces have struck the missile carrier on several previous occasions.
The Security Service of Ukraine and Ukraine's defence forces struck the Russian frigate on the night of 1-2 March 2026. At the time, a Ukrainska Pravda source in the service said that the damaged vessel was unable to launch Kalibr missiles.
In August, Ukraine's Defence Intelligence and defence forces also struck the Russian missile carriers Admiral Essen and Admiral Makarov, as well as the patrol ship Vasily Bykov.
Background:
- On the night of 8-9 September, monitoring Telegram channels reported that drones had attacked Novorossiysk, causing a fire at a fuel oil terminal.
- The mayor of Novorossiysk confirmed that a fire had broken out but claimed it had been caused by falling debris. He did not name the facility that had been attacked or provide details about the extent of the damage or possible casualties.
- OSINT analysts reported that facilities at the port complex had been struck, damaging at least one tank at the Novorossiysk fuel oil terminal.
- The terminal is one of the key facilities of the Novorossiysk transport hub and forms part of the Novorossiysk Commercial Sea Port, Russia's largest port by cargo turnover.
- On the morning of 9 September, Robert "Magyar" Brovdi, Commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, confirmed that the naval base in Novorossiysk, Russia's Krasnodar Krai, had been struck overnight.

articles.title: Oil tops $100 as Middle East conflict intensifies
articles.body:
Oil tops $100 as Middle East conflict intensifies
Global oil prices have surpassed $100 per barrel as escalating fighting between the US and Iran, and Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure, raised fears of further supply disruptions. Brent crude broke the threshold for the first time in nearly two months.
Brent futures climbed 2.2% to $100.07 per barrel in Asian trading, their highest level since July 24. US benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI) rose 1.83% to $94.73, while Brent has gained around 25% since early August as hopes of a lasting settlement to the US-Iran conflict have faded.
“Recent developments only reinforce the view that we’re still some way from a restart in talks. In the meantime, the market is likely to continue to price in a sizeable risk premium,” ING commodities strategists Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey wrote in a note early Wednesday.
The latest price surge followed a sharp escalation at sea. US forces struck five Iranian crude carriers on Tuesday, and Iran later claimed that it hit two US vessels and eight oil tankers in the Persian Gulf in retaliation, inflicting “significant damage.”
The attacks came after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) issued an “urgent warning” to tanker crews near Bahrain and Kuwait to abandon their ships, saying vessels in the area would be targeted. Ballistic missiles were subsequently launched from Iran toward US military facilities across the region, including those in Jordan, where air defenses intercepted 18 of 20 incoming missiles, according to the military.
The maritime confrontation has become an increasingly prominent front in the conflict. The US has restricted traffic to and from Iranian ports, while Tehran has imposed controls on passage through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital energy route that handled around a fifth of global oil supplies before the war.
Supply concerns have also intensified after Yemen’s Houthis launched missile and drone attacks on energy facilities in southern Saudi Arabia on Tuesday. The strikes reportedly forced temporary shutdowns and sparked a fire at the Jazan refinery, a major Saudi Aramco facility capable of processing 400,000 barrels of crude oil per day.

articles.title: Russia attacked Ukraine with missiles and 196 drones: air defenses shot down 165 UAVs
articles.body:
Russia attacked Ukraine with missiles and 196 drones: air defenses shot down 165 UAVs
Kyiv • UNN
At night, Russia launched ballistic missiles and 196 attack drones at Ukraine. Air defenses destroyed or suppressed 165 unmanned aerial vehicles.
During the night of September 9, Russian forces attacked Ukraine with Iskander-M ballistic missiles, S8000 "Banderol" missiles, as well as 196 Shahed-type attack UAVs (including jet-powered ones), Gerbera UAVs, and Parodiya-type decoy drones. This was reported by the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, according to UNN.
Details
The strikes were launched from the waters of the Sea of Azov, occupied Crimea and Donetsk, as well as from Russia’s Oryol and Kursk regions. The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
Air defense shot down/suppressed 165 enemy Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera UAVs, and drones of other types.
Hits by enemy missiles and attack UAVs were recorded at 23 locations, as well as the fall of downed targets (debris) at 4 locations.

articles.title: US missile reserves hit hard by Iran war
articles.body:
Wars are not measured only by the number of attacks, the missiles fired, or the areas gained on the battlefield. One of the most important criteria is the cost that war imposes on the military power, economy, and deterrence capacity of the parties; a cost that sometimes shows its effects months and even years after the end of the conflict.
It is within this framework that the recent report by the Los Angeles Times on the state of US missile stockpiles after the war with Iran takes on particular importance. Citing published estimates about US defensive missile reserves, the report says Washington consumed a significant portion of its advanced Patriot and THAAD missiles during the war, and rebuilding these stockpiles at the current capacity of the US defense industry could take several years.
According to the report, the United States consumed about 60 percent of its advanced defensive missile stockpiles in the first five months of the war. The estimate by the Center for Strategic and International Studies also indicates that US global Patriot and THAAD reserves declined from about 2,800 missiles at the start of the war to about 1,100 by the end of July.
These numbers become even more significant when we consider that the production speed of the US defense industry falls considerably short of the rate at which these missiles are consumed in a major war. Based on the same estimates, American factories were producing about 620 Patriot missiles and 96 THAAD missiles annually before the war; a figure that is not sufficient to quickly replace what has been consumed in the war. As a result, restoring Patriot stockpiles to prewar levels will take at least several years, and rebuilding THAAD reserves will take even longer.
This issue is not just a logistical problem for the US military; it is directly tied to the question of deterrence.
Unlike many countries, the United States must simultaneously prepare for multiple security scenarios in different regions of the world. In its defense calculations, Washington considers China its most important long-term rival in the Indo-Pacific region, and in Europe, the possibility of a large-scale conflict with Russia is one of the key scenarios in military planning. Under such circumstances, every missile consumed in one war is part of a stockpile that will no longer be available for a potential crisis in East Asia or Europe.
For this reason, the issue is not simply whether the United States can produce several thousand new missiles. The issue is that the war with Iran showed that America's production and stockpiling capacity is not as flexible as was imagined for a high-intensity, prolonged war.
This is precisely the point at which the cost of the war for America moves beyond the tactical level and becomes a strategic issue.
Over the past decades, Washington has built a large part of its military power on technological superiority, weapons precision, and missile defense systems. But new wars have shown that this superiority faces a serious challenge when one side can place the other side's expensive defensive systems under sustained pressure through the extensive use of missiles and drones.
Under such conditions, an economic equation also takes shape: if a very expensive interceptor missile is consumed to counter a relatively cheap threat, the continuation of the war can quickly deplete the defending side's stockpiles. Therefore, the issue is not only the number of available missiles; the ratio of attack cost to defense cost also becomes important.
From this perspective, the war with Iran has imposed yet another cost on America: the erosion of part of the military capacity that Washington had stockpiled for its larger and longer-term rivalries.
This has occurred at a time when the United States is also facing other problems; from the financial costs of the war to pressure on the defense industry's supply chain, the need to increase weapons production, and the necessity of maintaining the readiness of American forces elsewhere in the world.
In other words, the end of a war does not necessarily mean the end of its costs. The conflict may stop, but rebuilding stockpiles, repairing equipment, replacing weapons, and restoring the military's operational capacity can continue for years.
From this very angle, it can be said that one of the most important consequences of the war with Iran for the United States is the cost that remains on the balance sheet of the country's military power. Washington must now strike a balance between rebuilding consumed stockpiles, increasing production capacity, and maintaining readiness for other potential crises.
This situation becomes more significant when placed alongside the political and military outcome of the war. If the United States, despite possessing one of the largest and most advanced militaries in the world, has not been able to achieve its expected objectives in a costly war, then the massive consumption of stockpiles and the multi-year need to rebuild them is not merely a financial or logistical cost; it could mean a reduction in part of Washington's strategic freedom of action.
In fact, the bill of war for America is not just the money spent or the missiles fired. Part of this bill is the depletion of stockpiles, the erosion of defensive capacity, the pressure on the military industry, and most importantly, the reduction of part of America's ability to enter another major crisis simultaneously.
And perhaps the most important consequence is this: a war that was supposed to showcase American military power may, in the end, confront Washington with a difficult question; if the next major crisis occurs in East Asia or Europe, how quickly can America bring its consumed capacity back to the field?
MNA
