articles.title: Who should be in charge of the war?
articles.body:
Who should be in charge of the war?
This article is based upon my experiences in MOD UK and Army and Joint staff during the first Gulf War, Bosnia and with NATO in Kosovo.
I turned for support to my US defence academic friend and author Dr Thomas Durell Young a former member of staff at the US war college, and a former Policy Director in MOD Bulgaria Retired Colonel Vladimir Milenski. We all worked variously together with MOD Ukraine in 2014 and 2015 and between us on reform in over 15 other countries worldwide.
I apologize in advance to my female military friends for using he throughout this article, but it reflects simplicity of writing before translation not denigration of your amazing contribution to the national war effort.
Introduction: War Does Not Suspend Democratic Defence Governance, it severely tests it
In a democratic state at war, the defence system must be able to fight effectively while remaining politically controlled, legally accountable, strategically coherent and operationally agile.
War increases pressure on institutions, but the defence system must not become insular or a power on its own. War does not remove the need for clear authority, lawful responsibility and public accountability. On the contrary, the greater the stakes, the more important it is to know who governs defence, who advises government, who generates forces, who plans strategy and campaigns, who commands operations, and who answers for results. Today this is not totally clear in Ukraine.
The institutional question is therefore not primarily one of terminology. Different democratic states use different titles for organisations and posts.
What matters is whether these offices form a coherent system in which authority, responsibility, military advice, operational command, force generation, political control and accountability are clearly separated where necessary and integrated where useful – and most importantly society can see who is in charge and responsible for each task.
There is no doubt that to achieve a well–oiled, well–managed system the key requirement is outstanding teamwork. The fastest and best process is always two friends working together with a common purpose. Lack of trust, institutional arrogance, poor teamwork, bureaucracy or unclear tasks lead to delay – and delay kills.
In this regard the Minister and senior commanders, MOD, General Staff (GS) and Joint Staff (JS) must function as a single organism, working closely together not in opposition.
I have been lucky to work in a combined MOD/General Staff in UK with teams of officers and civil servants serving together. Meetings contained staff from all relevant HQs from MOD to units and many key decisions could be made and implemented immediately without need for bureaucracy. The civilian component came with different, less narrow thinking and skills, and added to achieving results hugely. Sharing work openly is vastly better than strict ownership.
In Ukraine, the main headquarters are the MOD and the General Staff (GS) (Most countries would call this HQ, Defence Staff as it is more than just army). We suggest a third strand is needed as Joint Staff, which should manage the fighting. UK and many NATO countries have an operational Joint Staff HQ and US have the regional combatant commands (COCOMS) reflecting their world view. Together, these three HQs would form a leadership triangle with clear and separate tasks. I have worked variously at all three levels. Depending on the issue in need of resolution, one headquarters leads the staff work, while the others support it.
The next day the task and leadership requirement may be totally different. States that inherit command structures from the Soviet military tradition and then introduce institutions associated with modern democratic and NATO ways of defence management are always challenged in who does what, how and when.
The problem is not that one idea, or vocabulary is "Eastern" and another "Western." The problem is that mixed systems often create parallel chains of authority, overlapping staff, unclear responsibility and commanders who are held accountable for outcomes without being given the authority or resources to achieve them. The current Ukrainian Joint Staff is a case in hand. It was given a role on the battlefield for which it was not intended. And in truth, it was never Joint either.
For a democratic state at war in 2026, the central principle should be simple: responsibility must follow authority. No institution or part of an institution should be able to use power without accountability, and no commander should be given responsibility without sufficient authority and resources to complete the task.
The Ministry of Defence: Civilian Authority, Policy, Resources and Accountability
The Ministry of Defence is the civilian political–administrative authority responsible for governing and enabling defence. In a democratic state, MOD is an arm of government and not an operational headquarters. It should not function as a parallel military command. Its legitimacy comes from constitutional authority, ministerial responsibility, parliamentary oversight and the rule of law.
In wartime, the responsibilities of the Minister remain the same, but he must do them faster and with more focus. He not only has to lead the whole defence system but also be a hands–on manager for MOD encouraging the staff to be proactive, supportive, innovative, and fast working. His ministry must also be operational 24/7, ready and able to react to emergencies. And the strong political role of this post is why a civilian, preferably an experienced politician, should always be appointed.
Military ministers may think and understand well the fighting task but are unused to the political and civil signals. They rarely understand the requirements for political briefing, networking and consensus building to get the best overall defence result.
The ministry task is complex. It must translate national political objectives into defence policy and strategic guidance; managing resources, the budget, procurement, mobilisation policy, personnel policy, international assistance, defence industry and sustainment. It must coordinate with government, parliament, other ministries, allies and civil emergency structures; and at the same time ensure legality, transparency, democratic oversight and anti–corruption controls.
The minister must also personally keep the defence committee constantly briefed about problems with any of the above tasks and especially the possible requirements for new or changed laws. Some Ministers in Ukraine have seen working with Parliament as the enemy instead of a vital and fundamental part of the defence system. The failure to pass many vitally needed laws in 12 years of war highlights this mistake exactly.
The ministry must also hold the military leadership accountable for readiness, plans, performance and use of resources. This does not mean political micromanagement of operations. It means that civilian authority as part of government sets objectives, provides means, defines limits, demands professional advice, evaluates performance and accounts to the democratic state. Its role is not to be military but to brief government and parliament, set strategic direction, provide the maximum resources available, oversee performance and carry political–administrative responsibility.
There is no doubt that to achieve a well–oiled, well–managed system the key requirement is outstanding teamwork across the whole system. I learned this well in MOD, but I also learned that we military are poor at arguing and getting our point across. Too often we use emotions and military arrogance to make our point where our civilian colleagues want hard logical arguments and facts. I learnt the hard way with papers and briefs returned covered in red ink and questions like "Why?" and "where is the proof?" spread all over them.
In this regard the Minister and senior commanders, MOD, General Staff (GS) and Joint Staff (JS) must function as a single organism, working closely together not in opposition. To do this, however, they all need common and high–quality briefings from the staff. They usually only know what the staff presents to them; they are not deity. Honesty is everything. Where there is a combined MOD/GS with teams of officers and civil servants working in tandem such as in UK or the Pentagon, most decisions can be made and implemented immediately.
In Ukraine with a separate MOD and General Staff the leadership must constantly look for new processes and better ways to design coordinated and collective team work to get the fastest and most coordinated results. The NATO or Continental Staff system for the military is arguably the best method for this, but it must be used in all its concepts and methods not just a renaming of the old methods. Ukrainian staff still have not grasped the essence of this tool. But this needs another article.
The Chief of Defence / Commander–in–Chief: Strategic Military Leadership and Professional Advice
The Chief of Defence, or Commander–in–Chief (CinC) of the Armed Forces is the senior professional military authority of the state. The title may vary, but the function must be totally clear. This officer is the principal military adviser to the President, government, Minister of Defence and national security bodies, and is responsible for the strategic military leadership of the armed forces as an institution. All three authors agree they have seen more Commanders–in–Chief fail than succeed.
The main reason is failing to grasp that they are not there to run defence like a CEO, and they are not just king of the castle as too many want to be. They must be the expert conduit between society and government, and the military system, ensuring that information and activity flows both ways smoothly and correctly.
The role requires translating political objectives into military strategic options; advising honestly on risk, feasibility, costs and consequences; directing the development of campaign–level plans through the staff system; ensuring jointness and equality across every aspect of the defence system; maintaining morale, readiness, discipline, professional standards and strategic coherence. The list and scope is enormous in its breadth and importance. This is why the Commander–in–Chief should not be the fighting commander. When he takes this role to himself the other key defence tasks that need his time suffer from neglect of proper command attention – and then like the TCC and mobilisation, the whole system degrades.
A further key role for any Commander–in–Chief is to select and provide advice to the President on which officers of all services, not just army, are suitable for high ranks, especially for operational command. Equally, the Commander must advise the President about senior officers who must be moved for failing to achieve results because of lack of ability, staleness or physical tiredness.
Accountability for the Commander–in–Chief flows upward to the civilian leadership through lawful oversight mechanisms like briefing President, Minister and Parliament regularly.
The Commander–in–Chief is responsible for the professional quality of this personal military advice, which means that those below him must also brief him honestly with trust that even when giving bad news they will not be judged or punished for this as has happened too often in the past. He is also responsible for the strategic employment of the armed forces, the integrity of the command system and the readiness and morale of the force.
The Commander–in Chief should be strong enough to lead the military institution through good and bad, but he must always remain subordinate to democratic authority.
The Chief of Staff: Staff Authority, Not Independent Command
The role of Chief of Staff is often the most sensitive in a mixed system. Chief of Staff is subordinate to the Commander–in–Chief and in Ukraine should be the daily manager of the defence system on his behalf by managing the General Staff. He is responsible for staff processes and quality at all levels, planning quality, coordination, staff discipline and ensuring military options developed inside the Joint Staff are fully supported by the system. This officer may be powerful in practice because good staff work shapes strategic decisions, but the authority should be exercised under the Commander–in–Chief and not as an independent command function.
If the Chief of General Staff issues orders, those orders should be staff orders issued under the authority of the Commander–in–Chief not personal command directives. The guiding formula is straightforward: the Chief of General Staff should be powerful as a staff coordinator and the lead manager of the armed forces, but not independent as a commander.
The General Staff: Strategic Staff, The Engine Room of Change and Creating a Stronger Future.
The General Staff, or Defence Staff as named in many contemporary systems, should be understood as the strategic staff that serves the Commander–in–Chief. Its purpose is to convert political direction and strategic military guidance into business plans, force development, mobilisation arrangements, readiness systems, doctrine, training policy, logistic priorities and strategic assessments. With these activities General Staff has a simple three–fold role.
First is supporting the Joint Force Commander with the resources he needs to conduct the fight.
Second is to create new and innovative military resources for the future, and third is to ensure that the whole defence system in the rear is focused upon supporting war as efficiently as possible. This means creating tight processes and effective organisations everywhere with no waste or delays.
Thus, the General Staff is the military brain of the institution and must remain focused upon the future. It should not become a rival command chain and should not be involved in the daily direction of the war or pull tasks to itself that are proper tasks of the subordinate services and agencies like the army or air force.
This distinction is especially important in countries shaped by the Soviet military inheritance. In Soviet–derived systems, the General Staff often accumulated planning, force management, mobilisation, operational direction, intelligence and direct command functions. That model reflected a different political–military logic: centralised control, vertical authority, limited civilian policy capacity, staff–driven command and secrecy over accountability.

The more intense the war becomes, the more damaging these frictions and disfunctions become to the fighting force.
The General Staff should therefore not directly command operational formations and be involved in warfighting. When they are the staff risk being busy with the wrong tasks, slowing decision–making, weakening operational commanders and destroying the clear link between authority and responsibility. They also lose the focus of their own key tasks and create delays that slow the others they deal with.
The Joint Force Commander: Commander of all Current Joint Warfighting Operations
The Joint Force Commander should be the operational commander responsible for the conduct of assigned campaigns and operations. His task is to win the war. This role is essential because modern war is Joint by nature. Every single capability including civil–military cooperation cannot be managed as separate single service efforts. They must all be integrated under an operational commander with real authority over assigned forces.
The Joint Force Commander's responsibilities should include commanding assigned forces in the operational area; planning and executing campaigns and major operations; identifying needed resources for the upcoming operations, integrating service and functional components; allocating operational priorities; synchronizing effects; reporting progress, risk, losses, needs and opportunities; and adapting operations within the strategic guidance received. He must also highlight operational gaps and weaknesses.
The key is that the title must be matched by authority. If every significant tactical or operational decision is controlled by the General Staff or the political center, the appointment becomes hollow and accountability disappears. A Joint Force Commander who is responsible for operational outcomes must have the authority to command assigned forces, set operational priorities and make timely decisions within strategic guidance.
The Joint Force Commander should be accountable to the Commander–in–Chief for his military performance, and through that chain to civilian authority. This accountability should be based on mission, resources, constraints and delegated authority. It should not be reduced to blame after failure or praise after success; it should be continuous discipline of reporting, assessment, adaptation and lawful command.
Joint Staff: The Operational Warfighting Machinery of Joint Integration
The Joint Staff should manage and coordinate the war fighting organization. It should focus on fighting the war through Joint operational and intelligence integration, translating and directing strategy to subordinate formations and then supporting their operations. It is the staff mechanism through which the armed forces integrate all possible capabilities into a coherent and coordinated war fighting system focused on a single warfighting strategy. When a state has both a General Staff and a Joint Staff, the distinction between them must be precise and with no overlap of cause for misunderstanding.
A well–designed Joint Staff enables the Joint Force Commander to plan, coordinate, assess and adjust joint operations on behalf of the country. His staff support operational–level planning both for close, medium and deep operations with a key aim to both focus battlefield effect and to direct resources where the strategic and operational needs demand. The staff prepare orders and directives for joint operations, work closely with MOD and the General Staff on resource requirements, maintain the recognized operational picture, coordinate with allied headquarters and link national military strategy with campaign execution.
There is always a danger that a Joint Staff can become either redundant if the General Staff take too much operational power, or too weak to integrate the services effectively if the legal authorities are not strong enough. Either outcome is deeply harmful for the war effort. Equally if the Joint Staff try to duplicate the General Staff, they add bureaucracy without authority. When the staff lack influence and real authority, joint operations remain dominated by service and agency interests or by improvised ad–hoc coordination. The result is operations that lack focus, coherence and coordination. Operations and ammunition are wasted on activities that do not have the desired cumulative effect of defeating the enemy. The Joint Staff must therefore have a defined role and clear access to the Commander–in–Chief. It is also vital that the Joint Commander and Chief of Staff have common purposes, are like minded with shared experiences, and even better, are good friends.
The Central Democratic Principle: Responsibility Must Follow Authority
The principle that responsibility must follow authority is the normative heart of democratic wartime defence governance. It protects the state from two equally dangerous failures: institutions that exercise power without accountability, and commanders who are blamed for outcomes they were not empowered or resourced to influence.
In such a system, accountability should be distributed as follows:
- Political leadership is accountable for political objectives, war aims, mobilisation of society, alliances, national resilience, and acceptable risk.
- The MOD is accountable for defence policy, resources, institutions, procurement, personnel, sustainment, and oversight.
- The Commander–in–Chief is accountable for professional military advice, strategic military leadership, readiness, and use of the armed forces.
- The General Staff is accountable for the quality of development plans and R&D, assessments, readiness systems, mobilisation, force development, and staff work.
- The Joint Staff is accountable for war fighting, joint integration and operational planning.
- The Joint Force Commander is accountable for the conduct of assigned operations.
- Armed forces (army/navy etc.) are responsible for delivering trained forces ready and equipped for combat
This distribution of accountability does not fragment command; it clarifies it. Political leaders remain responsible for political aims and national risk. Civilian defence authorities remain responsible for policy, resources and oversight. Senior military leaders remain responsible for professional advice, readiness and strategic coherence. Operational commanders remain responsible for the conduct of assigned operations. The system works when each level has enough authority to discharge its responsibility and enough oversight to prevent abuse.
Each principal defence office should therefore have a statutory duty list that answers five questions: what decision or product the office must deliver; by when it must be delivered; to whom it must be submitted; what authority is granted to deliver it; and what evidence will be used to assess compliance. Legal accountability should include periodic reporting to the Minister of Defence, government, President or parliament; written records of military advice and decisions; deadlines for operational assessments and readiness reports; audit trails for resources; and explicit consequences for failure to perform lawful duties.
Conclusion: Clarity Is a Strategic Capability and Battle Winner
For a democratic state at war in 2026, the decisive institutional test is not the number of headquarters, staff or command titles, but the clarity of authority, responsibility and accountability among them. A state may have a Ministry of Defence, a Chief of Defence or Commander–in–Chief, a General Staff, a Joint Staff, a Chief of General Staff and a Joint Force Commander. But unless their roles are clearly distinguished, the result may be duplication and weakness rather than strength.
Ukraine's challenge is especially demanding because it must fight a high–intensity war while transforming inherited command structures. The aim should not be cosmetic adoption of Western terminology, nor rejection of every inherited practice simply because of its origin. The aim should be a genuinely democratic and joint wartime defence system: civilian–led, professionally advised, operationally effective, legally accountable and clear enough that every major decision and action has an identifiable owner.
Institutional clarity is not an administrative luxury. It is a strategic capability. It shortens decision cycles, strengthens trust between civilian and military leaders, improves the use of resources, enables joint operations, reduces politicisation and makes accountability possible. In war, these are not secondary virtues. They are the key conditions for endurance, adaptation and victory.

articles.title: Who should be in charge of the war?
articles.body:
Who should be in charge of the war?

I turned for support to my US defence academic friend and author Dr Thomas Durell Young a former member of staff at the US war college, and a former Policy Director in MOD Bulgaria Retired Colonel Vladimir Milenski. We all worked variously together with MOD Ukraine in 2014 and 2015 and between us on reform in over 15 other countries worldwide.
I apologize in advance to my female military friends for using he throughout this article, but it reflects simplicity of writing before translation not denigration of your amazing contribution to the national war effort.
Introduction: War Does Not Suspend Democratic Defence Governance, it severely tests it
In a democratic state at war, the defence system must be able to fight effectively while remaining politically controlled, legally accountable, strategically coherent and operationally agile.
War increases pressure on institutions, but the defence system must not become insular or a power on its own. War does not remove the need for clear authority, lawful responsibility and public accountability. On the contrary, the greater the stakes, the more important it is to know who governs defence, who advises government, who generates forces, who plans strategy and campaigns, who commands operations, and who answers for results. Today this is not totally clear in Ukraine.
The institutional question is therefore not primarily one of terminology. Different democratic states use different titles for organisations and posts.
What matters is whether these offices form a coherent system in which authority, responsibility, military advice, operational command, force generation, political control and accountability are clearly separated where necessary and integrated where useful – and most importantly society can see who is in charge and responsible for each task.
There is no doubt that to achieve a well–oiled, well–managed system the key requirement is outstanding teamwork. The fastest and best process is always two friends working together with a common purpose. Lack of trust, institutional arrogance, poor teamwork, bureaucracy or unclear tasks lead to delay – and delay kills.
In this regard the Minister and senior commanders, MOD, General Staff (GS) and Joint Staff (JS) must function as a single organism, working closely together not in opposition.
I have been lucky to work in a combined MOD/General Staff in UK with teams of officers and civil servants serving together. Meetings contained staff from all relevant HQs from MOD to units and many key decisions could be made and implemented immediately without need for bureaucracy. The civilian component came with different, less narrow thinking and skills, and added to achieving results hugely. Sharing work openly is vastly better than strict ownership.
In Ukraine, the main headquarters are the MOD and the General Staff (GS) (Most countries would call this HQ, Defence Staff as it is more than just army). We suggest a third strand is needed as Joint Staff, which should manage the fighting. UK and many NATO countries have an operational Joint Staff HQ and US have the regional combatant commands (COCOMS) reflecting their world view. Together, these three HQs would form a leadership triangle with clear and separate tasks. I have worked variously at all three levels. Depending on the issue in need of resolution, one headquarters leads the staff work, while the others support it.
The next day the task and leadership requirement may be totally different. States that inherit command structures from the Soviet military tradition and then introduce institutions associated with modern democratic and NATO ways of defence management are always challenged in who does what, how and when.
The problem is not that one idea, or vocabulary is "Eastern" and another "Western." The problem is that mixed systems often create parallel chains of authority, overlapping staff, unclear responsibility and commanders who are held accountable for outcomes without being given the authority or resources to achieve them. The current Ukrainian Joint Staff is a case in hand. It was given a role on the battlefield for which it was not intended. And in truth, it was never Joint either.
For a democratic state at war in 2026, the central principle should be simple: responsibility must follow authority. No institution or part of an institution should be able to use power without accountability, and no commander should be given responsibility without sufficient authority and resources to complete the task.

Its legitimacy comes from constitutional authority, ministerial responsibility, parliamentary oversight and the rule of law.

He not only has to lead the whole defence system but also be a hands–on manager for MOD encouraging the staff to be proactive, supportive, innovative, and fast working. His ministry must also be operational 24/7, ready and able to react to emergencies. And the strong political role of this post is why a civilian, preferably an experienced politician, should always be appointed.
Military ministers may think and understand well the fighting task but are unused to the political and civil signals. They rarely understand the requirements for political briefing, networking and consensus building to get the best overall defence result.
The ministry task is complex. It must translate national political objectives into defence policy and strategic guidance; managing resources, the budget, procurement, mobilisation policy, personnel policy, international assistance, defence industry and sustainment. It must coordinate with government, parliament, other ministries, allies and civil emergency structures; and at the same time ensure legality, transparency, democratic oversight and anti–corruption controls.
The minister must also personally keep the defence committee constantly briefed about problems with any of the above tasks and especially the possible requirements for new or changed laws. Some Ministers in Ukraine have seen working with Parliament as the enemy instead of a vital and fundamental part of the defence system. The failure to pass many vitally needed laws in 12 years of war highlights this mistake exactly.
The ministry must also hold the military leadership accountable for readiness, plans, performance and use of resources. This does not mean political micromanagement of operations. It means that civilian authority as part of government sets objectives, provides means, defines limits, demands professional advice, evaluates performance and accounts to the democratic state. articles.title: Child among four killed by Ukrainian drone attacks – Russian governor
articles.body:
Child among four killed by Ukrainian drone attacks – Russian governor
Four people, including a child, were killed overnight in Ukrainian drone attacks on the Russian Black Sea port city of Novorossiysk, Krasnodar Region Governor Veniamin Kondratyev has said.
Another 29 people were injured across the city, the official said on Wednesday morning. Three of the victims are in a serious condition, he added.
Novorossiysk is a key hub for Russian maritime trade, which Kiev has been trying to disrupt with regular long-range attacks on ships and port infrastructure.
Kondratyev stressed that only civilian sites were targeted by Ukrainian forces. A church and a kindergarten were damaged, as well as three private homes and five apartment blocks, he reported. Ukrainian strikes also damaged homes in the resort town of Anapa, located some 40 km northwest of Novorossiysk.
Gelendzhik, another resort town in Krasnodar Region to the southeast of Novorossiysk, came under what Mayor Aleksey Bogodistov described as a “most massive and lengthy” drone raid. He did not report any casualties.
Russian air defenses intercepted 596 Ukrainian drones in 12 hours overnight into Wednesday, the Defense Ministry said.
In June, Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky ordered mass attacks on Russian ships, which was part of Kiev’s bid to cause more economic damage. Moscow responded to Zelensky’s “40-day pressure campaign” by ramping up its own long-range strikes, leaving Ukraine effectively cut off from maritime trade.
On Tuesday, Zelensky reiterated his calls for a pause in hostilities in the Black Sea, claiming it would come as a relief for the entire world. Both nations are major exporters of wheat, a key food commodity.
A Türkiye-mediated agreement that ensured free shipping in the Black Sea and provided for inspections of incoming cargo ships to ensure that they were not carrying weapons existed in the early phase of the conflict. Moscow ultimately pulled out of the deal after accusing Kiev of using designated safe routes to launch naval kamikaze drones at Russian ports.

articles.title: US allies lack resources to keep pace on AI, top Pentagon official says
articles.body:
The Pentagon’s top artificial intelligence official said on Tuesday that America’s closest allies lack the resources to keep pace with the US military’s adoption of AI, and that Washington is working to steer them away from mistakes it made along the way.
“They don’t have the resources that we do, they don’t have the experience that we do, they don’t have the scale that we do,” Cameron Stanley, chief digital and artificial intelligence officer at the Department of Defense, said at an event at the Billington Cybersecurity summit. Of Nato and the Five Eyes, an intelligence-sharing partnership of the US, UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, Stanley said Washington was “actively working with a number of our partners” so “they don’t make the same mistakes that we make”.
The comments come less than a year into Stanley’s tenure, during which the Pentagon’s AI office has rolled out several new tools while losing a number of senior staff. Since January, Stanley has overseen the launch of GenAI.mil, an internal chatbot platform he says has reached 1.7 million users, and Agent Network, a system designed to shorten the time between intelligence-gathering and a commander’s decision. The defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has directed Stanley’s office to report AI deployment speed as a monthly metric, part of a wider push to expand military computing power.
Much of Stanley’s appearance focused on speed. He described watching a commander halt a scheduled briefing to take a 30-second phone call and issue an order on the spot, without a formal decision brief or a review of the room’s security clearance level. He called the moment “revolutionary”.
“I know it sounds simplistic,” Stanley explained. “It’s only simplistic because we’re good at it now.”
It’s a term he has used before. Project Maven, the Pentagon’s original AI targeting program launched in 2017, became the Palantir-built Maven Smart System, which the US leaned on heavily during its 2026 air campaign against Iran, helping strike more than 13,000 targets over the first 38 days, according to Stanley at conference in May. Speaking at Palantir’s AIPCon 9 conference in March, Stanley called Maven “revolutionary” too, saying it let commanders go from identifying a target to launching a strike within a single platform.
But the campaign has drawn scrutiny. More than 120 members of the US Congress signed a letter demanding answers from the Pentagon regarding civilian casualties and the use of artificial intelligence, following a 28 February strike on an elementary school in Minab, which Iranian officials say killed at least 168 people, many of them children.
Stanley ended by telling the audience that the department’s old habits were now its biggest liability.
“The way we’ve always done it is the most risky course of action,” he said, adding that the department needed to “think differently” if it wants AI tools in the hands of warfighters faster.

articles.title: New record set: Ukrainian drones strike Russian gas facility over 3,000 km away in Siberia
articles.body:
New record set: Ukrainian drones strike Russian gas facility over 3,000 km away in Siberia
Ukraine's Special Operations Forces (SSO) carried out Kyiv's deepest strike into Russia so far in the full-scale war, attacking a natural gas facility 3,200 kilometers (1,988 miles) from the Ukrainian border on Sept. 9, the military said. 
Ukraine's General Staff announced a successful strike on the Novy Urengoy Gas Condensate Treatment Plant (GCTP) in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug. 
Novy Urengoy is located in northwestern Siberia, over 3,000 kilometers from Ukraine's border. The attack marks the first time Ukrainian forces have struck Russia's Yamalo-Nenets region.
"Until today, this area was considered completely safe territory for the aggressor," the SSO wrote on Telegram.
The GCTP facility processes 19.5 million tons of crude oil and natural gas annually and produces diesel fuel and other petroleum products for Russia's military. The record-breaking strike also targeted the nearby Purovsky Gas Condensate Processing Plant.
Ukrainian weapons manufacturer Fire Point, producer of the Flamingo missile, said that its FP-1 drone model was used to carry out the strike.
Fires and smoke billowing from the plant were visible in footage shot by residents of Novy Urengoy. Monitoring channel Exilenova-Plus posted footage of the facility releasing excess gas through flare stacks to prevent explosions.
The attack was confirmed by Dmitry Artyukhov, governor of the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug.
The strike on the GCTP facility was 600 kilometers (about 372 miles) from a major Russian liquefied national gas (LNG) site: the Yamal LNG project, located on Russia's Arctic Yamal Peninsula.
Yamal LNG is one of the country's largest LNG projects, accounting for over 60% of its total LNG exports — most of which flow to the European Union.
Alexander Kirk, sanctions campaigner at the German environmental and human rights organization Urgewald, said Ukraine's attack should serve as a wake-up call to Europe.
"The war has reached Russia's Arctic gas heartland, close to Yamal LNG, just days before this weekend's European Arctic Summit," Kirk said in a statement.
"The EU needs to get a grip. It should use the upcoming 22nd sanctions package to sanction all 14 Arc7 tankers sustaining Yamal LNG and close the sanctions gap around the European maritime and maintenance services keeping them operational."
Kirk urged EU countries to impose economic penalties against Russian LNG "before potential kinetic sanctions are applied to the Russian gas infrastructure supplying the European market."
The Yamalo-Nenets strikes demonstrate how Ukraine has increasingly extended the range of its unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in a campaign against Russia's energy infrastructure. 
In one of its previous farthest-reaching strikes, Ukrainian forces struck an oil refinery in Omsk, nearly 2,500 kilometers (around 1,550 miles) from Ukraine's border, the General Staff said on July 6. Ukrainian long-range drones also recently targeted oil refineries in Russia's Perm Oblast, located more than 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) from Ukraine, on Sept. 7.
Emphasizing Ukraine's success with long-range UAVs, President Volodymyr Zelensky warned airlines, insurers, and foreign governments that Russian airspace "will be de facto closed" because of Ukrainian drone strikes.

articles.title: Putin’s meeting with Trump envoys convinces Kyiv’s allies war will continue into 2027 – Bloomberg
articles.body:
Putin’s meeting with Trump envoys convinces Kyiv’s allies war will continue into 2027 – Bloomberg
Bloomberg reports this, citing sources, according to Ukrinform.
According to the publication’s sources, U.S. President Donald Trump’s envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff made no significant progress during talks in Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend. Putin showed no willingness to soften his position despite signals from Washington that new ideas were needed to revive negotiations. The Russian president continues to seek control over the Donbas.
One source said Putin used the visit by the U.S. special envoys to project strength at home ahead of the State Duma elections, which will be held September 18–20. He kept the U.S. delegation waiting until evening for a meeting at the Kremlin. Witkoff and Kushner were forced to spend several hours having lunch with Putin’s representative Kirill Dmitriev at an upscale restaurant in central Moscow.
According to the sources, trilateral talks involving representatives of the United States, Russia, and Ukraine could resume after the State Duma elections. However, they are unlikely to bring a peace deal significantly closer.
According to one of the publication’s sources, Russia plans to intensify strikes on Ukraine’s energy and heating infrastructure over the next six months, while also stepping up hybrid attacks and political interference in Europe in an effort to weaken support for Kyiv.
Putin expects Russia to be in a stronger position to end the war next spring while maintaining the stability of an economy facing mounting pressure, one source told Bloomberg. In their view, serious negotiations are unlikely to begin before at least 2027.
For now, Ukraine’s allies should focus on supplying interceptor missiles for air defense systems to help Kyiv protect its infrastructure and population, the sources said. European countries plan to purchase Patriot missiles from the United States to help Ukraine repel an expected intensification of Russian attacks this winter. According to Bloomberg sources, allies are finalizing a mechanism for using NATO funds under the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) to purchase interceptor missiles and subsequently transfer them to Kyiv.
As reported by Ukrinform, U.S. Under Secretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby said at a meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group in the Ramstein format that allies should be prepared for the possibility that Russia’s war against Ukraine will be prolonged, stressing that support for Kyiv, primarily from European partners, is crucial in this situation.

articles.title: The Promise of the Kurdish Peace
articles.body:
August brought some truly transformative good news for Turkey, the Kurds, and Turkey’s immediate neighborhood in the Middle East. On Aug. 10, the Turkish Parliament passed a law establishing a legal framework for the dissolution of the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK), the Kurdish militant group, and creating a phased pathway for reintegration of its members into society.
For more than four decades, the Kurdish issue has run like an electrified barbed wire through conversations in Turkey. The armed conflict between the PKK and the Turkish government has killed around 40,000 militants, soldiers, and civilians, and cost Turkey losses estimated to be around $2 trillion since 1984. Following peace talks, in July 2025, the PKK held a symbolic weapon-burning ceremony, starting a process of disarmament and moving toward ending the armed conflict.
The law offers legal protections to former PKK militants who have not committed specific crimes and helps suspend prison sentences for some members of the group. Thousands of sympathizers, activists affiliated with the PKK, and Kurdish politicians have been living in exile in Europe and elsewhere to escape legal prosecution. The law opens a path for them to return to Turkey. And the passage of this law in the Turkish parliament with broad support is a transformative step toward lasting peace and the creation of a new social contract between Turkey and the Kurds, domestically and regionally.
How to make peace
In the past decade, Turkey established clear military dominance in the fight against the PKK. Changes in military technology, intelligence, and surveillance systems, especially the rise of Turkish drones, strengthened the country’s counter-insurgency efforts. Yet Turkey’s military capacity to suppress an insurgency was not the sole factor in persuading the PKK to give up arms. Turkey did suppress waves of Kurdish rebellions in the past without creating space for Kurdish aspirations, and each suppression was followed by a more formidable and more violent rebellion.
Turkey’s embrace of a political process—instead of simply pursuing a decisive military path—to end the conflict made it more acceptable to the PKK leadership and the Kurdish movement. Abdullah Ocalan, the leader of the PKK, had to persuade his comrades to dissolve their organization, abandon the armed struggle, and choose political struggle. Unfavorable broader regional trends against armed militancy may have helped convince Ocalan and his comrades to make that consequential choice.
The legitimacy of the political solution, in the eyes of the Kurds, determines its sustainability and transformative impact. The current peace process seeks to end the insurgency and transform the struggle for Kurdish rights and aspirations into a nonviolent political one. It could transform Turkey’s relations with its own Kurdish community and the Kurdish communities in Iraq, Syria, and Iran. Leaders of the Kurdish movement believe that they can achieve more through politics than through armed struggle, and that it isn’t only they who are transforming, but that the state, political, and legal systems in Turkey can also change. The promise of the future, rather than being beholden to the grievances of the past, is the way forward.
The Turks and the Kurds managed it without relying on foreign peacemakers or mediation. The disarmament and demobilization process for the PKK was designed, executed, and monitored domestically, without involving any foreign mediators. The talks were held between Turkey’s National Intelligence Organization, Ocalan, and several other leaders of his group based in the Qandil Mountains in Iraqi Kurdistan and across Europe. The process involved the Turkish parliament and political parties through a Parliamentary Committee, formed in Aug. 2025 to work on legal and political dimensions of the PKK’s dissolution, which helped garner broad support for the peace process across political divides in Turkey.
Turkey and the Kurds have entered a new phase that demands greater buy-in for the peace process from politicians, lawmakers, ordinary people, and from the institutions that will implement the new law. To ensure the peace process has broader societal support, the political class will need to make clear why it matters and what it promises. The stakes of getting that right are high for Turkey and extend beyond its borders.
Seeing like a state
The nation-state in the 20th century largely adopted a conception of nationhood based on a single identity and was intolerant, assimilationist, or exclusionary toward other identities. The effect was to politicize and mobilize the very groups it sought to submerge. This was true of Turkey as well. The Turkish Republic was based on a single identity and an overly centralized state with its own insecurities, largely stemming from the traumatic experience during the collapse of the Ottoman Empire.
Today, Turkey needs a new conception of the nation-state that is inclusive of different identity groups, and a new idea of a strong state that is premised on broader societal legitimacy. Centralization coupled with exclusion is a recipe for societal discontent, which weakens, rather than strengthens, the state. Turkey’s real challenge is building an inclusive national identity that recognizes distinct identity groups without losing the thread of what binds them together. The task of the ongoing Kurdish peace process, and the Kurdish politics that will follow it, will be to achieve exactly this: an inclusive notion of national identity capacious enough to accommodate Kurdish identity and aspirations.
The current political mood in the Middle East and elsewhere is not one of militant groups and insurgencies. The broader trend runs toward their integration into state structures or their disarmament and demobilization. How these processes of demobilization and integration are carried out will be highly consequential. If they rely solely on coercion, rather than embracing persuasion and the prospect of mutual transformation, disarmament risks being a prelude to the next cycle of violence, waged under new names and banners.
Demobilization of insurgent groups succeeds when it rests on the prospect of mutual transformation. The armed groups dissolve themselves and remake themselves as political actors, who cease to be adversaries of the state and work as agents of its transformation.
The state and the polity, in turn, must transform alongside them, arriving at a more inclusive conception of national and geopolitical identity. In Turkey, it would mean embracing Kurdishness and honoring Kurdish political, democratic, and cultural rights, and regarding the Kurds outside of Turkey’s borders not as threats but as allies.
The PKK’s demobilization will reshape Turkey’s threat perception, and with it, Turkey’s approach to Kurds in Iraq, Syria, Iran and their countries. Already, in step with the pace of the PKK disarmament, the language used by Turkish officials and Kurdish actors across the region towards each other has improved significantly.
Fruits of peace
Turkey and its neighborhood have already benefited from the peace process and the demobilization of the PKK. That process faced two formidable tests in Syria and Iran and passed both. Turkey treated the PKK’s demobilization at home and the integration of Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF)—led by a Kurdish militia with close ties to the PKK—into the Syrian state as parts of a single process.
After the fall of the Assad regime, reuniting a fractured Syria became one of the most formidable tasks for the new government. The SDF controlled almost a quarter of Syrian territory. Limited fighting and military pressure earlier in the year helped shift the balance, stripping the SDF of a large portion of the land it had held.
What helped make the SDF’s integration into the Syrian state relatively smooth was the peace process already underway in Turkey, given the SDF’s close ties to the PKK. August brought two momentous developments: Turkey’s parliament passed the landmark legislation providing for the disbanding of the PKK, the reintegration of its fighters and the dismissal of charges against thousands of its sympathizers and prisoners; and the SDF announced its own dissolution.
A parallel drama played out during the Iran War. There were fears that the Iranian Kurdish militant group known as the Party for Free Life in Kurdistan, or the PJAK, might join the American war against Iran. Given its close ties to the PKK, such a move could have weakened the PKK’s commitment to disarmament and risked a new phase of conflict among Turkey, the PKK, and the PJAK. Despite pressure from the Trump Administration and Israeli plans to draw them into the conflict, Iranian Kurdish groups stayed out of the war. The peace process in Turkey was a major factor in persuading them to remain on the sidelines.
Together, the Syrian and Iranian cases reveal the power of political imagination and legitimacy in advancing national security. In both instances, Turkey has achieved more through political engagement than through military force. Any national security doctrine devoid of political imagination or legitimacy remains incomplete. The tests posed by Syria and Iran have demonstrated the PKK’s commitment to demobilization, confirmed that its decision is strategic rather than merely tactical, and helped build trust between Turkey and the PKK.
This process will also have considerable implications for Turkey’s relations with major powers. No issue has bedeviled Turkish-American relations more than the Syrian civil war did before the collapse of the Assad regime. At its core, that crisis reflected the conflicting American and Turkish approaches to the Syrian Kurds, specifically the People’s Protection Units (YPG), a PKK affiliate that, with American military advice and support, was later rebranded as the SDF.
By enabling the SDF’s integration into the Syrian state, the PKK’s demobilization has removed the most formidable sticking point in Turkish-American relations, clearing the way for closer cooperation between the two countries in Syria and beyond. Ocalan framed the recently passed Turkish law as the first step of a 1000 kilometer journey. The Turkish model, and the peace it promises, are still a story in the making. Despite the milestones already reached, formidable challenges remain, demanding persistence and commitment.
No two conflicts or two peace processes are alike. Yet the central message is universal: peace is possible and leadership matters. Long-running conflicts around identity are not fates to be endured but political questions to be settled. In a world still defined by war and insecurity, the story of peacemaking is, inherently, a global one.

articles.title: Kremlin reveals new details of Putin-Trump call
articles.body:
Kremlin reveals new details of Putin-Trump call
Washington could help bring the Ukraine conflict to an end sooner by stopping all assistance to Kiev, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov has said, commenting on the latest phone call between Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US counterpart Donald Trump.
The two leaders spoke by phone on Tuesday in the wake of a new round of shuttle diplomacy that saw Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visit Moscow and Kiev over the weekend.
The issue came up as the two presidents discussed ways to reach a settlement of the conflict, Ushakov told journalist Pavel Zarubin on Wednesday. Asked what Washington could do to bring the hostilities to an end sooner, the Kremlin aide said that “first and foremost, [it could] probably stop providing any assistance to Kiev.”
The official acknowledged that US assistance to Ukraine had already “declined significantly” since Trump returned to the White House, compared with the previous administration, when military aid “was provided on a massive scale.”
The two presidents also discussed resuming talks with the Ukrainian side, including in trilateral format that would include the US mediators, Ushakov added.
Trump said he had a “great” conversation with Putin, adding that the Russian president did want “to make a deal.” If Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky “is wanting to make a deal, that’d be very nice,” he told reporters on Wednesday before boarding Air Force One en route to Dallas for the GOP National Convention.
Moscow has repeatedly said it is ready to settle the Ukraine conflict as long as its root causes are addressed and the realities on the ground are taken into account.
Russia’s demands include Ukraine abandoning its plans to join NATO and adopting neutral status, accepting restrictions on its armed forces, and formally recognizing Crimea and four other former Ukrainian regions as Russian territory. Crimea voted to join Russia shortly after the 2014 Western-backed coup in Kiev. Donetsk, Lugansk, Zaporozhye and Kherson regions held similar referendums in September 2022.
Kiev has consistently rejected Moscow’s demands on territorial and security issues, insisting on restoring control over all territories it lays claim to and joining NATO.
Moscow has repeatedly cited Kiev’s aggressive posture, as well as the position of its European backers as major obstacles to a peace settlement.
On Tuesday, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said that the several European leaders calling for a ceasefire were actually seeking to preserve an “openly Russophobic and aggressive neo-Nazi regime” in Kiev, adding that the Russian people would never accept this outcome.

articles.title: Trump predicts Iran war end, says Putin ready for Ukraine deal
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump said Wednesday that the war with Iran could end immediately after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, while signaling possible diplomatic openings on both Tehran and the war in Ukraine.
Speaking to reporters before traveling to Dallas, Texas, for the Republican Party's first midterm convention, Trump claimed Iran was seeking to influence the elections and could not sustain the conflict much longer.
"I think the war will end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer," Trump said.
Asked about the possibility of renewed nuclear negotiations with Tehran, Trump said his administration was not actively pursuing talks but did not rule them out.
"We're not looking for it. Yes, a negotiation could possibly happen, but it's not something we're looking at," he said.
Trump said any potential agreement with Tehran would extend beyond its nuclear program, suggesting other issues would also be included in negotiations.
"There is a lot more than nuclear," he said.
He also said recent U.S. strikes in the Strait of Hormuz had incapacitated about nine Iranian tankers and suggested further military action could follow.
Trump separately struck an optimistic tone on efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war following a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, saying the Russian leader was "wanting to make a deal."
Trump described his conversation with Putin as "good" and said a trilateral meeting involving Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy "could happen."
"If Zelenskyy is wanting to make a deal, that'd be very nice," Trump said.
His comments followed visits to Moscow and Kyiv last weekend by U.S. mediators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, though no significant breakthrough toward ending the war has been announced.
The Kremlin said Putin told Trump that Moscow had no "aggressive plans" toward Europe and provided the U.S. president with an assessment of developments on the battlefield.
Putin also outlined what he believed Washington could do to help bring the fighting to an end, according to Kremlin foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Washington has stepped up mediation efforts since Trump's return to the White House, including a meeting between Trump and Putin in Alaska last year.

articles.title: West Braces for Ukraine War to Stretch Into 2027 as Putin Rejects Peace Push
articles.body:
US and European officials increasingly expect Russia’s war against Ukraine to continue into 2027 after the latest push to restart peace talks with the Kremlin failed to deliver a breakthrough, Bloomberg reported on Tuesday, Sept. 8, citing people familiar with the matter.
US special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow before traveling to Kyiv, but the diplomatic effort failed to produce significant progress, according to the report.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Putin spent three hours with the US envoys at the Kremlin but showed no willingness to soften his position, European officials told Bloomberg. Instead, he is expected to intensify attacks on Ukraine as winter approaches.
Russia is also preparing a new campaign against Ukraine’s energy and heating infrastructure over the next six months, one source told Bloomberg. The goal would be to make life increasingly difficult for civilians while Moscow steps up hybrid attacks across Europe to weaken Western support for Kyiv.
Putin is betting that Russia will enter next spring in a stronger position, the source said, while seeking to keep the country’s increasingly strained economy afloat.
“Serious negotiations” are unlikely before then, according to the source.
Putin uses US envoys to project strength
Another Bloomberg source said Putin used the high-profile visit by Witkoff and Kushner to project strength to a domestic audience ahead of Russia’s September State Duma elections.
How Russia Is Trying to Paralyze Kyiv Without Occupying It
Three-way Russia-Ukraine talks involving the US could take place after the vote, following announcements by Witkoff and the Kremlin. But Bloomberg’s sources said the meeting is unlikely to bring the sides significantly closer to a peace deal.
The diplomatic deadlock is putting renewed pressure on Europe to bolster Ukraine’s air defenses ahead of another winter of Russian attacks.
The UK announced an additional £100 million ($135 million) in military assistance to Ukraine on Tuesday.
Germany is also preparing an urgent transfer of Patriot interceptor missiles from its own stocks, Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said.
“I realize that it is not easy to balance between my own security requirements and the urgently necessary support for Ukraine,” Pistorius said.
Ukraine’s Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said on Tuesday that contracts are being signed with allies for the supply of about 1,000 Patriot missiles using the EU loan.
“I ask you to adopt the necessary financial decisions by November, so we can already see results on the battlefield this winter,” Khmara said according to Interfax-Ukraine, adding that “up to 90% of our success on the battlefield depends on drones.”
The latest warnings come as Kyiv’s allies increasingly prepare for the possibility that diplomacy will not end Russia’s war this year – and that Ukraine will once again face a winter under sustained Russian missile and drone attacks.

articles.title: Moldovan President Sandu condemns Russian drone strike on border crossing point that killed two, injured three
articles.body:
Moldovan President Sandu condemns Russian drone strike on border crossing point that killed 2, injured 3
Moldovan President Maia Sandu condemned an overnight Russian drone strike on the Starokozache international border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, in a Sept. 9 statement on X.
Russia struck the Starokozache border crossing overnight with drones, killing two civilians and injuring three others, Odesa Oblast Governor Oleh Kiper said. Rescuers evacuated another 16 people from a bus, according to Kiper.
Sandu also said that a Russian drone forced Moldova to close its airspace temporarily, warning that the Russian advance in Ukraine is moving further west.
"I urge more air defense support for Ukraine," Sandu said.
Earlier in the day, referring to Russian attacks on the border crossing, among others, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on X that "there has been too little response from the international community to these strikes."
The Southern Regional Directorate of Ukraine's State Border Guard Service announced in a Facebook post on Sept. 9 that border operations had resumed.
"The operation of this border crossing point will help to avoid congestion and traffic build-up on other routes along the border with Moldova. At the same time, security measures for citizens crossing the border will continue to be implemented in response to any (Russian) attempts to attack border infrastructure," the statement reads.
Russia most likely wants to disrupt logistics with its attacks on border crossings, Andriy Demchenko, the spokesman for Ukraine's State Border Guard Service, said during the national telethon, Suspilne reported.
The attack was the fourth one on a border crossing between Moldova and Ukraine, Demchenko added.
A Russian Shahed-type drone strike overnight on Aug. 25 damaged the Vynohradivka border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova in Odesa Oblast, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said at the time.
In a post on X, Sybiha called on the international community to "condemn Russia's systematic targeting of civilian transport corridors and critical border infrastructure."
Moldova's Foreign Ministry reported on Aug. 27 that five drones violated Moldovan airspace on the night prior.
"We have repeatedly warned about the unacceptable risks posed by Russia's war against Ukraine," the ministry wrote.
A suspected Russian Shahed-type drone violated Moldovan and Romanian airspace on Sept. 8, forcing airspace closures, emergency alerts and the scrambling of NATO fighter jets.
The Moldovan military detected an "unmanned aerial vehicle" at 4:20 p.m. local time on Sept. 8, the Moldovan Defense Ministry said in a statement, identifying it as a "Shahed-type" drone that entered the country's airspace from the "direction of … Ukraine."
Spanish F/A-18 fighter jets, deployed as part of a NATO air-policing mission, were scrambled from Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base in Romania as the drone entered Romanian airspace.

articles.title: How the US post-9/11 overreaction built today's illiberal world
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
How the US post-9/11 overreaction built today's illiberal world
There are events that happen within history, and there are events that change its direction. The attacks of 11 September 2001 unquestionably belonged to the latter.
Twenty-five years ago, Al-Qaeda's attacks on New York and Washington killed almost 3,000 people, traumatised the US and produced images that became instantly seared into global consciousness.
But 9/11 was more than an atrocity. It altered the course of an era.
Barely a decade after the collapse of the Soviet Union, the US stood as the world's sole superpower and liberal democracy appeared to have no serious ideological rival. Francis Fukuyama's famous declaration of the "end of history" captured the extraordinary confidence of the age.
Liberal democracy, globalisation and an international system supposedly governed by universal rules appeared not merely ascendant, but inevitable.
Then the planes hit.
A quarter of a century later, that world seems almost unrecognisable. Liberal democracy is in retreat, the far right is ascendant across much of the West, most notably in the US, Russia is waging a war of territorial conquest in Europe, and the international rules supposedly restraining state power appear increasingly conditional.
This week provided another remarkable marker of how far we have travelled. The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won 43.8% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, its greatest electoral result to date, bringing a party once considered beyond the limits of respectable German politics tantalisingly close to governing a German state.
None of this can be solely blamed on 9/11. But nor can the world of 2026 be understood without examining what the US and its allies did in response to it.
The Global War on Terror (GWOT) transformed more than US foreign policy. It changed the relationship between security and liberty and helped normalise the idea that extraordinary threats demanded extraordinary powers.
The Patriot Act vastly expanded surveillance. Guantanamo Bay became a legal black hole in which alleged "enemy combatants" could be detained indefinitely without charge. The CIA abducted suspects and transferred them through an extraordinary rendition programme to states where torture was routine. The invasion of Iraq showed that even the world's leading liberal democracy was willing to bypass the international order it claimed to defend.
The Bush administration was not pursuing an explicitly illiberal project. Quite the opposite: it believed US power could protect and ultimately spread liberal democracy.
But it pursued liberal ends using profoundly illiberal means.
That distinction matters. Donald Trump is not simply George W. Bush with the mask removed, nor did the Patriot Act somehow inevitably produce the AfD. But the GWOT created a political world in which exceptional measures became increasingly normal and showed how easily restraints on state power could be discarded once "security" was invoked.
I have previously called what followed the "procession of illiberalism": ideas and machinery created for the War on Terror being taken up and repurposed by movements with very different, explicitly illiberal goals.
The Western front
Orban's Hungary became perhaps the clearest European example.
During his 16 years in power, Orban openly set about building what he called an "illiberal state". His governments expanded Hungary's counterterrorism apparatus while increasingly depicting Muslim migrants as an existential threat to Hungary and Christian Europe.
The terrorist became the extremist; the extremist became the Muslim migrant; those helping migrants became accomplices; and eventually multiculturalism, LGBT rights, liberal civil society and "globalism" itself were portrayed as threats to the survival of the nation.
Orban may have lost power this year, but the politics he helped pioneer travelled far beyond Hungary.
The AfD's victory in Saxony-Anhalt cannot be reduced to this history. Economic stagnation, anger at Germany's established parties and the particular history of eastern Germany all matter.
But today's European far right operates on political terrain profoundly shaped by the post-9/11 era. Borders become front lines and migration becomes invasion. Muslims are treated as a civilisational danger, while multicultural liberal democracy itself is presented as something weakening the nation from within.
In Trump's US, the process has become almost absurdly literal.
Guantanamo, perhaps the ultimate physical symbol of the GWOT's suspension of normal rules, has been repurposed for the detention of migrants. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), itself created by the Bush administration during the War on Terror, has become the frontline institution of Trump's mass-deportation programme.
The machinery and language built to confront foreign terrorists have turned inwards.
The targets have changed, but the logic is familiar. Identify an existential enemy, strip away normal protections and invoke security to justify extraordinary state power.
The War on Terror never left the Middle East
If the GWOT has turned inward in the West, in the Middle East its original logic never really disappeared.
Israel's genocidal war on Gaza made this explicit. Israeli leaders repeatedly invoked 9/11 and presented the war as part of the same civilisational struggle against terrorism. Benjamin Netanyahu described 7 October as Israel's own 9/11 and compared Israeli military action beyond its borders to what the US did after the attacks.
The comparison is revealing.
Once again, an appalling terrorist attack became the justification for an overriding security imperative. Once again, exceptional violence was presented as necessary because the threat was existential. And once again, international law was treated as secondary to the state's claimed need to destroy its enemy.
The results in Gaza have been catastrophic - the enclave devastated, tens of thousands of Palestinians killed and most of its population displaced, while the US supplied the military and diplomatic support that allows the genocide to continue.
Gaza is not simply another version of the GWOT. But the political logic is recognisable. Terrorism becomes more than a crime or military threat. It becomes a condition under which normal restraints can be suspended - even one under which genocide can be justified in the language of security.
The US-Israeli war on Iran has revived another defining feature of the post-9/11 era, namely the crime of preventive war.
In February, the US and Israel attacked Iran amid under the guise of negotiations over its nuclear programme, wiping out its entire leadership, bombing civilian targets, most deplorably a girls school, and civil infrastructure. The war has since spread across the region, with Iran attacking US bases and neighbouring pro-US Arab states and fighting engulfing the economically vital Strait of Hormuz.
Once again, the language is strikingly familiar - nuclear danger, terrorism, national survival and a threat that cannot be allowed to materialise.
This was one of the central ideas behind the GWOT, namely that waiting for a threat to become imminent could itself be too dangerous.
Twenty-five years after 9/11, the War on Terror has therefore taken two different paths. In the West, its security politics have increasingly been redirected from terrorists towards migrants and other supposed internal enemies. In the Middle East, many of its original assumptions about preventive war, existential threats and exceptional violence remain alive.
When the rules stop being universal
Vladimir Putin shows how the same era also helped weaken the international order from another direction.
Putin initially enthusiastically embraced the GWOT. Russia was already waging a brutal war in Chechnya when 9/11 occurred, and he rapidly recast Moscow's campaign as another front in the global struggle against terrorism. Bush, in turn, described Putin as a partner in that struggle.
But by Putin's 2007 Munich Security Conference speech, Russia was openly attacking the US-led order and accusing Washington of violating international law.
The War on Terror had given Putin both an opportunity and, later, an alibi. Russia borrowed its language of existential security while pointing to Iraq and US exceptionalism as proof that the liberal international order was hypocritical.
That does not mean Iraq justifies Russia's invasion of Ukraine. It does mean the US weakened the very principles needed to condemn such aggression consistently.
Gaza has deepened that crisis further. When Western governments invoke sovereignty, international law and civilian protection in Ukraine while giving Israel the means to devastate Gaza, the damage goes beyond charges of hypocrisy.
If the rules depend on who is breaking them and against whom, they stop being universal rules at all.
Before 9/11, the US emerged from the Cold War claiming to lead a liberal world order grounded, however imperfectly, in international law, human rights and democratic government.
The GWOT did not destroy that order. It fractured it.
Its deeper tragedy is that the Bush administration believed US power could be used not simply to defeat terrorism, but to preserve and spread liberal democracy. Torture, rendition, indefinite detention and illegal war were justified by supposedly liberal ends.
Twenty-five years later, even the ends have changed.
The ascendant illiberals of our age do not promise to improve the liberal order. They promise to replace it: universalism with ethno-nationalism, international law with raw sovereign power, multiculturalism with civilisational identity, and the restraints of liberal democracy with the permanent demands of "security".
Nor is this solely the work of those who openly seek liberalism's destruction. As during the GWOT, the rise of illiberalism has also been made easier by governments that defend international law selectively, tolerate its violation by allies and then wonder why appeals to the "rules-based order" carry less and less weight.
Modern illiberalism would almost certainly have emerged without 9/11. But the response to those attacks hastened its rise, furnished it with powerful political tools and helped knock the world off its liberal democratic axis.
Perhaps the most enduring legacy of 9/11 and the War on Terror is therefore neither Afghanistan nor Iraq, but the spread of its central proposition: when the threat is grave enough, the rules no longer apply.
Twenty-five years after the towers fell, the state of exception has escaped the emergency that created it.
The enemies have multiplied, the exceptions are becoming the rule, and the world that once proclaimed the inevitable triumph of liberal democracy increasingly resembles an age of monsters.
Sam Hamad is a writer and History PhD student at the University of Glasgow, focusing on totalitarian ideologies.

articles.title: Rutte warns delays in Ukraine aid cost lives
articles.body:
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has urged allies to accelerate military support for Ukraine, warning that delays in delivering weapons and funding are costing lives.
Speaking at the latest Ukraine Defence Contact Group meeting, Rutte said Ukraine’s war against Russia was directly affecting the wider security environment across NATO and called on countries to increase their contributions.
Rutte said: “Ukraine’s fight shapes the entire Euro-Atlantic security environment. It directly impacts, as we all know, our own security, and as we work on modernising the alliance and building a stronger Europe and a stronger NATO, we must continue to support Ukraine’s security and help them defend from Russia’s brutal attacks.”
He added: “That means supporting Ukraine with the utmost urgency. And here, let me say that delays simply cost human lives.”
Rutte said the level of civilian deaths had reached its highest point since May 2022 and told members of the group that more military assistance was required. He said: “Nations must dig deeper. We do not have a choice, I believe.”
The NATO Secretary General identified air defence, drones and extended-range ammunition as priority requirements for Ukrainian forces. Rutte also said allies were seeing changes in the weapons employed by Russia, including greater use of North Korean missiles and jet-powered attack drones.
He stressed the continuing role of the PURL mechanism, under which NATO allies and partners finance the purchase of American weapons for Ukraine. According to Rutte, around $10 billion had been allocated over the previous year through PURL and US foreign military sales for Ukraine, including $3.5 billion originating from the Ukraine support loan.
He described those figures as evidence of European countries taking on a greater share of the effort to sustain Ukraine. Rutte said continued deliveries were particularly important for maintaining Ukrainian air defences and enabling forces to hold positions on the front line.

articles.title: Ukraine hits Russian naval base in Novorossiysk – videos
articles.body:
Ukraine hits Russian naval base in Novorossiysk – videos
Robert "Magyar" Brovdi, Commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces (USF), has confirmed a strike on the naval base in Novorossiysk in Russia's Krasnodar Krai on the night of 8-9 September.
Source: Brovdi on social media
Quote: "The Novorossiysk naval base has lost a number of military vessels, including missile carriers, as a result of a combined strike by Ukraine's defence forces and the USF on the night of 8-9 September."
Details: Overnight, the USF also destroyed an Su-33 carrier-based fighter jet, an Mi-8 helicopter and two radar systems in the Gelendzhik area near the Russian city of Anapa.
Brovdi noted that the average number of Russian personnel killed per day has increased so far in September compared to August, reaching 411 personnel per day, up from 355 in August.
In total, between 1 and 8 September, the USF had wiped out 3,395 Russian troops and struck 16,720 Russian assets.
Background:
- On the night of 8-9 September, monitoring Telegram channels reported that drones had attacked the city of Novorossiysk, causing a fire to break out at a fuel oil terminal.
- The mayor of Novorossiysk confirmed that a fire had broken out but claimed that it was caused by drone debris that had landed at the site. He did not name the facility that was attacked or provide information about the extent of the damage or any casualties.
- According to OSINT analysts, the strike had hit facilities at the port complex, damaging at least one storage tank at the fuel oil terminal.
- Novorossiysk Fuel Oil Terminal is one of the main facilities in the Novorossiysk transport hub, which forms part of the Novorossiysk Commercial Sea Port, Russia's largest seaport in terms of cargo throughput.
