articles.title: “I will continue to work just as productively”: former intelligence chief Budanov shrugs off third Russian arrest order as an acknowledgment of his effectiveness
articles.body:
Russia has arrested Ukraine's presidential chief of staff in absentia for a third time, and he is treating it as a compliment. Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Office of the President and the former military intelligence chief, calls the Moscow court's ruling a "masterpiece of absurdity" and a sign his work is landing, writing on Telegram that such Russian decisions mean nothing to him.
Budanov ran Ukraine's military intelligence through the war's boldest operations on Russian soil before taking over Zelenskyy's office in January. The charges Moscow has stacked against him track the strikes the Kremlin blames on him. A Russian ruling carries no force outside Russia, where Budanov is already on the country's list of terrorists and extremists. What it marks is how central a target he remains three and a half years into the war.
Moscow charges him over warfare methods
A Moscow court has ordered the in-absentia arrest and accused Budanov of using prohibited methods of warfare, according to Russian state media. Budanov has answered with contempt.
"The decisions of the so-called Russian 'court' have no significance for me, nor for the rest of humanity," he states.
He adds that the only thing that matters for him is his work, which "forces the enemy to panic and issue such masterpieces of absurdity." He framed the case as proof that he is on the right track.
"I consider such actions by the enemy a kind of acknowledgment of my effectiveness. I cannot lower the bar. I will continue to work just as productively," he says.
The arrests track his intelligence record
Each Russian case has followed one of the operations Moscow attributes to Ukrainian intelligence. In April 2023, the Lefortovo court arrested Budanov over alleged terrorism and put him on an international wanted list, after Russia's FSB named him as an organizer of the Crimean Bridge blast, as per Suspilne.
Late that year, the Basmanny court arrested him a second time over more than 100 drone strikes on Russian territory. This week's ruling is the third.

articles.title: Germany pledges more missiles and shells for Ukraine
articles.body:
Germany will transfer additional Patriot and AIM-9 missiles from Bundeswehr stocks to Ukraine while financing tens of thousands of long-range artillery rounds, Defence Minister Boris Pistorius has announced.
Speaking at the opening of the latest Ukraine Defence Contact Group meeting, Pistorius said Berlin would urgently provide PAC-2 Patriot interceptor missiles and called on other countries to examine whether they could release weapons from their own inventories ahead of the winter.
Pistorius acknowledged the tension between maintaining national reserves and supplying Ukraine, but told participants: “I am aware that it is not easy to strike a balance between one’s own security requirements and urgently needed support to Ukraine. But please, if in doubt, decide in favor for Ukraine.”
Germany will also increase deliveries of AIM-9 air-to-air missiles from Bundeswehr stocks, with Pistorius saying the weapons were already being supplied to Ukraine. The additional missiles form part of a wider effort to strengthen Ukrainian air defences before temperatures fall, with the German minister warning that Russian attacks against power stations, ports and other infrastructure could increase during the winter.
Germany is also continuing deliveries of IRIS-T air defence systems and missiles. Pistorius said Ukraine was preparing to order several thousand additional IRIS-T guided missiles using funding from the EU-Ukraine Defence Loan.
According to Pistorius, the size of that procurement will allow industry to expand production by establishing another missile production line. He said the order represented an example of how support for Ukraine could also increase European defence manufacturing capacity, allowing production to serve both Ukrainian requirements and wider European rearmament.
Pistorius also referred to the City Dome project, through which Germany is supporting the establishment of additional defences for Ukrainian cities against missile and drone attacks. Beyond air defence, Germany will finance several tens of thousands of long-range artillery rounds for Ukraine. The ammunition will be procured through the British Artillery and Air Defence Consortium before being transferred to Ukrainian forces.
Pistorius thanked UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and his team for helping arrange the procurement, describing it as an example of cooperation between countries participating in the Ukraine Defence Contact Group.
Germany will also continue deliveries of drones and long-range ammunition as part of its support for Ukrainian forces operating on the front. The commitments were announced as members of the contact group focused heavily on preparing Ukraine for another winter of Russian air attacks, with air defence missiles identified by Kyiv as its most immediate requirement.

articles.title: Drones attack fuel oil terminal in Novorossiysk, sparking fire
articles.body:
Drones attack fuel oil terminal in Novorossiysk, sparking fire
Drones attacked the Russian city of Novorossiysk in Krasnodar Krai on the night of 8-9 September, causing a fire at a fuel oil terminal.
Source: Russian media outlet Astra; Novorossiysk Mayor Andrei Kravchenko; monitoring Telegram channels
Details: Around midnight, residents of Novorossiysk reported hearing drones flying overhead, Russian air defence systems responding and explosions. Videos of a fire near the city's port infrastructure appeared online shortly afterwards.
Kravchenko confirmed that a fire had broken out but claimed that it was caused by drone debris that had landed at the site. He did not name the facility that was attacked or provide information about the extent of the damage or any casualties.
Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) analysis by ASTRA has established that the fire broke out at the Novorossiysk Fuel Oil Terminal.
According to Dnipro Osint, the strike had hit facilities at the port complex, damaging at least one storage tank at the fuel oil terminal.
Novorossiysk Fuel Oil Terminal is one of the main facilities in the Novorossiysk transport hub, which forms part of the Novorossiysk Commercial Sea Port, Russia's largest seaport in terms of cargo throughput. It handles the storage and transshipment of fuel oil and light petroleum products, with a throughput capacity of approximately 4 million tonnes per year.
Background:
- The Monitoring Group of the Black Sea Strategic Studies Institute previously reported that in July, systematic Ukrainian Armed Forces and Security Service of Ukraine attacks on Russian infrastructure and tankers in the Black and Azov seas reduced Russia's oil product shipments by 45.6% compared with June.
- On 12 August, Russia's two largest grain terminals in the southern port of Novorossiysk suspended operations following Ukrainian drone strikes.
- During the first 20 days of August, exports of Russian crude oil from Black Sea ports fell by a factor of 3.2 to around 1.7 million tonnes, compared with 5.5 million tonnes in July.
- According to Reuters, Russia suspended crude oil exports from the Sheskharis terminal at the port of Novorossiysk following a drone attack.
- In addition, Mediterranean Shipping Company (MSC), the world's largest container shipping company, has cancelled all new bookings for cargo bound for Novorossiysk because of the risks to shipping.

articles.title: UN nuclear watchdog board reports Iran to Security Council for first time in 20 years
articles.body:
UN nuclear watchdog board reports Iran to Security Council for first time in 20 years
The agency says Iran failed to cooperate in a long-running investigation into uranium traces detected by inspectors at undeclared sites
The UN atomic watchdog’s board on Wednesday reported Iran to the UN Security Council for the first time in 20 years, citing it for failure to cooperate in a long-running investigation into uranium traces detected by inspectors at undeclared sites.
Western officials suspect that the traces could provide evidence that Iran had a secret nuclear weapons programme until 2003. Iran says that it is not pursuing nuclear weapons and that its programme is entirely peaceful.
Reporting Iran to the Security Council opens the country to possible sanctions and asset freezes, though such punitive measures are unlikely because Iran’s allies Russia and China hold veto power on the panel.
Twenty-three countries on the International Atomic Energy Agency ’s 35-member board of governors voted for Wednesday’s resolution at IAEA headquarters in Vienna.
China, Russia and Niger opposed it, while eight countries abstained and one did not vote as it was in arrears, according to diplomats who spoke on condition of anonymity to describe the outcome of the closed-door vote.
The resolution was put forward by the US, Britain, France and Germany.

articles.title: Ukrainian Intelligence Hacks Corporation Linked to Oreshnik System Development
articles.body:
Cyber specialists from Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence have hacked the information systems of the Russian Moscow Institute of Thermal Technology (MITT).
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence reported the results of the operation.
The data obtained includes information about the institute’s structure, management, and employees, as well as its current and prospective developments.
At the institute’s facilities in Moscow and other regions of Russia, engineers develop designs, software, engines and other components for missile weapons. They also conduct mathematical modeling and testing of control-system components.
The institute’s enterprises are involved in work on:
Another area of the Moscow Institute of Thermal Technology’s work is developing and improving satellite communications systems for the Russian military.
One key project is the Start-1M launch vehicle. If implemented, it will allow Russia to deploy low-Earth-orbit satellite networks.
The institute is also developing the Tiporyad unified space platform. It is intended to strengthen the Russian military’s intelligence, communications and command capabilities and increase the resilience of its space infrastructure.
During the operation, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence obtained the personal data of 2,648 institute employees whom Ukrainian intelligence considers to be involved in producing weapons used against Ukraine.
The individuals identified include Reserve Lieutenant General Sergei Ponomaryov, the institute’s CEO, as well as his deputies.
Moscow Vympel Machine-Building Plant, which, according to OSINT Varta, manufactures, tests, and services equipment for technical and launch systems used in rocket and space technology. This includes cable systems, gas supply systems, lighting equipment, shock absorption systems, and systems for maintaining temperature and humidity conditions.
Prozhektor State Design Bureau, which develops signaling equipment and control and power supply systems for civilian and military airfields. The enterprise has also participated in developing autonomous power supply systems for mobile complexes operated by Russia’s missile forces and air defense forces and carries out state defense orders.
Iskra Research and Production Association develops and manufactures solid-fuel rocket motors, nozzle assemblies and composite components for Russian missile systems. The enterprise supplies engines and other components for the Topol-M, Yars, Bulava, Oniks, and Yakhont missiles and also participates in fulfilling Russia’s state defense order.

articles.title: Poland secures further $4bn financing from US to buy American military equipment
articles.body:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Poland has signed an agreement for a further $4 billion (14.8 billion zloty) from the United States Foreign Military Financing (FMF) programme, which provides grants and loans to fund the purchase of American military equipment.
Defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz called the development a “great honour”, because FMF is “granted only to the best allies”. The agreement is not only “another important step in the modernisation of the Polish armed forces” but also “strengthens the strategic partnership between Poland and the US”.
The US embassy in Warsaw likewise hailed the agreement as “reaffirming the strength of the US-Poland partnership as we work together to strengthen NATO, deter aggression, and support peace and security in Europe”.
.@UnderSecT took part in the signing of a $4 billion Foreign Military Financing (FMF) loan guarantee—an important step in U.S.-Polish security cooperation. Poland’s significant investments in its defense capabilities and the U.S. defense industrial base reflect our shared… pic.twitter.com/Dz3huAp8pj
— US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) September 9, 2026
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has embarked on an unprecedented military procurement spree, with its defence budget rising to the highest relative level in NATO.
Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was also the largest importer of arms in NATO. Around 44% of those purchases came from the US, including Abrams tanks, Patriot air defence batteries, and HIMARS rocket artillery.
The new agreement marks the sixth time Poland has received funds through FMF, for a total of almost $20 billion. Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the latest financing would be used to “accelerate the implementation of existing contracts, including for Apache helicopters”.
In 2024, Poland signed a $10 billion deal to buy 96 AH-64E Apache attack helicopters, along with a logistics and training package and a stockpile of ammunition and spare parts. It will make Poland the second-largest operator of Apaches in the world, after only the US itself.
Thomas DiNanno, the US under secretary of state for arms control and international security, said that the new agreement “signifies our commitment to assistance, but also Poland’s commitment to ensuring security, building defence capabilities, and ensuring the security of NATO’s eastern flank”.
“Poland is not only a trusted partner; it is not only an ally on the front line; it is a model ally of the United States,” he added, repeating recent remarks by US defence secretary Pete Hegseth.
The terms of the financing have not been revealed, but Marta Postuła, vice president of Poland’s national development bank, BGK, through which the funds will be channelled, said it was “on more favourable terms than the last two [FMF] loan guarantee agreements”.
This, she added, was “due to the subsidisation of a portion of the financing costs through a grant awarded for this purpose by the US government”.
💬 Obecna umowa została zawarta na korzystniejszych warunkach niż dwie poprzednie umowy z gwarancjami pożyczkowymi dzięki subsydiowaniu części kosztów finansowania w ramach grantu przyznanego w tym celu przez Rząd USA. To kolejny wyraz bardzo bliskiej, transatlantyckiej… pic.twitter.com/Ipd4cYDeFo
— Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego 🇵🇱 (@BGK_pl) September 9, 2026
The issue of who Poland should buy military equipment from, and how such purchases should be funded, has become embroiled in domestic political disputes this year.
President Karol Nawrocki and the right-wing opposition with which he is aligned have criticised the government for signing Poland up to the EU’s SAFE programme, which is providing €43.7 billion (188.7 billion zloty) in loans for defence and security spending.
They argue that provisions requiring most of the money to be spent within Europe itself could damage Poland’s relations with the US and South Korea, who have in recent years been the main sources of military procurement.
However, speaking today, Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the new loan agreement with the US shows that SAFE and FMF “do not compete with one another; they complement one another”.

Łącznie w ramach amerykańskiego programu Foreign Military Financing pozyskaliśmy już blisko 20… pic.twitter.com/hhzXcE1hoC
— Magdalena Sobkowiak (@magdasobkowiak) September 9, 2026
While Nawrocki is a close ally of President Donald Trump, who endorsed him ahead of last year’s Polish presidential elections, the more liberal government, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, has at times clashed with Washington.
In May this year, the sudden and unexpected cancellation of the rotational deployment of almost 4,000 US troops to Poland raised concern in Warsaw.
Shortly afterwards, Trump declared that he would deploy 5,000 additional troops to Poland. However, since then, no clear details of that plan have been announced, although Poland has formally submitted a request for the US to establish a new permanent US military base on its territory.
On Wednesday morning, Polish deputy defence minister Paweł Bejda told broadcaster TVP that an American delegation was in Poland this week to visit potential locations for the base and discuss the issue further.

articles.title: German foreign minister proposes sharing data on military-age Ukrainian men living in Germany with Kyiv
articles.body:
German foreign minister proposes sharing data on military-age Ukrainian men living in Germany with Kyiv
Ukrainian men of military age living in Germany should return to Ukraine, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said in an interview with a podcast published by the German newspaper Bild.
Wadephul said the German government could help Kyiv track them down. “We know who lives here, who receives welfare payments, for example, who is registered here, who has residency status,” he said.
Ukraine’s government could use that data to notify men of military age that they must report for service, he said. “I think this can be discussed, and that it needs to be discussed,” the German foreign minister added.
Berlin also wants Ukraine to place more defense orders with German defense companies.
“We are Ukraine’s biggest supporter in terms of financial and military assistance. And naturally, the German defense industry should benefit from that. […] At the moment we are not entirely satisfied with the volume of orders being placed in Germany. So we have now asked the Ukrainian government to look into this and ensure the situation improves,” Wadephul said.
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius announced a day earlier that Germany would send Ukraine part of its own stockpile of PAC-2 interceptor missiles for American-made Patriot air defense systems. “I am aware that it is not easy to strike a balance between one’s own security requirements and urgently needed support for Ukraine. But please: if in doubt, decide in favor of Ukraine,” he said.

articles.title: Europe is playing a dangerous game with Russia
articles.body:
Europe is playing a dangerous game with Russia
History doesn’t repeat itself, not even as farce, and thus the latest chapter in the centuries-long confrontation between Russia and Europe will look different from those that came before it.
Today, the German authorities are closing Russian cultural and diplomatic institutions on flimsy pretexts and Norway is seizing Russian research vessels – and while the methods are new, the underlying impulse is familiar. Europe has sought to constrain Russia’s independence since at least the late 15th century.
For now, however, European governments aren’t seeking direct military confrontation, but this should not be mistaken for pacifism in Berlin, Brussels, Paris, or London – nor should we take seriously their ritual declarations about dialogue and a new regional security architecture, given there are more practical reasons for their restraint.
First, Western Europe’s largest states lack the human and material resources for a war with Russia, and although their position is somewhat better when it comes to weapons, much of that capacity is already being directed toward Ukraine, whose population is being asked to make enormous sacrifices in pursuit of European objectives.
However, the European people show little appetite for these sacrifices, mainly because living standards haven’t deteriorated nearly enough to persuade ordinary Germans, Italians, French, and British people to march into a conflict with Russia. Nor should anyone place much faith in Poland or the rest of Eastern Europe because Warsaw’s increasingly belligerent rhetoric disguises a much weaker willingness to actually fight.
Second, the Europeans understand that their American patrons have no desire to become embroiled in a potentially fatal confrontation with Moscow. The supposed American nuclear umbrella over Europe has always contained an element of mythology, and the region’s leaders understood this even during the Cold War.
France’s development of an independent nuclear deterrent was itself an acknowledgement that Europe could not assume that the US would risk its own destruction on their behalf. Charles de Gaulle and his successors didn’t build this arsenal because they were confident of American guarantees.
Nobody in Europe, therefore, seriously believes that Russia can be easily defeated in a war, because if they did, the temptation to attempt it would be much greater.
Yet these rational calculations run up against a more subjective danger, and we shouldn’t overestimate the European elite’s instinct for self-preservation.
Unlike Russia or China, Western Europe has experienced no comparable replacement of its ruling elites over the past 150 years, meaning today’s political establishments are, in an important sense, descendants of those that led Europe into the First and Second World Wars.
Western European politicians, particularly German and British, have historically displayed a tendency towards adventurism. Indeed, George Kennan, an astute observer of political cultures, drew a revealing contrast in his 1946 Long Telegram where Russian foreign policy, he wrote, “is neither schematic nor adventurist” and “doesn’t take unnecessary risks,” but the same cannot always be said of Europe.
The US, for all its willingness to use military force, generally prefers overwhelming odds, which is why its habit is to attack when it is confident that the opponent can’t inflict unacceptable damage in return. This makes the Americans, in a certain sense, more predictable and therefore more amenable to diplomacy. Even at the height of American unipolar power, Washington harbored few illusions about what a direct war with Russia would entail.
Europe has a more troubling historical record and its powers have repeatedly created dangerous situations that ultimately escaped their control, with World War II as the supreme example. Napoleon’s invasion of Russia and Germany’s invasion more than a century later were also enormous gambles, courses of action that appeared reckless even to many contemporaries.
For the moment, Europe is conducting its struggle against Russia primarily through indirect means because it lacks the resources for something more ambitious and retains enough sound judgment to recognize the dangers of escalation – but it would be reckless for Moscow to assume this restraint will last forever.
With every new stage of confrontation, European governments are burning bridges that might have otherwise supported a more balanced system of coexistence. Seen in this context, Russia’s decision to close the Goethe Institutes isn’t merely a symmetrical response to German measures, but also makes sense in the long term.
Whether we like it or not, cultural and humanitarian cooperation has increasingly become an instrument of state policy, though exceptions remain. Russian and French museum professionals, for example, continue to work together on some projects, as do academics and cultural figures in other fields, but these relationships have become increasingly subordinate to the logic of soft power.
Even seemingly innocuous forms of international cooperation are now expected to serve national objectives, and this is regrettable – but it reflects the expansion of modern foreign policy far beyond traditional diplomacy. Governments can use funding and institutions to influence almost every sphere of international contact.
Russia isn’t entirely different in this respect. We too often judge educational and cultural cooperation by its political consequences, and governments and the public naturally ask why money should be spent on international projects if they produce no discernible benefit for the country that funds them.
But in Western countries, these demands are particularly pronounced, so institutions such as the Goethe-Institut cannot realistically be separated from Germany’s broader foreign-policy objectives, and German officials inevitably expect publicly supported cultural organizations to influence attitudes towards Germany and advance the country’s interests.
The result is paradoxical: The political burden placed upon cultural institutions eventually undermines the very value of the relationships they were created to foster.
Perhaps the erosion of these old forms of cooperation is therefore unavoidable and it may even prove necessary if future cultural and academic contacts are to become less dependent on the political climate in European capitals.
For now, however, Russia faces a more immediate problem, in which European leaders remain afraid of direct confrontation, yet their own decisions are steadily pulling them deeper into a spiral of confrontation.
Their caution is real, but history gives Russia little reason to assume that caution will always prevail over adventurism – and that requires vigilance from Moscow and the resolve to act accordingly.
This article was first published by Vzglyad.ru, translated and edited by the RT team.

articles.title: FSB opens treason case against Ruslan Sidiki, who is already serving 29 years for attacks on Russian military airfield and railway bombing
articles.body:
The Ryazan region branch of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) has opened a new criminal case against Russian and Italian dual-citizen Ruslan Sidiki, who was sentenced in May 2025 to 29 years in prison for an attack on the Dyagilevo military airfield near the city of Ryazan, blowing up railway tracks, and preparing another act of sabotage.
The rights project Ogni Svobody (lit. “Fires of Freedom”) reported that Sidiki is now also being accused of treason. According to information obtained by The Insider, investigators accuse him of passing information to Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, carrying out sabotage in Kyiv’s interests, and transferring money through the cryptocurrency exchange Binance to support Ukraine’s armed forces. However, Sidiki’s alleged cooperation with Ukrainian military intelligence had already featured in his 2025 conviction, meaning some of the same alleged conduct that the FSB is now classifying as treason was already used to justify the 29-year sentence he is already serving.
In July 2023, Sidiki organized a drone attack on the Dyagilevo military airfield. Then, in November of that year, he blew up railway tracks in the Ryazan Region, derailing 19 cars of a freight train. He was also convicted of preparing another attack on the railway, though Sidiki denied involvement in that episode.
In May 2025, a court sentenced him to 29 years in prison. He is to serve the first nine years in a prison, a stricter form of incarceration under the Russian penal system, and the remaining 20 years in a high-security penal colony. On July 1, 2026, the Military Court of Appeal upheld the sentence.
After the judgment took effect, Sidiki was supposed to be transferred to prison. However, he is currently being held at Ryazan’s SIZO-1 pretrial detention center, where he was transferred in August from SIZO-2 in Ryazhsk. Ogni Svobody said the transfer to prison has now been delayed because of the new criminal case.
Under Russian law, treason can be punished by up to life imprisonment.
Sidiki holds both Russian and Italian citizenship. Franco Fausto Salamena, an assistant to the Italian consul in Russia, was in attendance during closing arguments and the announcement of Sidiki’s verdict in May 2025. Sidiki’s defense had also sought access for representatives of the Italian consulate.
After his arrest in November 2023, Sidiki said security officers tortured him in order to force a confession. He said he was beaten, subjected to electric shocks using a field telephone and a stun gun, suspended by his handcuffed arms, and threatened with sexualized violence.
When he was placed in a temporary detention facility (and later a pretrial detention center), medical staff documented numerous wounds, abrasions, hematomas, and bruises.
Russia’s Investigative Committee repeatedly refused to open a criminal case into the torture allegations. However, those decisions were later overturned by prosecutors and by senior officials in the regional branch of the Investigative Committee, and as of April 2026, an additional review of Sidiki’s allegations was still underway.
Sidiki’s lawyer, Igor Popovsky, had pushed for an investigation into the alleged torture. He obtained medical records documenting his client’s injuries, challenged the Investigative Committee’s refusals to open a case, and argued that Sidiki should be treated as a prisoner of war due to the fact that, according to the prosecution’s own version of events, he had acted in the interests of Ukrainian military intelligence.
In May 2026, Popovsky was detained by the Russian authorities on suspicion of large-scale fraud.
Sidiki acknowledged carrying out the attack on the airfield and the railway bombing but disputed prosecutors’ classification of the acts as terrorism. He argued that the targets were military aircraft and railway infrastructure used for military logistics, rather than civilians, and that his aim was not to intimidate the population.
Sidiki also said he had been in contact with representatives of Ukrainian intelligence, but maintained that he chose the specific targets and methods of attack himself.

articles.title: Pakistan warns Iran to rein in Houthis amid Yemen conflict
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Pakistan warns Iran to rein in Houthis amid renewed Yemen conflict
Pakistan has delivered a Saudi warning to Iran to rein in its Yemeni Houthi allies after they stepped up attacks on the kingdom, in a coordinated effort to prevent the crisis from spiralling, Saudi, Pakistani and Iranian sources said.
The Houthis struck an airbase in Khamis Mushait and oil infrastructure in nearby cities on Tuesday, wounding 73 people, in one of the biggest attacks on Saudi Arabia since the start of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran in February.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Wednesday that Saudi warplanes carried out 54 airstrikes across various Yemeni provinces over the past 12 hours, adding that they would "not go unanswered and unpunished".
The escalating conflict, which represents a second theatre of war threatening global energy supplies, comes as Iran and the United States wage their biggest declared wave of tit-for-tat attacks on shipping in the Gulf region since their war began.
Pakistan's warning to Iran carries significant weight because of its recently signed Mecca Defence Agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkey.
While officials in Islamabad stressed any military role would be confined to defending Saudi territory, Pakistani Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said attacks spilling into the kingdom could trigger a joint security arrangement involving Riyadh, Ankara and Islamabad.
"An aggression on one country will be considered an aggression on all three countries," Asif said on Pakistani TV.
"There is no ambiguity or doubt... Unprovoked aggression or spillover... into Saudi Arabia will definitely make this agreement operational."
The Pakistani defence ministry, foreign ministry and the military did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.
Fears of regional conflict
Pakistan’s intervention, after years of balancing ties with Saudi Arabia and Iran, has underscored the seriousness of the Houthi attacks. The message to Tehran is clear: rein in the Houthis or risk turning a proxy conflict into a broader regional security crisis, the sources said.
A senior regional diplomat said Pakistan had conveyed the message to Iran over the past 24 hours, urging Tehran to use its influence to halt Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
A senior Iranian official confirmed that Pakistan conveyed the message to Tehran on Tuesday and Tehran's response was that "Iran does not control the Houthis".
However, two Iranian sources said Tehran had told the Houthis last week to carry out attacks on Saudi Arabia. Tehran promised additional funding and weapons, they said, while several Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commanders had travelled to Yemen to help coordinate the attacks.
The regional diplomat said Islamabad was seeking to restrain the Houthis before the escalation reached a point where Riyadh could press Pakistan to play a more active role in defending it.
"Pakistan has an agreement with Saudi Arabia, but I am hopeful the situation will not reach the point where Pakistan has to practically step in," the diplomat told Reuters. "It will pursue a diplomatic solution for now."
Pakistani support for Saudis
The Pakistani source said Saudi officials had met senior Pakistani and Turkish military representatives in Riyadh to coordinate their response. The three countries agreed that their troops would not enter Yemen and that any response would be launched from Saudi territory, the source added.
A second Pakistani source said no decision had been made to join retaliatory strikes, stressing that its military pact with Riyadh was defensive and limited to protecting Saudi territory. Pakistani forces could provide military, technical, ground or air support within Saudi Arabia, but would not take part in combat operations on foreign soil, the source said.
The pressure campaign waged by Iran and the Houthis could have the opposite effect to that intended by Tehran, the regional diplomat said.
By targeting Gulf security in a bid to pressure Washington over its blockade of Iranian ports, Tehran risks driving Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkey and other U.S.-aligned states into closer security coordination rather than fracturing their ties.
Trump's blockade of Iran set to continue
Regional officials also see little sign that Washington is prepared to relent.
President Donald Trump appears committed to maintaining the US.blockade until Iran reaches an agreement with Washington, the diplomat said, while Qatar is quietly exploring new proposals aimed at bringing both sides back to negotiations.
Another regional source said Saudi Arabia's military response would remain focused on the Houthis rather than Iran itself. Nor do Saudi officials believe Houthi attacks will achieve Tehran's broader objective of ending the U.S. blockade.
Riyadh is not expected to press Washington to lift the blockade, that source said, stressing that Trump believes sustained economic coercion is the most effective pathway to negotiations.
"The question is how much pain Iran can absorb, and for how long," the source said. "Trump does not want a military solution. He wants to squeeze them through the blockade."

articles.title: Will it kill off humanity? Computer scientists and politicians wrestle with risks of AI
articles.body:
Does artificial superintelligence really pose a risk greater than nuclear weapons? Is there a significant chance of “a Chornobyl-sized catastrophe”. Might there even be a greater than 10% chance that AI could “kill all humans” in the next decade?
These warnings were issued over the past 48 hours on both sides of the Atlantic about the potential impact of a technology that most people still think of as a more talkative search engine.
Some of the threats were raised in the UK as MPs and peers began to wrestle with the danger of AI outperforming human capabilities. The nuclear warnings came from Des Browne, a former defence secretary, and Prof Stuart Russell, an eminent Berkeley computer scientist.
Beatrice Fihn, who won the 2017 Nobel peace prize for leading the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons, told parliamentarians: “It is not the first time we’re confronted with abilities that could end up killing us all.”
The session on Monday was convened by Control AI, a lobbying group pushing for international regulation of the technology. It is backing a bill tabled in parliament this week by the Labour MP Alex Sobel and aimed at banning the creation of artificial superintelligence (ASI).
On Tuesday night, a senior employee at Anthropic admitted he believed there was a greater than 10% chance the technology could “kill all humans” in the next decade and warned that his AI company did not have a plan to ensure ASI was aligned, meaning it did no harm. Predictions for when ASI might be reached vary from several years to more than a decade.
Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead at Anthropic, posted the comment after Jacob Coxon, a 28-year-old researcher at the San Francisco company and previously at OpenAI, resigned, claiming “neither company was acting responsibly”. He said they were “gambling with our lives”.
Coxon said the risks at Anthropic were well understood but they were “locked in a race to get there first”. In a glimmer of hope, he added that he was optimistic about the potential for coordination between US labs on pacing their progress in the race.
Anthropic has been approached for comment on the issue. OpenAI pointed to a statement from its chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, who said last week: “International coordination on future AI development needs to become a top priority for governments around the world.”
The push for wider coordination to control ASI was at the heart of events at Westminster this week. According to the Financial Times, government officials voiced concern that Anthropic had declined to submit its latest model – Mythos 5.1 – to the UK’s AI Security Institute for pre-release testing.
Only a few US organisations have had access to Mythos 5.1, the Cabinet Office confirmed. A spokesperson added: “The AI Security Institute continues to collaborate closely with industry partners, including Anthropic.”
The Labour MP Darren Jones has written to the prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the heads of the UN and the OECD calling for a “multinational treaty for the regulated and safe development of superintelligence – not a ban on innovation or scientific endeavour but a safety-first approach to the rapid development of this technology”.
Citing Coxon’s resignation, Jones added: “The debate ranges from the end of humanity to claims of ‘marketing hype’. Either way, governments must now step in.”
On the other side of the Atlantic, Bernie Sanders ratcheted up his AI safety campaign this week by again calling on Congress to regulate the technology. He pointed to polling suggesting that 81% of Americans believed their politicians should take action.
The independent senator for Vermont said: “We can’t allow a handful of greedy people to play God and determine the future of humanity – our economy, environment, democracy, privacy and more – without public input.”
ControlAI is funded by Jaan Tallinn, the multi-billionaire founder of Skype who calls himself an “anti-extinctionist”. He has dedicated part of his fortune to campaigning for AI safety and says some senior AI executives would be happy for humanity to be wiped out.
Despite being an early investor in Anthropic and Google DeepMind, two of the leading AI labs, Tallinn estimates that 10-15% of AI employees believe the technology will be a worthy successor to humanity.
He said in an interview earlier this summer: “A fairly known AI researcher said to me ‘Jaan, don’t worry about this. Humans are a disposable species’. From what I understand he was fine with becoming extinct.”
Tallinn’s lobby group ran the session for MPs and peers at Westminster on Monday and urged them to back measures to curb the most powerful AI models. On every chair was a copy of the book, If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: The Case Against Superintelligent AI.
The politicians heard from Russell, who made the Chornobyl warning and said: “The other possibility is a much larger catastrophe, in which humanity loses control irreversibly. But we have no say over whether we continue to exist.”
Browne said that when he was defence secretary he thought nuclear war was the most likely threat facing humanity. Now he believed “a superintelligent AI poses a threat on the same, possibly, a greater scale”.
Other contributors were more cautious. Dr Andrew Rogoyski, of the Surrey Institute for People-Centred AI, said: “In reality, these systems are nowhere near as versatile as humans, let alone humans acting collectively. I suspect we’re heading towards ‘the great disappointment’ where advanced AI turns out to be too expensive and not useful enough to continue in its current form.”
David Barber, director of Sofair, a state-backed AI research lab combining academics from Oxford, Cambridge, Edinburgh and UCL, said he was worried about people “throwing the baby out with the bathwater”.
“AI is not going to go away,” he said. “It’s incredibly useful, whether or not you allow it in a fully unconstrained way to access the internet and various systems that’s potentially problematic. We may need to learn how to better control these things. There are vulnerabilities in the software frameworks that need to be patched. But that’s doable.
“What we need as a country is to get to grips with the duality that is both an incredibly important and useful technology, and at the same time, it’s something that needs to be carefully thought about and carefully controlled.”
Sandra Wachter, a professor at the Oxford Internet Institute, said she did not believe in “Terminator scenarios” but that AI posed real threats including its environmental impact, spreading of misinformation and replacing jobs.
“These problems are real and urgent and need addressing now,” she said. “Terminator scenarios are a big distraction from real issues.”
Gary Marcus, an AI industry commentator and academic, said: “There is a difference between superintelligence that is aligned (if such a thing is possible) and superintelligence that is not.
“It is at least conceivable that the former might be net positive. So far we have neither, but a superabundance of hype combined with a striking lack of prudence on OpenAI’s part has gotten us where we are, with intense mistrust all around.”

articles.title: Russian drone strike hits Ukrainian checkpoint on border with Moldova, killing two
articles.body:
Russian drone strike hits Ukrainian checkpoint on border with Moldova, killing two
Russian drones struck border infrastructure in Ukraine’s Odesa region, according to the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine. The strike hit the international vehicle checkpoint in Starokozache, on the border with Moldova.
According to preliminary data, the attack killed two people and injured three others, the Odesa regional military administration reported. Operations at the border crossing have been suspended.
The Russian Defense Ministry confirmed the strike, saying the checkpoint had been used “to deliver military cargo into Ukraine.”
The day before, Moldova’s Defense Ministry reported that a drone had entered the country’s airspace from Ukraine, prompting authorities to close it to flights. The drone later headed toward Romania, prompting local authorities to scramble two F-18 fighter jets.
The drone later returned to Moldovan airspace and came down in the country. No casualties were reported.

articles.title: Vietnam’s Communist Leader Meets With Putin in Kremlin
articles.body:
Russia and Vietnam signed a framework agreement Wednesday to cooperate on establishing a strategic oil reserve in Vietnam, as the two countries moved to deepen energy ties during President To Lam’s visit to Moscow.
Following talks with To Lam, President Vladimir Putin also said Russia was working to introduce visa-free entry for Vietnamese citizens “in the near future,” though he gave no timetable.
Vietnam’s Deputy Foreign Minister Le Thi Thu Hang previously said Hanoi expected a “breakthrough” in Russian-Vietnamese oil, gas and nuclear power cooperation.
To Lam, who last visited Moscow in May 2025 to attend the Victory Day parade on Red Square and sign a strategic partnership agreement with Russia, held a joint press briefing with Putin after talks between Vietnamese and Russian officials.
In addition, Putin and To Lam presided over the formal launch of a joint infectious disease research laboratory via video link.
During his three-day state visit to Moscow, which began Monday, To Lam has so far met with Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin, Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev and upper-house Federation Council Speaker Valentina Matvienko.
To Lam also met with Russian Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov, Russian war veterans and members of the Vietnamese diaspora at the embassy in Moscow, where he emphasized Vietnam’s transition toward diversified international integration.
Russia remains Vietnam’s top arms supplier and is involved in nuclear power and South China Sea gas projects, including in waters also claimed by China, though Hanoi has been diversifying its military sourcing.
Reuters contributed reporting.

articles.title: Russian drone attack kills two at Ukraine-Moldova border crossing
articles.body:
At least eight people killed in Russian attacks across Ukraine
Death toll in Russia’s Novorossiysk rises to four, including a child, after Ukrainian attacks on naval base.
At least eight people have been killed in Russia’s attacks on Ukraine, including along the Ukraine-Moldova border and in the southeast, according to regional officials.
Two civilians were killed and three others were injured overnight when Russian drones hit the Starokozache border crossing with Moldova, in the southern Odesa region, Governor Oleh Kiper said on Wednesday. The attack caused a fire and briefly halted crossing operations, which Ukraine’s customs agency confirmed had resumed by mid-afternoon.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Iran and Ukraine wars: Why ship fuel is running short, and why it matters
- list 2 of 4Witkoff says peace talks have been ‘very meaningful’ in Ukraine
- list 3 of 4US envoys hold ‘substantive’ talks with Zelenskyy in first visit to Kyiv
- list 4 of 4Will Trump succeed in restarting Russia-Ukraine peace talks?
In the southern port city of Kherson, two civilians – a 73-year-old man and a 55-year-old woman – were killed in separate Russian drone attacks on Wednesday morning, the regional prosecutor’s office said, adding that a war crimes investigation was opened.
Two separate Russian drone attacks killed a 34-year-old man and injured a 52-year-old woman in the town of Kushuhum in the Zaporizhia region, according to Ivan Fedorov, a regional defence council co-chair.
An early-morning Russian assault on the southern city of Mykolaiv killed one person and wounded five others, Ukraine’s emergency services agency said, adding that homes, cafes, shops and warehouses were damaged and a large fire broke out at one site.
In the eastern Donetsk region, regional military administration head Vadym Filashkin said on Wednesday that an aerial bomb struck the city of Sloviansk, killing one person, wounding another and destroying a home, while five further bombs hit near the city of Kramatorsk, wounding eight people and damaging 27 homes in the village of Bilenke.
The Russian Defence Ministry said its forces had struck a Ukrainian cargo vessel, carrying military equipment, in the Black Sea, en route to the port of Odesa, as well as a warehouse in Kyiv, allegedly belonging to a company manufacturing drones, Russian news agencies reported.
Moscow resumed its near-constant air attacks on Kyiv on Tuesday after a brief halt during a visit by US peace negotiators. Officials said five people were killed in the capital.
Meanwhile, Russian forces shot down 596 Ukrainian drones during the night, the Defence Ministry said Wednesday.
In Russia, Ukranian attacks killed four people, including a child, in Novorossiysk in the southern Krasnodar region. Another 29 were injured, three of them seriously, Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said on Telegram.
Mayor Andrei Kravchenko said drone debris fell on several businesses and close to a residential building in Novorossiysk late on Tuesday.
Ukrainian authorities confirmed attacks in the area, saying that military vessels at a naval base in Novorossiysk were hit overnight, the commander of Ukraine’s drone forces, Robert Brovdi, said.
Brovdi said missile carriers were among the vessels “lost” at the base, but did not say how many vessels had been struck.
Novorossiysk, a frequent target of Ukrainian drone attacks, is a key outlet for Russian oil, oil products and grain exports, among other commodities.

articles.title: Ai-Petri’s maker began building EW gear after Russia took Crimea in 2014. It’s now shown system, named for peninsula’s highest peak, at Polish expo
articles.body:
Ukraine has shown its Ai-Petri, an electronic-warfare system that jams drones and can even disrupt Russian glide bombs at Poland's MSPO 2026 expo. It was named after the highest peak in occupied Crimea, a representative of its maker, Storkway, told the outlet Oboronka. The company began developing electronic-warfare gear in 2014, the year Russia annexed Crimea.
Ai-Petri takes on two of its hardest jobs at once. It jams the control links that strike and reconnaissance drones need to fly and see, and it can interfere with the guided glide bombs, or KABs, that Russia drops on Ukrainian positions from a distance.
The company says roughly 400 are already deployed along the line of contact. The scale matters as much as the specifications, because coverage is what turns a jammer into a shield.
Ai-Petri jams drones and glide bombs
Ai-Petri's tactical versions have gone to the front since 2024, working with the 12th Special Purpose Center, the representative said.
The system can scan a full 360 degrees and detect targets 20 to 30 kilometers out, depending on terrain, across radio bands from 300 to 6,000 megahertz.
A pickup carries the whole system
Ai-Petri comes in fixed and mobile forms. The mobile one is carried on a pickup and set up by two crew in about 10 minutes.
It is built around a rotating platform of jamming modules, each with two channels, plus a detection antenna and a radar that listens for the radio signatures of approaching drones. In detection mode, it draws 250 watts, with jamming a target pushing that to 2,000.
The maker patches it like an antivirus
The pitch is adaptability, the company's representative said.
"If Russia invents a virus, we immediately make an antivirus," the Storkway representative said, describing how feedback from troops informs new jamming profiles that are quickly built to counter each new Russian system.
The company wrote its own software for Ai-Petri around a situational-awareness tool called Lira, which pulls in data from other radars to build a single picture for spotting and countering aerial threats.

articles.title: “We found the key to the Russians”: Ex-Defense Minister Fedorov returns from the US, planning Ukraine’s largest venture fund for defense tech and war think tank
articles.body:
Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov has returned to Kyiv after a trip to the US and shared the results of his meetings. He announced plans to establish a major venture fund for Defense Tech in Ukraine and launch a think tank to help forecast how the war will evolve.
As defense minister, Fedorov drove Ukraine's shift toward drones, robotics, and data in warfare. His firing in July set off the rare wartime protests that reshaped the military's top command.
The fund targets military startups
The fund will be based in Kyiv and invest in defense technology, Fedorov said, backing not only new military startups but established companies that can scale their systems. He credited contacts built around the US firm Palantir, a tech giant whose clients include the CIA, FBI, Pentagon, and the US military, with helping him raise the resources.
In 2023–2024, Palantir signed memorandums of understanding with Ukraine’s Ministry of Digital Transformation, Ministry of Education and Science, and Ministry of Economy.
"I've published information about Palantir, and we managed to attract resources that will let us create in Ukraine, in Kyiv, the largest venture fund in the defense-tech direction," Fedorov said.
The company’s products are already helping Ukraine in wartime in areas including security, education, reconstruction, and demining.
He did not disclose the fund's name, its size, or a firm launch date.
A center would forecast Russia's moves
The second project is an analytical center meant to study the war rather than react to it. Its task, Fedorov said, would be to map Russian weaknesses and anticipate Moscow's next steps.
"Over the last seven or eight months, we found the key to the Russians: how to find their vulnerabilities, how to strike and seize the initiative in the sky and on the ground," he said.
Fedorov argued that Ukraine should forecast the war's next moves and prepare solutions in advance rather than only respond.

articles.title: Oil terminal ablaze and four dead in Novorossiysk, two dead at Moldova border crossing in Ukraine as Moscow and Kyiv exchange drone strikes
articles.body:
Russia and Ukraine exchanged large-scale drone strikes overnight into Sept. 9. In the Russian Black Sea city of Novorossiysk, a Ukrainian attack killed four people, including a child, and injured 29 others, according to local authorities. In Ukraine, Russian drones struck several targets, including a border crossing with Moldova, where two people were killed.
Krasnodar governor Veniamin Kondratyev reported that three of the 29 injured in the strike on Novorossiysk were in serious condition. Three private homes and five apartment buildings were damaged, along with an Orthodox church and a kindergarten.
In Anapa, falling drone debris damaged three more private homes and a kindergarten. No injuries were reported there. Damage from the attack was also recorded in the Krymsk and Temryuk districts.
Several industrial sites in Novorossiysk caught fire during the attack. The independent outlet Astra used footage posted by witnesses to geolocate the blaze to the grounds of the Novorossiysk fuel oil terminal. The facility is part of the Novorossiysk transport hub and handles the transshipment of petroleum products.
Satellite data from NASA’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) also showed a fire in the area of the Novorossiysk fuel oil terminal. According to its map, heat signatures were recorded near the terminal between 2:05 a.m. and 3:45 a.m. Moscow time on Sept. 9, with the strongest readings at 3:45 a.m.
The fire radiative power (FRP) in the terminal area reached between 25 and 27 megawatts, a level consistent with a noticeable fire, though FIRMS data alone cannot establish exactly what was burning or the size of the blaze. The system records heat anomalies, while the location of the readings near the fuel oil terminal provides additional support for Astra’s geolocation of the fire.
Robert “Magyar” Brovdi, commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, later confirmed that Ukrainian forces had carried out a coordinated strike overnight on the Russian naval base in Novorossiysk. He claimed that several military vessels, including missile-carrying ships, were damaged or destroyed.
Brovdi also said Ukrainian drones destroyed a Su-33 carrier-based fighter jet, a Mi-8 helicopter, and two radar systems in the city of Anapa. According to him, the radars were a Kasta-2E2 system and a 92N6 radar used with S-300 and S-400 air defense systems in the Gelendzhik area.

articles.title: Russia is switching its cheap Molniya strike drones to digital video. When the change is complete, Ukraine’s analog detectors go blind, Flash warns
articles.body:
Russia is fitting its cheap Molniya strike drones with digital video, a quiet upgrade that threatens to blind the detectors Ukrainian troops rely on to spot drones coming. Digital transmission is turning up on more and more Molniyas and will eventually replace analog altogether, making today's portable detectors useless against them, President Zelenskyy's defense-technology adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov told UNIAN.
Front-line soldiers depend on cheap detectors that pick up a drone's analog video signal, buying the seconds of warning that let them take cover. Digital video is invisible to that gear.
The Molniya is the drone Ukraine can least afford to lose track of, a $300 plywood aircraft that Russia already churns out in numbers and keeps re-engineering to slip past detection. Beskrestnov's point is that Ukraine has to answer the change before the switch is complete, not after.
Digital video slips past the detectors
"Digital video transmission is increasingly found on Molniyas," Beskrestnov said, urging Ukraine to prepare for a future in which its current gear is useless against them.
The fix, he continued, is to build digital-video detection into interception systems now, before the switch is complete. Such a system would not show what the drone sees, but it would flag the signal and point to its source.
"We will not see the image, but we will see the presence and determine the bearing, warning the user of the threat," he explained.
A $300 drone keeps outrunning detection
The Molniya is among the cheapest weapons Russia fields: an aircraft-shaped kamikaze drone built from plywood, foam, and off-the-shelf Chinese electronics, making it easy to mass-produce and upgrade. Russia launches up to 10 of them a day in the Zaporizhzhia direction alone.
It has already moved its Molniyas onto video frequencies of 4.1 to 4.5 gigahertz that most detectors barely register, and has begun fielding an autonomous, AI-guided version that flies with no radio link for a detector to catch at all.
Ukraine is racing to close the gap
Ukraine has lagged on this exact tool. It only fielded its first portable, mass-produced drone detector in July, while Russian soldiers had long carried a Chinese-made device that identifies drone types.
Each fix Ukraine builds risks being overtaken by the next cheap change Russia bolts onto a drone that costs less than a smartphone.

articles.title: Yemen's Houthis report dozens of new Saudi airstrikes
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Yemen's Houthis report dozens of new Saudi airstrikes as conflict exacerbates
Yemen's Houthi rebels reported dozens of Saudi airstrikes on Wednesday as daily attacks continued in a conflict that has reignited during the Middle East war, with hundreds of people killed in fighting near the Red Sea.
More than 50 attacks targeted several regions including Taiz and Hodeida, the scene of fierce clashes between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed internationally recognised government, the Houthis said.
"It's a catastrophe, and the attacks are ongoing," said Mohammed Khudairi, one of nearly 20,000 people who fled the fighting, according to the International Organization for Migration.
"We managed to leave, but others remain trapped there," he said at a displacement camp of wood-and-straw huts near Khokha, on the Red Sea coast.
The latest salvos in Yemen's previously dormant conflict come a day after the Iran-backed Houthis set oil sites ablaze and wounded 73 in their heaviest missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia in years.
The Houthis' Al-Masirah TV Channel reported on Wednesday the toll from Saudi strikes on a prison days earlier had climbed to 32 dead and seven injured as rescue and recovery efforts continued.
The fighting comes against the backdrop of the Middle East war, which erupted in late February with US-Israeli strikes on Iran.
Over 500 killed; Hodeida in Saudi crosshairs
The fighting in Yemen has killed more than 500 people since the Houthis launched a major offensive last week to seize territory around the Bab al-Mandeb strait, gateway to the Red Sea shipping route.
The Houthis have also been attacking Saudi oil tankers, and are trying to tighten their squeeze on the shipments, analysts say -- a lifeline for exports after Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
"During the past 12 hours, the Saudi enemy's air force conducted 54 airstrikes targeting the provinces of Al-Jawf, Marib, Taiz, Hodeida and Saada," said Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree.
Footage released by the Iran-backed group showed what it said were attacks on Saudi-backed forces on Al-Jawf province's frontlines, with missiles heard flying overhead before impact, followed by flaming wreckage.
There was no official comment from Saudi Arabia.
Analysis by the Institute for the Study of War said the city of Hodeida, held by the Houthis, could be the "ultimate objective" of the Saudi backed forces.
The Red Sea port is "critical to both Houthi civilian and military goods, and its loss would be a significant setback for the Houthis", a report published by the institute said.
Saudi warnings
Saudi civil defence issued warnings twice for the southern governorate of Khamis Mushait, near Yemen, and once for Abha city, but quickly lifted the alerts without elaborating on the cause.
On Tuesday, Saudi authorities vowed to respond to the Houthi attacks, saying they caused fires and temporary shutdowns at oil sites.
The Houthis triggered the return to hostilities in July, when they let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace.
Yemen's internationally recognised government, which controls Aden and the south of the country, retaliated by striking the airport, an attack the Houthis blamed on its sponsor, Saudi Arabia.
The ongoing exchanges risk returning Yemen to a conflict that left hundreds of thousands of people dead and sparked one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
The Houthis, after seizing Yemen's capital Sanaaand forcing out the internationally recognised government, fought a Saudi-led coalition from 2015 until a United Nations-brokered ceasefire in 2022.

articles.title: Drones Strike Fuel Oil Terminal at Novorossiysk Port
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones struck a fuel oil terminal at the port of Novorossiysk in Russia’s Krasnodar Krai overnight on September 9.
GEOINT analysis from Militarnyi confirmed the strike, as did photos and videos published by monitoring channels.
The attack caused a fire at the terminal.
Around midnight, residents of Novorossiysk began reporting the sound of drones flying overhead, Russian air defense systems operating, and explosions.
Later, videos of a fire near the port infrastructure began appearing on Telegram channels.
Russian local authorities warned of a Ukrainian drone attack, and a missile threat was also declared in the region.
Novorossiysk Mayor Andrey Kravchenko later confirmed reports of strikes on industrial facilities, saying they were caused by “falling debris.”
NASA FIRMS satellites detected several fire hotspots in Novorossiysk following an overnight drone attack.
According to available information, a fire broke out at the Novorossiysk fuel oil terminal, where at least one storage tank was damaged.
The Novorossiysk fuel oil terminal is part of the Novorossiysk transport hub and operates within the Novorossiysk commercial seaport.
The terminal specializes in storing and handling fuel oil and light petroleum products, with an annual capacity of around 4 million tonnes.
Overnight on September 7, Ukrainian drones struck Russian Mi-35 and Mi-8 helicopters at Taganrog-Central military airbase in the Rostov region.

articles.title: Seven of my colleagues were killed in Gaza. There and in Ukraine, aid workers are no longer safe | José Andrés
articles.body:
In times of war, the hard and vital work of supplying food, water and medicine has been protected by international agreements for almost 80 years. Yet those protections have been systematically and repeatedly ignored in the two most bloody wars of recent years: Ukraine and Gaza.
Russia has attacked healthcare targets in Ukraine more than 3,200 times since the full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to the World Health Organization: about twice a day on average. That includes many “double-tap” attacks on the same target in quick succession, which are especially lethal for first responders.
In April, the UN security council heard that in the past three years, at least 1,010 humanitarian workers had died in 21 countries. More than half of those were in Gaza and the West Bank. That is three times more than the 377 killed in the previous three years.
“This is not an accidental escalation,” said Tom Fletcher, the UN’s undersecretary-general for humanitarian affairs. “It is the collapse of protection.” This collapse of protection has led directly to the airstrikes on aid workers in Gaza, including seven of my own World Central Kitchen (WCK) team, who were killed by the IDF in April 2024 despite full cooperation and coordination with the military.
At the time, the IDF concluded that the attacks had been “a grave mistake” and a breach of its own standard operating procedures. It stated: “We consider the vital humanitarian activity of international aid organizations to be of utmost importance, and we will continue to work to coordinate and assist their activities, while ensuring their safety and safeguarding their lives.” The reserve colonel who ordered the strikes, Nochi Mendel, was dismissed for his actions.
However, these fine words were undercut by the IDF itself, when its military prosecutor decided last month not to open a criminal investigation into the airstrikes on our convoy. Now we understand, because of a Guardian investigation, that the targeting of the WCK convoy was the result of a military tactic of guilt by association. It means that lethal force can be triggered by suspicions, shadows, or simply prejudice. This undefined, unjustified and unlawful tactic is a mortal threat to all humanitarians. What are the protections under these conditions?
It is worth remembering why the fourth Geneva convention was created in 1949 and embraced by the world, with the express intention of protecting civilians in war and meeting basic humanitarian needs. In the immediate aftermath of the second world war, the scale of civilian suffering shocked the world’s conscience. Indeed, one of the key architects of the convention was Georges Cahen-Salvador, a French Jewish civil servant, whose family was imprisoned at the Drancy internment camp. They were being deported to Auschwitz in 1943 when they managed to escape to Switzerland. He was one of several survivors who drafted the fourth convention.
The convention’s assertions of shared values in war are not lost today, but they are struggling to survive.
David Ben-Gurion, Israel’s founding father, famously said: “The fate of Israel depends on two things: its strength and its righteousness.” It’s something that Israel’s military leaders like to quote, but their record falls far short. Humanitarian values are the foundation of righteousness; they are what separate responsible nation states from terrorist groups or rogue states who don’t care about civilian suffering. The protection of aid workers allows the world to ensure that civilians are cared for.
We might be numb to the sight of Russia disregarding our values. But we surely cannot tolerate the only democracy in the Middle East behaving the same way.
- 
  José Andrés is the founder of the food aid charity World Central Kitchen, and a Michelin-starred chef
-

articles.title: What Did US Envoys Achieve in Moscow and Kyiv?
articles.body:
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and with Ukrainian President Volodomyr Zelensky in Kyiv on the weekend to discuss how to end the war between the two countries. Afterwards, Witkoff called on both sides to make compromises. Zelensky said that security and economic guarantees for Ukraine had been discussed. Moscow described the talks as “extremely frank” and “constructive”.
Washington has embarassed itself again
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The visit to Moscow on Saturday was a diplomatic faux pas, rants journalist Edward Lucas (Lithuania) in Delfi:
“We should have been shocked by US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff’s repugnant fawning over Putin. And also by the fact that Witkoff and his equally unimpressive sidekick, Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, travelled in a convoy of Russian government vehicles and relied on an interpreter from the Kremlin during the Moscow meeting. Unfortunately, repugnant rhetoric and actions from Washington seem to have become the norm. ... Much like the US president’s daily tirades on social media, unpleasant episodes only shock us until they are overshadowed by the next alarming piece of news.”
Time is on Putin’s side
Journalist and former deputy minister for infrastructure Mustafa Nayyem (Ukraine) analyses the situation on Facebook:
“Donald Trump has made his ability to bring wars to a swift end an integral part of his political image. Furthermore, the political calendar is piling on the pressure: the mid-term elections are just around the corner and the presidential election campaign begins about a year from now. ... The more urgently Washington needs results, the more sense it makes for Moscow to play for time, continue the war and wait for the next offer. This is why I would focus less on the number of visits by Witkoff and instead ask what has changed in Putin’s calculations after each of these visits. Right now the answer seems to be pretty clear: nothing.”
Abramovich Loses Third Bid to Escape EU Sanctions
At least a functioning channel of communication
This diplomatic initiative must be taken seriously, political scientist Bernardo Ivo Cruz urges in Diário de Noticias (Portugal):
“The EU and Kyiv’s allies have made it clear: only Ukraine will decide the terms for ending the war. This means that we may have to accept a settlement that is acceptable to the Ukrainians but which results in tangible gains for Russia. An imperfect peace that would neither fully restore the justice violated by the aggression nor wholly uphold international law. ... Yet after four and a half years of war, the mere return of a diplomacy capable of engaging with both Moscow and Kyiv must be taken seriously.”
Too early for diplomacy
Diplomacy can only begin once Russia has lost, Le Point (France) argues:
“At this stage there will be no diplomatic solution to this war. Some conflicts end around a negotiating table. But there are others where the negotiating table only comes into play once an imperialist regime has realised that it has lost. That was the case with Germany in 1945. And with Serbia in 1995. And it is exactly what will happen with Russia too: the diplomats will only get to work once the reality of the battlefield has, in one way or another, been acknowledged in the Kremlin’s inner circles. Until then, the winter will be brutal, and we must help Ukraine to hold out.”
A small step in the right direction
Military expert Oleksiy Kopytko (Russia) is optimistic in a Telegram post republished by Echo:
“There is no doubt that the path to genuine agreements will involve heavy-handed pressure. Right now it looks like the US is intent on exerting pressure primarily, or even exclusively, on Ukraine, because the country is heavily dependent on external support. With regard to Russia, only China could assume this role, but Beijing has yet to intervene. ... This round of negotiations will not lead to an immediate end to the war. That would take a miracle. ... But it is a small step in the right direction. I am confident that by winter serious attempts will be made to initiate genuine negotiations leading to a ceasefire.”
Putin’s final bid with Trump
So far Putin’s hopes regarding Trump have been dashed, Gazeta Wyborcza (Poland) concludes:
“Putin and his entourage had hoped that Trump would do for them the job they themselves are unable to do on the front line, and force the Ukrainians to hand over to the Russians what they demand but have been unable to secure despite heavy losses. ... That was their aim at the summit in Anchorage in August 2025, but it failed. ... Trump’s shelf life is coming to an end. It looks as though his fellow Republicans will suffer a defeat in the mid-term elections on 3 November and his hands will be tied by a hostile Congress. ... So if the Kremlin can still get anything out of him, it has to be now.”
No hope without concessions by Zelensky
In a Telegram post republished by Echo, journalist Fyodor Krasheninnikov (Russia) sees the Ukrainian president playing a key role:
“I am wholeheartedly in favour of ending the war as quickly as possible, but in September 2026 there is only one way this will be possible – namely, if Trump’s envoys persuade Zelensky to accept Putin’s humiliating and unjust terms. Should this prove impossible for Zelensky, talks is all there will be. To those who want to jump to conclusions about my stance and ask, ‘Well what do you propose?’ I say: I am not proposing anything. I am merely saying that the war will continue and there are no other options unless Zelensky is prepared to make concessions.”
Russia wants to eliminate the Ukrainian state
All Russia’s demands call into question Ukraine’s very existence, making concessions on Ukraine’s part practically impossible, argues journalist Vitali Portnikov on TSN (Ukraine) :
“Russia has a clear ambition: the elimination of Ukrainian statehood and the expulsion of a large part of the Ukrainian population from the territories in which they live. ... It will not seek a compromise with a nation whose statehood it seeks to eliminate. That is why, since 2014, there has been no alternative but to stand firm against it; there will be no other option in 2026, nor beyond that. ... What is at stake here is nothing less than the right of Ukraine and the Ukrainian people to an independent existence.”
