articles.title: ‘Miserable and impossible’: food scarce in Kyiv as Russia targets supply chains
articles.body:
Stocking up on cured sausages from the half-empty shelves in her local supermarket, Valentyna Sveshnikova is worried about money. The 68-year-old grandmother lives off her small pension and has already noticed the cost of several goods increase, including sausages. Russia wants “to make our life miserable and impossible. And they’re actually succeeding in it,” she says.
Russian strikes on food warehouses and logistics supply chains around several Ukrainian cities have left gaps on supermarket shelves and risk causing price increases.
Kyiv has faced a particularly intense barrage of attacks. A temporary truce that was in place between Moscow and Kyiv to ensure the safe passage of US negotiators over the weekend ended abruptly on Monday night when jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles pounded Ukraine’s capital, killing two people.
Many shelves at the Novus supermarket where Sveshnikova is shopping for groceries are empty. But customers, hardened by four years of war, are sanguine. “It’s scary, but I don’t plan to go anywhere,” says 40-year-old Dariya Malyukova.
The agrarian policy and food minister, Taras Vysotsky, has warned that food prices could increase by 2.5% because of the attacks on warehouse infrastructure.
But Dmytro Krymskiy, the co-founder of Bureau of Wine, which operates several high-end retail brands in Ukraine, including the supermarket chain Goodwine, says the impact could be as high as 15%.
One of Krymskiy’s warehouses near Kyiv was hit on 1 September, wiping out €4m (£3.4m) of stock. The attacks “seriously hurt our business”, he says.
Krymskiy says that prices will increase not because of a shortage of supplies, but because of the cost of reorganising supply chains to make them more resilient against strikes.
He is exploring several options, including moving his warehouses to a neighbouring country such as Poland, using underground storage facilities and splitting his stock across several smaller sites. “We understand that we cannot have only one big warehouse,” he said. Krymskiy thinks his prices could rise by about 5%.
The latest strike did not come as a complete surprise; it was the third time since the start of the full-scale invasion that his warehouses had been hit. The first, in 2022, destroyed €15m of supplies, while another attack in July this year annihilated €1.5m-worth of goods.
“It was really a matter of time,” he says. “The problem is, we had 3,000 pallets there, and you simply cannot move it,” he says. The recent onslaught of airborne attacks also meant that warehouse staff could only work for three to four hours per day, reducing the company’s ability to shift stock.
The raids come at a difficult time for Ukraine. Kyiv has been hit by a torrent of daily drone and missile strikes since late August, killing dozens of people and destroying key infrastructure. As well as the food warehouses, Russia has targeted e-commerce logistics hubs and stockpiles of medical supplies.
On Wednesday night, one of the World Health Organization’s main warehouses storing humanitarian aid on the outskirts of Kyiv was hit.
At the warehouse of Biokon, a pharmaceutical company, the air was thick with the smell of burnt fuel on Friday as firefighters picked through the wreckage of the building. The company said in a statement that three months of medicines had been destroyed and that it had suspended all operations.
Shopkeepers and customers say that most people are not panic-buying food in the way that they were in 2022.
“What’s the point?” says Iryna Mesyanzhynova, a 54-year-old woman shopping for groceries at ATB, a low-cost supermarket in Brovary, near some of the burnt-out warehouses. “I have a bit of extra products, like porridge oats, but for the rest – vegetables, fruits – why would I buy them? They will just rot.
“I’m trying to deal with today’s problem,” she says. “I try not to think about the future.”
In a statement to the Guardian, Vysotsky, the agrarian policy and food minister, said that the logistics hubs of all of Ukraine’s leading supermarket chains, including Novus, ATB, Silpo and Fora had been destroyed or significantly damaged in the recent strikes.
“This wave of strikes is the most massive since the beginning of the full-scale invasion,” Vysotsky said.
“If in 2022 the enemy attacked mainly export-agricultural infrastructure, and in the following years destroyed the energy sector, then the attacks of August-September 2026 are a systemic attack on the internal civilian life support system. The enemy is purposefully trying to destroy the logistics that provide Ukrainian cities with food.”
Aside from growing their own food, which many people already do, Ukrainians have few options other than trying to continue as normal. The attacks are “not our first of the war”, says Olena Zhuk, a 36-year-old travel manager shopping at a central Kyiv farmer’s market. “We will survive. We will not die from the hunger.”
Additional reporting by Illia Dyadik

articles.title: How Emmanuel Macron brought France’s AI darling to the world stage
articles.body:
It’s not every AI company that can count the French president as its top salesman.
On June 11, 2025, the founder of French AI company Mistral took to the stage alongside Jensen Huang, the powerful CEO of chip giant Nvidia, to announce a partnership between the two companies. As President Emmanuel Macron joined them, the Taiwanese-American executive turned to Mistral’s young CEO Arthur Mensch and said something just audible to the Parisian audience of techies and public officials: “Your president worked really hard for you.”
The Nvidia boss was referring to the deal his company had just sealed with Mistral to roll out AI infrastructure across Europe. “I told the president that Arthur and Mistral needed support from France’s biggest companies. Mr. President said to me: ‘Which ones? Let me call them!’” Huang said.
Advertisement
By the time the deal was official, the companies could announce that BNP Paribas, Orange, SNCF and Thales had all expressed interest in the partnership — boosting Mistral’s official entry into the global race for computing power.
Even for the head of Nvidia, the world’s most valuable company, such presidential proactivity was remarkable, illustrating the French government’s dedication to championing its homegrown startup and showing how Mistral has leveraged ties to the executive branch in Paris to try and reach the level of some of the biggest generative AI companies.
Mistral’s rise over the past three years, according to a dozen public officials and representatives of France’s tech ecosystem interviewed by POLITICO, owes much to the privileged relationship it built with Macron — enabling the company to secure both strong ties with the French state and a seat at the table with the world’s leading AI companies.
Now, with a French presidential election bringing to a close Macron’s two-term reign, details on the depth of that relationship — many of which are reported here for the first time — also raise questions about Mistral’s future under a different president.
The company on Tuesday announced a new €3 billion funding round including investments from the European Union and South Korea’s electronics giant Samsung, valuing Mistral at more than €21 billion. While that falls well short of the valuations of Anthropic and OpenAI, the news confirms the French startup as the only serious European player in the AI race.
As Europe questions its ability to challenge Chinese and American tech giants, Mensch and his team must now plan for life after Macron.
‘Fairy godmothers around the cradle’
Launched in 2023 by three co-founders — Mensch, Guillaume Lample and Timothée Lacroix — Mistral AI set out to build a full-fledged large-language model to compete with the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic. To do so, the Paris-based startup put forward a clear strategy from day one: cultivate a relationship with the French executive, and Macron in particular.
From its first funding round, the startup — which declined to respond to questions for this article — made a point of forging ties with the public sector. First among them was Bpifrance, France’s public investment bank and one of its earliest investors.
“We were aware of the sovereignty issues linked to AI,” recalls Arnaud Caudoux, deputy CEO of Bpifrance. “We had a good idea of the few — a few hundred in the world at the time — credible experts in the sector, among whom were Mistral’s founders.”
Advertisement
The BPI investment was part of a record €105 million total for a French seed round. But Caudoux noted: “There were a lot of fairy godmothers around the cradle.”
Those looking out for the startup came from the cream of French business and tech, playing crucial roles as matchmakers, patrons and fundraisers. They included telecom billionaire Xavier Niel, as well as Jean-Charles Samuelian-Werve and Charles Gorintin, co-founders of insurance startup Alan.
They were driven by the same goal: helping a European AI giant emerge. They tapped their networks to identify the most promising French AI researchers. These three businessmen were the ones who played matchmaker, bringing together Mensch, Lacroix and Lample.
When the Alan team struck a deal with the three young co-founders, it secured a strategic recruit to forge ties with the public sector: Cédric O, a former digital affairs secretary of state and early Macron supporter, would play a crucial role in the startup’s launch.
It was O who went into battle in Brussels to try to secure looser rules under the European Union’s AI Act, first proposed in April 2021. For Mistral, the burgeoning legislation posed a threat: How could Europe build a giant of its own if it stifled innovation?
In 2023, O intervened on Mistral’s behalf in EU talks in an effort to influence the negotiations — to the point that some lawmakers accused him of a conflict of interest. He also drew a rebuke from Thierry Breton, then European commissioner for the internal market.
Advertisement
Mistral “is lobbying, that’s normal,” French-born Breton said during the final weeks of negotiations over the AI Act. “But we are not fooled by anything. It is defending its business today, and not the general interest.”
“Cédric O’s role was, in a way, that of a lightning rod,” said a private-sector official who followed Mistral in its early days. By taking the hits, O allowed Mensch “to grow and develop as a CEO.”
Behind the scenes
From the outset, Mistral played the French and European card. The three co-founders may have built their careers in U.S.-based AI labs — Google DeepMind for Mensch and Facebook AI for Lample and Lacroix — but the first concept notes drafted for the startup’s launch put technological sovereignty at the heart of the project.
At the time, Mensch was a discreet 30-year-old engineer who needed to transform himself into the public face of Mistral on the international stage. Just a few months after launching the startup, the alum of the prestigious École Polytechnique made his first public appearance at VivaTech 2023 — Europe’s largest annual technology event — alongside Macron, who had already begun making the appeal for European technological autonomy.
The two were clearly in sync. “How do France and Europe intend to enable European champions to emerge, and how do we make sure that AI regulation does not hinder innovation?” the young sneaker-wearing entrepreneur asked the French president on the main stage.
Mensch would himself be tasked with helping come up with the answers. A few months later, the prime minister’s office formed a committee of experts to devise a French AI strategy. Alongside Mensch and O, its members included Gaël Varoquaux, a top researcher at France’s national digital research institute and Mensch’s former Ph.D. supervisor, as well as future Nobel economics laureate Philippe Aghion and Meta researcher and Turing Award recipient Yann LeCun.
By 2024, the committee delivered its report and Mistral unveiled Le Chat, its rival to OpenAI’s ChatGPT. But the AI landscape was already changing rapidly — and Europe was having second thoughts.
German rival Aleph Alpha, the continent’s other great hope in generative AI, announced it was moving away from developing its own models. Its CEO, Jonas Andrulis, offered a gloomy assessment: “Simply having a European LLM is not enough as a business model. It does not justify the investment.”
Advertisement
Mistral was not spared those doubts. Many observers feared its technology could fall behind American or Chinese rivals — even raising concerns that the startup might be acquired from abroad.
In 2025, reports of talks with Apple sparked panic at the highest levels of the French state. France’s embassy in the United States and the Elysée presidential palace asked Mistral whether the reports were true, according to two advisers who spoke to POLITICO. The company eventually reassured them: There had been no discussions “at the highest level.”
The French champion instead turned to a partner closer to home, and at the heart of Europe’s drive for technological sovereignty: the Netherlands’ microchip-printing giant ASML. The Dutch pioneer in the chips supply chain poured €1.3 billion of fresh investment into Mistral in September 2025 in a bid to speed up industrial AI development and keep Mistral’s know-how in European hands.
The deal was a boon for politicians — including Macron — seeking to keep the United States out of Europe’s most prized critical technology players.
Strategic partner
Three years into the company’s existence, the French government is no longer simply promoting a promising young startup. The state is now prepared to bend over backward to preserve a company whose technologies are being integrated across government.
After signing a strategic partnership with France’s national employment agency in early 2025, Mistral secured a deal with the French Armed Forces Ministry to develop AI for defense. Since 2025, Le Chat has also been in the process of being rolled out to 10,000 civil servants.
Advertisement
In public, Mensch has played down the importance of public subsidies and government support for his company. But Mistral’s teams in private conversations readily acknowledge that this privileged relationship is a major asset.
With Macron’s help, the French company has also opened the doors to the world’s biggest international summits — all the way up to the G7.
Mensch has been brought along on almost every presidential trip abroad in the past two years, giving him repeated opportunities to sharpen and spread his AI counter-narrative to contrast with the all-powerful Silicon Valley vision.
For several months, the Mistral boss — who readily appropriates the École Polytechnique motto, “For the Nation, Science and Glory” — has hammered home a position aligned with Macron’s: Europe must promote technological sovereignty and offer the rest of the world a model that is more sensitive to cultural and linguistic nuances than American and Chinese rivals.
In February, on stage at the New Delhi AI summit attended by Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Demis Hassabis of Google DeepMind and Sam Altman of OpenAI, Mensch defended AI as “a tool for empowerment, not domination.” He spoke about the importance of deciding who controls the deployment of AI, who benefits from it and how to ensure that it serves the general interest, not just a few powerful players.
That landed as countries across the world were scrambling to get insights from U.S. firms and the Trump administration into how new AI models were creating major new hacking risks.
Advertisement
And in June, in Evian-les-Bains at Lake Geneva, Mensch had lunch with G7 leaders and AI executives, including Altman. He once again took on the role of maverick to confront his American rivals, who were calling for technological standards to be drawn up under U.S. leadership.
“We still need to be very wary,” Mensch told POLITICO in an interview after the meeting. “It’s true that American actors tend to make that argument, which is, ‘Trust us—we’ll set standards here, and then we’ll export them to you.’”
Succession planning
As Mistral moves into infrastructure by building data centers and continues rolling out its solutions at major companies, some are beginning to doubt whether it can remain in the race to produce “frontier” models — the most powerful models available.
For Macron, the June G7 meeting was one of the last opportunities to leave his mark on the global AI debate before his presidency ends next spring. For Mistral, its relationship with Macron’s successor has yet to be built.
Gabriel Attal, former prime minister and presidential candidate for Macron’s pro-business bloc, readily showcases his ties to Mistral and has put AI at the heart of his campaign platform — even incorporating Le Chat into his communications toolkit. Attal’s centrist rival Edouard Philippe would also almost certainly continue backing Mensch.
Advertisement
While Mistral does not publicly associate itself with the far-right National Rally of Marine Le Pen, the nationalist party sees the company as a sovereign asset. On the left, the parties have unanimously backed the company — and called for sovereign AI — in response to the risk of American models being weaponized against European countries.
Yet Mistral relies on international funding and major partnerships with American giants including Amazon, Nvidia and Microsoft. While bringing in ASML as a key investor meant Mistral would remain firmly rooted in Europe, it also shifted some of the power to ASML’s headquarters in Veldhoven, the Netherlands.
This detail could undermine the French consensus in favor of Mistral, just as AI is emerging as a key campaign issue for the presidential election.
“We need to kill this very bar room idea that it would be feasible to own the capital, and therefore finance on our own, at French or European level, the hundreds of billions that AI infrastructure requires. It’s simply impossible,” said Bruno Bonnell, a French businessman who runs a major public investment program, France 2030, under the prime minister’s office.

articles.title: Yemen war threatens Saudi oil lifeline through Red Sea
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Yemen war threatens Saudi oil lifeline through Red Sea
Renewed fighting in Yemen is threatening a crucial Red Sea oil route that has become increasingly important to Saudi Arabia amid severe disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Houthi forces have pushed towards government-held territory near Mocha and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, while Saudi-backed Yemeni forces have launched a multi-front counteroffensive, raising fears that the most serious fighting in the country since a UN-brokered truce in 2022 could develop into a wider war.
The strategic significance of the fighting has been magnified by the wider regional conflict.
The disruption in the Strait of Hormuz followed the US-Israeli attacks on Iran, which Tehran has responded to by severely restricting shipping through the waterway. The strikes, widely condemned as a violation of international law, have forced Saudi Arabia to rely more heavily on alternative export routes bypassing the Gulf, including moving crude westwards towards the Red Sea.
Central to Saudi Arabia's efforts to bypass Hormuz is the East-West Pipeline, which carries crude from the kingdom's eastern oilfields across the country to the Red Sea export terminal at Yanbu.
The Houthis have already sought to disrupt that route. In July, the group said it targeted crude oil supply and transport infrastructure linking eastern Saudi Arabia to Yanbu, as Riyadh increasingly relied on the pipeline to circumvent disruption in the Gulf.
Between March and mid-July, Saudi seaborne crude exports through Bab al-Mandab were eight times higher than during the same period in 2025.
The Houthis, meanwhile, declared a blockade against Saudi shipping in the Red Sea in July and have sought to expand their control towards the strategically vital strait.
Bab al-Mandab, which connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, carried around 4.1 million barrels of crude oil and petroleum products per day in 2024, equivalent to around five percent of the global total.
The result is an increasingly dangerous convergence between Yemen's renewed civil war and the wider regional conflict.
While Hormuz remains severely disrupted, fighting is intensifying around the other major maritime entrance to the Arabian Peninsula.
Those fears grew further on Tuesday when the Houthis launched one of their largest attacks on Saudi Arabia in years, striking four southern cities with missiles and drones. The attacks targeted energy infrastructure in Abha, Najran and Jizan, as well as King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait, according to Saudi and Houthi officials.
Fires broke out at several oil facilities, and 73 people were wounded, including women and children. The Jizan refinery, situated on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast, can process around 400,000 barrels of crude per day and forms part of the kingdom's western energy infrastructure.
Oil prices rose above $100 a barrel on Wednesday amid the renewed escalation and further US-Iran fighting around the Gulf.
Yemen's war returns
The battle over the Red Sea is unfolding amid the most serious escalation inside Yemen in four years.
More than 500 people have reportedly been killed in the latest fighting between Houthi and government-aligned forces, overwhelmingly combatants but including at least 29 civilians.
Thousands more have fled their homes, particularly around Taiz and Hodeidah on Yemen's western front.
The Houthis launched their latest offensive last week, seeking to advance towards Mocha and territory bordering Bab al-Mandab.
Saudi-backed government forces subsequently launched counteroffensives across several provinces, with Yemen's internationally recognised government saying it ultimately intends to retake all Houthi-controlled territory, including Sanaa.
The fighting continued into Wednesday, when Houthi-run Al Masirah television said Saudi-backed forces had launched 32 airstrikes across Marib, Al-Jawf, Taiz and Hodeidah overnight.
Saudi Arabia has not confirmed carrying out the strikes.
Houthi authorities have separately said at least 21 people were killed in strikes in Al-Jawf over the past two days.
The Houthis said Tuesday's attacks on Saudi Arabia were retaliation for Saudi attacks inside Yemen, while Riyadh described the strikes as a dangerous escalation and vowed to take measures to deter further attacks.
Saudi Arabia led the military coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015 after the Houthis seized Sanaa, launching a years-long bombing campaign and blockade that devastated Yemen's infrastructure and contributed to one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
The 2022 truce largely ended direct Saudi-Houthi hostilities and froze the country's front lines, but the latest escalation threatens to pull Riyadh back into a conflict it had spent years attempting to extricate itself from.
The regional war has also changed the strategic stakes.
The Houthis have repeatedly demonstrated their ability to attack Red Sea shipping and Saudi energy infrastructure, while their latest ground offensive could give them greater strategic depth around Bab al-Mandab.
Recent reports have also pointed to increasing coordination between the Houthis and other Iran-aligned armed groups, including Iraqi factions, although the extent of Tehran's direct control over Houthi operations remains disputed.

articles.title: Romania trailed a Russian agent for seven months—then revealed what he was filming
articles.body:
Romania's domestic intelligence service says it prevented a Russia-coordinated sabotage operation on its soil, Militarnyi and Radio Svoboda reported. For months, it watched a Russian citizen who was filming military sites across the country—including, it says, Ukraine's Antonov cargo planes.
A wave of arson, drone incursions, and covert surveillance blamed on Russian handlers has spread across the continent, aimed at the logistics that keep Ukraine armed.
What the suspect was told to film
The Romanian Intelligence Service (SRI) announced on Tuesday that it had prevented the plot with national and international partners. The man had been under SRI monitoring since February 2026, part of a wider investigation into sabotage attempts on Romanian soil.
An intermediary instructed him to make photos and videos of targets of strategic military interest, SRI said. The list ran from NATO-used bases and communications nodes to defense institutions, critical infrastructure, and Ukraine's Antonov cargo planes.
SRI says the pattern matches saboteur networks run by Russian entities across Europe. It points to similar cases foiled in Romania in 2024 and 2025. The service added that Russia keeps leaning on people from vulnerable groups to carry out this work.
The Leipzig link
The case recalls an incident in Germany. On 4 August, workers found a drone rigged with explosives and a detonator beside an An-124 Ruslan at Leipzig airport. The Ruslan is a giant Antonov cargo plane. Ukraine's Antonov fleet moves oversized loads few other planes can carry, a standing target for a Kremlin trying to slow Western support without firing a shot.
Germany's government blamed Russia, and the attempt sharpened tensions between Berlin and Moscow. Russia denies any role in Europe's sabotage wave and has not addressed Romania's findings.
The disclosure comes days after Russian Shahed attack drones struck the Orlivka ferry crossing in Odesa Oblast, overnight on 1 September. The crossing sits on the Ukrainian-Romanian border.

articles.title: Pollard says he does not want kit that fails in Ukraine
articles.body:
Equipment that would not survive the war in Ukraine has no place in the British armed forces, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry has told an audience of financiers and defence firms at Mansion House, in a speech setting out how the government intends to bring private capital into defence.
Luke Pollard was speaking on Tuesday at an event hosted by the Lady Mayor, ahead of remarks by the Ukrainian Ambassador, and used the address to announce a Defence Finance Investment Strategy to follow the autumn budget along with a defence investment summit in December.
Warning that Britain must “discard the warm comfort blanket that we are used to, of polishing old things and pretending that that will protect us”, he put the test in a single sentence: “If our technology and kit will not work in Ukraine, I do not want it in our armed forces.”
That, he argued, opens the door to “new technology, new thinking, new weapons”, and to designing for “the conflicts of today and the battles of tomorrow”.
“The way that the United Kingdom would now fight is fundamentally different today than it was at the point when Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine only those four and a half years ago,” he told the room, adding that learning from Ukraine means changing how Britain itself operates.
Finding, funding and firing up
Much of the speech turned on speed, and on where the useful ideas are now coming from. Many of the most critical advances in defence, in the minister’s account, are emerging from technology startups and scale-ups, agile businesses “seizing the opportunities on offer and driving change at speed”. The challenge he set the room was framed as a question. “How can we get better at finding, funding and firing up the most creative minds and enterprise to get the best technology into the hands of our armed forces and those of our allies as fast as possible?”
He was unsparing about the position two years ago, describing a defence programme that was “to be honest and to be frank, unfit to counter the dangers that we now face”. Industry, he suggested, needs no reminding. “Those who work in our supply chains know how painfully slow, wasteful and costly the procurement the MOD previously undertook was,” he said, singling out small businesses and scale-ups with good products who “struggled sometimes to find the right buyer within the MOD”.
Small firms
Against that, Pollard set out the machinery now in place: a new National Armaments Director in Rupert Pearce, recruited from a FTSE 100 company and bringing what the minister called a new corporate approach and energy to procurement; the Defence Office for Small Business Growth, established to cut red tape and remove obstacles to entry; and an SME Action Plan published so the department can be held to account for the change.
The headline commitment is a 50 per cent increase in departmental spending with medium and small firms by summer 2028, which the minister described as “moving an extra two and a half billion pounds into the pockets of SMEs by changing the way we procure”.
Regional defence and security clusters have proved successful enough that more regions are developing them, he said, creating local routes that bring together major suppliers, devolved and local government, and giving investors a forum in which to meet them.
Bringing in the City
Running through the address was an argument that public money alone will not build the capacity required in the time available, however welcome rising budgets are. “As a defence minister, of course, I would like more defence spending,” he said.
“But it’s not just from the taxpayer that there’s opportunities for investing in defence. It’s how you crowd in private capital, how you use the institutions, the networks, the structures of the City of London and the UK’s place at the heart of global financial trade, to bring more private capital into defence, creating more good jobs and more deterrence.”
Waiting was not, in his view, an option: “In a more dangerous world, we need to build more capacity now, rather than just wait for the increase in defence money that we know is coming over the next 10 years.”
Whether the two sides can understand one another is a separate problem, and one he acknowledged. “There’s a risk that we sometimes speak past each other,” he said, arguing that a shared language and shared data would improve the department’s ability to deliver. The Defence Investment Unit announced in the Defence Investment Plan is meant to close that gap, giving investors a clearer interface with the department while bringing financial expertise in to turn priorities into market-facing propositions.
Companies already through the door
To show the approach producing results rather than remaining theoretical, the minister turned to firms that have already taken the route.
Thirteen British startups won contracts of up to £4 million in May under the Defence Unicorn Fund programme. Among them was Kraken Technologies, which builds maritime uncrewed surface vessels and has since raised $175 million in a Series B round on the back of a $1 billion valuation. Green Jets, one of three firms selected to develop a low-cost drone interceptor, has also secured significant funding. Both drew money from the National Security Strategic Investment Fund and the NATO Innovation Fund, with the British Business Bank financing Kraken as well.
JET Connectivity, a small business building 5G and 6G communications tools, was the only British firm admitted to the NATO DIANA mission track programme this year from more than three and a half thousand participants, which Mr Pollard called “fantastic recognition of British innovation at its best” while adding that it is “just the tip of the iceberg”.
There was a moment of self-deprecation over how the language has shifted under the current Prime Minister, with the Minister saying, “I used to be incentivised by the MOD press office to say defence is an engine for growth in all my interviews,” he told the audience. “With Andy Burnham in Downing Street I now say re-industrialisation, but the fundamental truth is there. Investment in defence creates good jobs. It provides opportunities in particular for our young people and we should be unafraid and unapologetic of saying that truth loudly.”
His closing argument was that none of this rests with his department alone, describing defence as “a whole of society endeavour, a whole of government endeavour” which the Ministry of Defence must lead but cannot deliver by itself.
He finished on deterrence, and on what follows if it does not hold, saying “That’s why increasing our deterrence matters with new technologies. But if deterrence fails, we must be ready to fight, and we must be ready to win.”

articles.title: CIA Director Ratcliffe may take lead in US negotiations on Ukraine – media
articles.body:
Director of the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency John Ratcliffe may take on a more prominent role in Washington's diplomatic efforts to end Russia's war against Ukraine, as President Donald Trump's administration is considering changing the composition and division of responsibilities within its negotiating team, the Financial Times reports.
According to the publication, the White House is considering reducing the involvement of U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, who have so far played a key role in contacts with Moscow and Kyiv.
"Officials close to Ratcliffe have told European peers that he will play a larger role in shuttle diplomacy between Russia and Ukraine – which is currently the purview of Witkoff and Kushner – while maintaining contact with intelligence officers in both countries… People close to the situation said Trump has not made a final decision." the publication said.
The potential expansion of Ratcliffe's role is viewed positively in European capitals, which are eager to see a return to a productive diplomatic process after a prolonged period without significant progress. The negotiations have effectively reached an impasse due to Putin's unwillingness to back down from the Kremlin's key demands.
The U.S. administration is considering a change in the negotiating team following the failure of U.S.-led attempts to reach a peace agreement in late February.
Despite the possible reshuffle, Ukrainian officials have not expressed a preference regarding who specifically should lead U.S. efforts to end the war. Three high-ranking Ukrainian officials told the FT that Kyiv has working relationships with Ratcliffe, as well as with Witkoff and Kushner.
"We're OK with [Ratcliffe], and with Jared and Steve too. The problem is the Russians," the publication said citing one of the Ukrainian officials.

articles.title: Syria no longer under IAEA probe
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Syria no longer under UN nuclear watchdog IAEA probe
The UN nuclear watchdog's board of governors on Wednesday decided to close a long-time probe against Syria launched under ousted leader Bashar al-Assad after the country's new authorities led agency exports to key nuclear sites.
Inspectors from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) last month visited two sites, one in Deir al-Zour and a second in an undisclosed location identified to them by Syrian authorities. IAEA head Rafael Grossi said on Monday that a near-complete nuclear reactor found in Deir al-Zour and built secretly during the rule of al-Assad would have been able to produce material to make nuclear weapons.
The IAEA board "adopted by consensus" a text stating that a 2011 resolution finding Syria in non-compliance with its obligations was "terminated", noting the current government's cooperation, two diplomats told AFP.
The resolution, seen by AFP, was submitted by Egypt, Jordan, Morocco and Saudi Arabia and "encourages Syria to continue its cooperation with the agency, including the excavation work at the Deir al-Zour site".
It also "requests the director general to update the board, as appropriate, on the outcomes of ongoing activities of the agency" in Syria.
'Clandestine' activities
Assad was toppled in December 2024 and the current Islamist government came to power.
Grossi said on Monday that it was "obvious that the previous government was pursuing a number of clandestine" activities.
Besides the reactor under construction at the Deir Ezzor site, the IAEA found a fuel fabrication plant where nuclear fuel for the reactor was manufactured, and a location where nuclear fuel as well as uranium scrap and waste were stored.
In a confidential report seen by AFP last week, the IAEA said it found around 73 tonnes of natural uranium metal.
Grossi has praised Damascus's "courageous decision" to report the undisclosed site.
The UN atomic watchdog had declared in 2011 that the location was "very likely" to host a nuclear reactor, adding that its information suggested it was being built with North Korean assistance.
Last month, Grossi visited the site in Deir al-Zour in the east, which has been shut for 18 years.
In 2018, Israel admitted carrying out a top-secret air raid on the site 11 years earlier.
In 2008, less than a year after the strike, US officials accused Syria of having sought to build a secret nuclear reactor and acknowledged that Israel had destroyed it in the raid.
Israel also has an undeclared nuclear arsenal.
Robert Kelley, a former director of IAEA inspections and now an associate fellow of the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, told AFP following the IAEA report that there was "no evidence of any weapons programme" in Syria.
Instead the aim before the site was destroyed may have been to produce plutonium for North Korea, possibly to sell to a third party, he added.
